studies.theologicalSignificance: The promise attaches to God's word, not to a schedule, and that changes what is asked of anyone waiting. Endurance is not confidence about timing. The passage also puts this messenger inside a series, so hardship stops counting as evidence against a mission. And it says help came, in the past tense, to people whose situation looked at the time just as open as yours.

crossReferences.why: Describes how late the help came: when the messengers had almost despaired, it reached them.
States the same principle about God's words, that there is nothing that can alter them.
Shows earlier communities who did not weaken under what struck them, and did not give in.

studies.applyIt: Think of something you are enduring with no visible end date. Write down what you would need in order to keep going for one more month, not for however long it lasts. Then arrange that one thing. This passage does not promise a date. It says endurance is measured in stages, and a stage is the unit you can actually plan.
studies.explainEasier: Other messengers before him were called liars too. They were hurt, and they kept going, and God's help came in the end. Nothing can change what God has said.

studies.title: A Tunnel Or A Ladder
studies.meaning: It begins by admitting the distress rather than correcting it. Then it offers two impossible options, and offers them seriously. Dig down through the earth, or climb up through the sky, and fetch them a sign. Early scholars read that offer as marking a limit, not as mockery. Gathering everyone onto guidance is then said to be within God's power, and it has not been done. The instruction at the end is short, and it is about the one carrying the grief, not about the deniers.
studies.historicalContext: Mecca, speaking to the Prophet during a stretch when steady refusal from people he had grown up among was taking a visible toll. The classical scholars describe his distress at their rejection. They do not attach this verse to any one incident. The surah returns to the theme several times, which suggests it was answering something ongoing rather than a single moment.

keyTerms.note: The word for a burrow with two openings, of the kind a desert animal digs. Its ordinary use is small and animal, which keeps the impossible suggestion concrete rather than grand.
An everyday object, used for reaching a roof. Setting it against the sky measures the gap between what effort can reach and what is being demanded, using the plainest tool available.
A noun from the verb used earlier in this surah for turning the face aside. Naming it as a thing that weighs on someone treats indifference as an event, which is how it is actually felt.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Wells were the great digging project of that world. Sinking one meant weeks of work and could fail completely, and the rights to a good well shaped a clan's fortunes for generations. Roofs were reached with a palm-trunk ladder. Both images in this verse come from ordinary labour, and both name the point where honest effort stops being able to help.
studies.didYouKnow: The warning at the end is against being among the ignorant, and that word did not mainly mean uneducated. In seventh-century Arabic it carried hot-headedness as much as lack of knowledge. Poetry from before Islam uses it for the man who acts on his own heat. So the instruction is about staying calm at least as much as about knowing things.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Guidance is placed outside the reach of the one calling, and that lifts a weight which would otherwise crush him. If everyone believing were the measure, every messenger would have failed. The passage separates the task from the outcome, and assigns you only the task. It also shows God speaking to grief without brushing it aside. The difficulty is named first, and only afterwards comes what to do with it.

crossReferences.why: States the same point directly: had your Lord willed, everyone on earth would have believed.
Names the same grief, warning that he might destroy himself with sorrow over their turning away.
Answers the same eagerness for their guidance, with the same limit placed on it.

studies.applyIt: Think of one person whose choices you have been trying to change, and count the hours you have spent on it this month. Then decide what part of that was yours to do, and stop at the edge of it. Keep the relationship and drop the campaign. This passage separates the two, and the separation is where the exhaustion goes.
studies.explainEasier: The Prophet found their refusal hard to bear. God told him that if God wanted, He could bring them all to the truth, and He has not. So the Prophet should not let it break him.

studies.title: Only Those Who Listen
studies.meaning: The sorting here is by capacity, not by verdict. Only those who hear respond. As for the dead, God will raise them, and most early scholars read that line two ways at once: as a picture of people who do not hear, and as a plain statement about the resurrection. Then the demand for a sign gets answered in two halves. The power to send one is there. And the demand itself rests on a mistake about what a sign would actually do.
studies.historicalContext: Mecca, where the demand quoted here keeps coming back through the surah in slightly different words. This version is the plainest of them: a request for something sent down from his Lord. The answer neither promises nor refuses. The classical sources attach it to no particular episode. They treat it as the standing shape of the argument during those years.

keyTerms.note: A form of the verb for answering a call, used in the Quran of God answering prayer too. Here it is turned toward people, so responding to a call becomes the same act in both directions.
The plain verb for hearing, though the sentence around it gives it the weight of attending. Arabic uses the same word for sound reaching an ear and for a request being granted.
An active participle stating a present capacity rather than a promise to act. The wording concedes everything the objectors assume about power while declining the conclusion they draw from it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A caller in that society had a set role. A man stood on a height or walked the lanes and made the announcement. A summons to a meeting or to a raid depended entirely on who answered it. Who came was public and easy to count. Saying that only those who hear respond described something everyone had watched happen. The crowd forms out of the people already listening.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran uses the image of the dead not hearing more than once, and each time it stops short of saying such people cannot be reached. Here the clause about God raising the dead sits right after the comparison. So the sentence describing an inability also names the one for whom it is not final.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Reception is made a condition here, not a result, and that changes how guidance is usually pictured. A message is not a force applied to a dead object. It meets something that is either open or shut. That puts the weight on the listener without making the speaker's work useless. The mention of the resurrection keeps the door ajar. The one who raises the dead is not bound by anyone's present state.

crossReferences.why: States the same comparison plainly: the living and the dead are not alike at all.
Turns responding into an invitation: answer God and the Messenger when called to life.
Repeats the limit exactly, that the dead and the turned-away deaf will not hear the call.

studies.applyIt: Pick a conversation today in which you usually prepare your answer while the other person is still talking. Do not prepare. Let a full second pass after they stop before you say anything. This passage makes hearing the condition of everything that follows it, and one second is enough to find out whether you were hearing.
studies.explainEasier: Only people who really listen will answer. God will raise the dead, and they all go back to Him. Some asked for a sign to come down. God is able to send one, but most of them do not know.

studies.title: Communities Like Your Own
studies.meaning: Every creature that walks and every bird that flies is called a community here. The word is the one the Quran uses of human nations, and the comparison is stated plainly and then left standing. Early scholars differ over how far it reaches. Some read it of their being ordered and provided for as we are. Others read it of their having their own ways of answering for what they do. Then comes a claim about the record, and a gathering that includes them.
studies.historicalContext: Mecca, inside a passage arguing with people who wanted a sign delivered on demand. The verse answers by pointing at signs already present in enormous number. The surah belongs to the later Meccan years, when the exchange had settled into a pattern of demands and refusals. Much of its method is to turn attention from the spectacular to what is already in view.

keyTerms.note: From a verb for moving slowly along the ground. The word covers every walking animal and is used elsewhere of human beings too, so the category the verse opens with already includes the listener.
The same word used of human peoples with their own messengers and appointed terms. Applying it to animals is the whole claim of the verse, and Arabic offers no gentler reading of the word.
The verb used of people driven together at the resurrection, taken from the herding of livestock and the mustering of armies. Here it is applied to the animals themselves rather than to their owners.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabs lived closer to animals than to most people. A herder knew his camels one by one, by temper. He tracked birds to find water and read the movement of gazelles for weather. Poetry of the period describes ostriches and wild asses with a precision that only comes from hours of watching. An audience like that would not have found animal societies a strange idea. They had watched the orders and the ranks.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase about the bird flying with its two wings has drawn comment since the earliest period, because flight already implies wings. Classical scholars read the extra words as a way of pinning the description to something actually seen. It holds the sentence to a real bird rather than to birds as a category.
studies.theologicalSignificance: This moves the human being off centre without putting him down. Other creatures are given the words for community and for gathering, which places them inside the moral shape of the world rather than beside it as furniture. The middle of the verse makes a further claim, that nothing has been left out of the record. Early scholars differ over what that record is. Some take it for this revelation, others for the preserved book of all things.

crossReferences.why: Says that birds in flight and all in the heavens each know their own prayer.
States that everything glorifies God, though people do not understand their praise.
Places the provision of every moving creature on God, in a nearby surah.

studies.applyIt: Watch one animal today for two full minutes: a bird on a wire, a cat crossing a wall, ants at a crack in the pavement. Do not photograph it. The verse calls what you are looking at a community. The claim only gets interesting once you have watched long enough to notice that something is being organised.
studies.explainEasier: Every animal that walks and every bird that flies lives in groups, just like people do. God knows about all of them, and nothing has been left out of His book. One day they will all be gathered to Him.

studies.title: Deaf And Dumb In Darkness
studies.meaning: Three things get stacked into one clause. Unable to hear, unable to speak, and set in darkness. Nothing can come in, and no request for help can go out. Early scholars note that the darkness is plural here, matching the way this surah opened. Then the verse says God leaves astray whom He wills and sets whom He wills on a straight path. The Quran holds that beside its constant address to human beings as responsible, and the classical tradition keeps both and drops neither.
studies.historicalContext: Mecca, in a passage arguing that the refusal on show is not a lack of information. The surah runs as one long case about revelation and how it is received, and this is among its bluntest lines. No occasion is reported. The people described had heard the recitation many times. Some of them defended it in private while opposing it in public.

keyTerms.note: The root also gives the word for something solid with no opening, like a rock with no crack in it. Deafness here is the quality of a sealed surface rather than a damaged organ.
Used of someone who cannot form words, and by extension of one who has nothing to say for himself. Pairing it with deafness closes both directions, so nothing enters and nothing is asked.
A broad open road rather than a track, borrowed into Arabic from a Latin word for a paved way. Its width matters: the image is not a narrow ledge but a road wide enough to walk without straining.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Travel in Arabia depended on hearing and on speaking. A guide called directions back along a line of camels. A party moving at night stayed together by voice alone. Losing the sound of the man ahead in the dark was how people vanished. The three conditions in this verse, put together, describe the exact case that killed travellers. Every listener knew someone it had happened to.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for the straight path here is one of a small number of Quranic terms that linguists trace back to Latin. It came through Aramaic or Greek, from a word for a paved street. Its most famous appearance is in the opening surah, recited in every unit of the daily prayer.
studies.theologicalSignificance: God's will and human responsibility sit in the same sentence here, and the verse does not resolve them into a formula. Mainstream scholars treat that pairing as deliberate. Read with the rest of the surah, being left astray follows a settled refusal rather than coming before it. What the verse rules out is any claim to have found the road by your own steering. That is why the same book teaches its readers to ask for the path every day.

crossReferences.why: Uses the identical three words for deaf, mute and blind, of those who bought error.
Turns the same road into a request, which is how the Quran teaches readers to hold this.
States the same double clause about leaving astray and guiding, right after mentioning clear speech.

studies.applyIt: In your next prayer, slow down on the line asking for the straight path and mean it as a request rather than a formula. You say it many times a day. Once today, put a specific decision behind it, something you are genuinely unsure about. This verse describes people who cannot ask. Asking is the thing you still have.
studies.explainEasier: People who turn down God's signs are like someone who cannot hear or speak, standing in the dark. God lets some go off the road, and He puts others on a straight one.

studies.title: Whom Would You Call
studies.meaning: The question is put as a thought experiment, and its force sits in the words at the end. Strip away everything comfortable. Bring either the punishment or the Hour. Then ask honestly who you would call on. Early scholars note that the appeal is to the listener's own experience, not to scripture and not to argument. The wording assumes the answer is already known to the people being asked, and the next verse states it for them without waiting.
studies.historicalContext: In Mecca the religion of the people addressed had a working split: lesser powers for ordinary needs, and a high God behind them for emergencies. The Quran points at that split again and again as the weak spot of the whole system. No specific occasion is attested here. The surah makes this argument several times, in different settings.

keyTerms.note: Literally a request to see, used as an invitation to imagine a case. This surah uses the form repeatedly to open arguments, turning each one into a question the listener answers inside his own head.

The verb for calling out to someone by name, which gives the Quranic word for supplication. Prayer of this kind is described as address rather than ritual, so the question is about who you would shout for.

From the root for truth-telling, applied here to the match between claim and conduct. The condition attached to the question asks not for honesty in reply, but for a reply that matches how they actually behave.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Sea travel from the Arabian coast was the standard emergency of that world, and the Quran returns to it often. A merchant caught in a storm on a Red Sea crossing had no options and no go-betweens. Traders who financed such voyages knew what the crews said when the wind turned, and it was not the name of a household idol. The question here leans on that common knowledge.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb for calling on God in this verse gives the ordinary word for supplication. The Quran uses it for prayer and also for shouting to someone out of earshot. Classical philology does not treat that overlap as an accident. The same act is being described, and it differs only in who is being called and how far away they are taken to be.
studies.theologicalSignificance: A crisis is treated here as a test reading, not as a lesson. What a person reaches for when the arrangements fail is offered as the truth about what they believe, and everything calmer is treated as a footnote on it. That is a claim about human nature, and the surah does not argue for it. It simply asks the audience to consult their own memory. That is a stronger move than a proof.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same test at sea: they call God sincerely, and add others once safely ashore.
Describes the same reversal, with those they call on failing them the moment the sea turns.
Narrates the storm, the vow made inside it, and the behaviour that follows deliverance.

studies.applyIt: Think back to the last time something frightened you badly, and remember the first words that came, before you had chosen any. Do not judge them. Just notice what they show about where you actually turn. Then, once today, turn there deliberately while nothing is wrong, so the reflex and the practice point the same way.
studies.explainEasier: God asks people to be honest with themselves. If real trouble hit them, or the last day came, they would not call on anyone but God. They already know that.

studies.title: You Will Forget Them
studies.meaning: The answer arrives without waiting for a reply: it is Him you call. Then two things are attached to it. The relief comes if He wills, so the calling is not a machine you operate. And afterwards you forget the rivals you had set up, which is offered as a description rather than a rebuke. Then the pattern widens. Hardship was sent to earlier communities for a stated purpose, that they might turn and plead.
studies.historicalContext: Mecca, where the argument keeps building on what the listeners already know about themselves. The mention of earlier peoples draws on stories the audience had heard from traders. Nearby communities who held earlier scriptures told the same stories. No occasion is reported for these two verses. They sit in a long passage that moves between the Meccan present and the peoples who received messengers before.

keyTerms.note: The verb for lifting a covering off something rather than destroying it. Distress is pictured as a cloth laid over a person, so relief is described as an unveiling of what was underneath all along.

A word for affliction from outside, often used of poverty, war and famine. It is paired here with a second term for bodily suffering, so the two together cover what comes at you and what is felt within.

From a root for lowliness and for a child at the breast. The word describes the posture of someone with no leverage, asking rather than negotiating, which is exactly what hardship strips a person down to.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Drought was the recurring trouble of Arabian life, and it produced a familiar pattern. Communities gathered, prayers were made in the open, and vows were pledged aloud about what would change when rain came. Then the rain came, and the season resumed. That cycle was known well enough that the verse can describe it in a clause and expect the audience to supply the rest.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb used here for humble pleading appears only a handful of times in the Quran. It is almost always tied to hardship rather than to formal worship. Its root also gives a word for a suckling child. So the language of asking is tied to helplessness, not to fine speech.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Hardship is given a purpose here, and the purpose is stated openly. It is about relationship rather than punishment: that they might turn and ask. That does not explain every affliction, and the Quran does not claim it does. What it shows is that trouble is not outside the plan. The forgetting described afterwards is the more sobering half, because it says relief itself can undo what the hardship began.

crossReferences.why: States the pattern as a rule: no town received a prophet without adversity coming afterwards.
Traces the forgetting in detail: he calls while lying down, then passes on as before.
Shows the same reversal, with a blessing granted after distress and the earlier prayer set aside.

studies.applyIt: Think of something you badly wanted last year. It arrived, and it has stopped being remarkable to you. Name it out loud today, once, as the thing you were asking for. This passage describes forgetting as the ordinary aftermath of relief, and the only repair that works is going back and looking on purpose.
studies.explainEasier: When trouble comes, it is God you call on. If He wants, He lifts it, and then you forget the things you used to put beside Him. Hard times came to people before you so they would turn and ask.

studies.title: But Their Hearts Hardened
studies.meaning: Trouble is supposed to soften people, and here it did not. The wish at the start never came true, and early scholars read it as regret over a chance missed rather than as surprise. Hardship arrived, and the softening it might have brought did not follow. Two reasons are given, and they work together. Hearts hardened, which changes what a person can take in. And their conduct was made to look good to them, which removes any sense that something needed changing. Hardship on its own is not enough.
studies.historicalContext: Mecca, in the same passage about earlier communities that received messengers and were tested. The verses around it describe a sequence rather than an incident: hardship, then no turning, then unexpected plenty. The classical sources do not attach this verse to any one people. It is written to fit the audience listening as much as those it describes.

keyTerms.note: Used of stone and of dry ground that will not take water. The image is a surface that repels rather than absorbs, so the failure described is one of reception, not of understanding.
An intensive verb for adorning or decorating something. Nothing is added to the deed itself; only its appearance is worked on, which is why the person sees no reason to reconsider anything.
A word for force and for the hardship it produces, used in Arabic of both courage in battle and calamity endured. The one term covers the striking and the suffering that follows it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Farmers in the oases knew the difference between ground that took water and ground left too long. Baked earth sheds a first rain. The water runs off, and the field looks watered without being watered. Everyone who had waited on a season knew that a downpour on hard ground was worse than useless. It gave the look of relief without the thing itself.
studies.didYouKnow: Even rocks split open and let water through. The Quran says that in another surah, in the same passage where it compares hardened hearts to stone. It uses the language of hardened hearts sparingly, and always with something physical in reach, usually stone or dry ground. It never treats the condition as permanent by nature.
studies.theologicalSignificance: This denies a comfortable idea, that suffering reliably improves people. It can, and it is sent with that in view. But the outcome depends on the state of the one receiving it. The second cause named is quieter and far more common. It is a settled story about yourself in which your conduct already looks fine. Once that story is in place, every experience confirms it, hardship included.

crossReferences.why: Compares hardened hearts to rocks, then notes that some rocks split and release water.
Warns against hearts hardening as time lengthens, which is how the condition usually arrives.
Asks about the one whose bad conduct looks good to him, so he considers it fine.

studies.applyIt: Take one thing you do that you have stopped examining because you settled long ago that it is fine. A way you speak to someone, a corner you cut at work. Do not resolve to change it. Just describe it to yourself in plain words, without the reasons attached. The reasons are the decoration this verse is talking about.
studies.explainEasier: Hard times came, and they did not soften. Their hearts went hard instead. Satan made the things they were doing look good to them, so they saw no reason to change.

studies.title: The Gates Of Everything
studies.meaning: This is the most unsettling turn in the sequence, because it makes plenty part of the process. Gates of every kind are opened, and the opening comes after the forgetting, not before it. Early scholars describe that as being drawn out by degrees. The giving increases while nothing gets put right. Then the turn arrives at the exact moment of delight, and that is where the seizure is placed. It closes with praise, which the tradition reads as praise for justice arriving, not satisfaction at ruin.
studies.historicalContext: Mecca was a prosperous trading town in a period of growing wealth. It sat on the caravan route and held the sanctuary, and both had made a small number of families rich. Their wealth was widely read as proof that their arrangements were sound. This passage takes the same wealth and sets it inside a completely different account of what it means.

keyTerms.note: The plain verb for opening a door or a city, used across the Quran for granting and for conquest. Here it takes gates as its object, so provision is pictured as access rather than as a delivery.
A word for someone whose hope is cut and who has nothing left to say. It is the root behind one of the names for the devil, and it names dumbstruck ruin rather than grief.

The hindmost part of something, the tail of a retreating column. Cutting it names the removal of what would have continued, so the phrase describes the end of a line rather than the death of a generation.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Meccan fortunes turned on caravans, and a good year showed itself at once. More animals, bigger houses, more clients at a family's door. The language had no separate word for luck and for blessing. Success at the market was read straight off as approval from above. That reading was the city's confidence in itself, and it is the exact assumption these two verses take apart, without ever denying that the wealth was given.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for their state at the moment of seizure shares its root with one of the Quranic names for the devil. Classical philologists linked the two through one sense: hope cut off entirely. So the same three letters name two things. A speechless despair, and a figure defined by being shut out of mercy.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Plenty is cut loose from approval here, as firmly as ruin was cut loose from bad luck earlier in the surah. Neither can be read as a verdict on you. That leaves a person with no way to score their own standing from the outside. It is unsettling, and it is also freeing. The praise at the end places the whole sequence inside justice rather than inside anger, which is why the tradition treats it as an answer and not a celebration.

crossReferences.why: Names the same gradual drawing out: they are led on by degrees, without perceiving it.
Asks directly whether wealth and children extended to someone mean good is being hastened to them.
Warns against admiring another's wealth and children, and says what such things are actually for.

studies.applyIt: Notice a stretch of your life that is going unusually well, and ask what you have quietly stopped examining during it. Ease removes pressure, and pressure is what most of us use for review. Pick one thing you would have checked in a harder year, and check it this week while nothing is forcing you to.
studies.explainEasier: They ignored the warning, so God opened every door of good things to them. When they were enjoying it all, He took them suddenly. That was the end of the people who did wrong.

studies.title: If He Took Your Hearing
studies.meaning: The argument works by subtraction. Take away hearing, take away sight, seal the heart, and then ask who could give any of it back. The three are not picked at random. They are the instruments this surah has been discussing all along, the means by which a message gets received at all. Early scholars note the climb from the senses up to the organ of understanding. Then the words at the end turn from the audience to the Quran's own way of arguing, which varies its approach and is still declined.
studies.historicalContext: Mecca, and this is one of a series of verses in this surah that begin by asking the listener to consider a case. The people addressed accepted a supreme God above their other objects of worship, and that is what the argument leans on. They would not have claimed that any lesser power could restore a sense once taken. The verse simply makes them notice it.

keyTerms.note: The verb for stamping a seal on a document or a container, closing it so nothing enters or is altered. It implies a completed act and an owner's mark, not a slow closing over time.

An intensive form meaning to turn something in different directions. Applied to the signs, it describes an argument presented from several angles rather than repeated, which is a claim about how the Quran is put together.
A less common verb for veering away from something, used of an animal shying off a path. The surah has already used two other words for turning away, and this is the third.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Blindness and deafness were common and had no remedy. Eye disease spread in dust and heat, and a man who lost his sight moved permanently into dependence on his household. Everybody knew someone in that position. There was no physician to appeal to and no shrine that claimed to reverse it. So the question this verse asks had a settled answer before it was asked.
studies.didYouKnow: Hearing, sight and heart appear together as a set more than ten times in the Quran, and the order is almost always the same. They usually come up with thankfulness, or with answering for what you do. The classical scholars found the order consistent enough to be deliberate. Two gateways, and then the place where what enters is handled.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Thankfulness is approached through the chance of loss, not through the pleasure of having, and that is the sharper tool. A faculty you have never been without is invisible to you. The verse makes it visible again by taking it away in an imagined case. There is an argument about worship inside that move too. Whatever cannot give back what it never gave has no claim on you, and the audience's own instincts already agree.

crossReferences.why: Names the same three gifts as given at birth to people who knew nothing at all.
Repeats the trio and notes how little thanks follows from having been given them.
Places the same set at the completion of the human being, after the body is shaped.

studies.applyIt: Close your eyes for sixty seconds somewhere you would normally be looking around, and try to keep track of what is happening near you. Then open them. This verse works by subtraction, and the demonstration takes a minute. Most people find the return of ordinary sight is briefly, unmistakably, a gift rather than a fact.
studies.explainEasier: God asks people to picture losing their hearing and their sight, with their hearts sealed up. No other god could hand any of it back. He explains this in many ways, and they still turn away.

studies.title: Bearers Of Good News
studies.meaning: The question narrows what punishment would mean if it came, by surprise or in plain view. Only the wrongdoing would be destroyed. Then a messenger's work is given in two words: good news and warning, in that order. Early scholars note that the good news comes first. They also note that the condition attached is doubled. Those who believe and put things right are the ones described. What they are promised is the absence of two things: fear ahead and grief behind.
studies.historicalContext: Mecca, where these verses answer demands to see the punishment the recitation kept mentioning. The community around the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) was small and under pressure. The promise here is addressed to them as much as the question is addressed to their opponents. No occasion is reported for these two verses in the classical sources.

keyTerms.note: Arrival with no approach visible beforehand. Paired here with its opposite, openly, the two words together close off every manner in which such a thing could come.
From a root for skin, since news shows first in the face. The word names a messenger by the effect he produces, and its placement before the word for warner sets the order of the work.
A verb for repairing what is broken, used of mending a wall, a quarrel or a life. Set beside believing, it makes the second half of the condition practical and outward facing.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A man who brought good news to a household was given something for it by custom, and the gift had its own name. He came ahead of the caravan to say that the goods and the men were safe. Arriving with bad news was a different role entirely, often given to someone senior enough to absorb the reaction. Both messengers were familiar figures at a Meccan gate.
studies.didYouKnow: The two words for a messenger's work here appear as a pair in more than a dozen places in the Quran. The bearer of good news is named first in nearly all of them. That is striking, given how much of the material around those passages is warning.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The pairing sets a limit on what a messenger is for. Neither the man nor the message is a tool of force, which matches this surah's earlier point about angels and being compelled. The promise attached is worth reading closely. It removes fear about what is coming and grief about what is gone. Those are the two directions a mind travels when it is unsettled. The present is left untouched and unpromised.

crossReferences.why: Gives the reason for sending messengers with news and warning: so no argument remains against God.
Attaches the same freedom from fear and grief to those who say God is their Lord.
Applies the identical phrase to the close friends of God, in another Meccan setting.

studies.applyIt: Write down the two things currently taking most of your attention: one you are dreading and one you regret. Look at the pair. The promise in this verse is aimed at exactly those two directions, and noticing how little of your worry sits in the actual present is a useful hour's work on its own.
studies.explainEasier: If God's punishment came, suddenly or in the open, only the people doing wrong would be ruined. Messengers were sent to bring good news and to warn. People who believe and put things right have nothing to fear.

studies.title: It Will Touch Them
studies.meaning: One short verse balances the promise just given. The verb chosen for the punishment is unusually mild in its plain sense: it means to touch, or to brush against, and early scholars note the restraint in that. Then comes the reason, and it names conduct rather than opinion. They were stepping outside a boundary they knew was there. The word for that is not the word for disbelief used earlier, so denial and defiance get told apart in the same sentence that links them.
studies.historicalContext: Mecca, immediately after the statement that those who believe and set things right have nothing to fear. The two verses are a matched pair, and this surah often works that way, placing a promise and its counterpart back to back. No occasion is attested. The audience included men who had heard the recitation for years and had made their position public.

keyTerms.note: The plain verb for physical contact, weaker than striking or seizing. Its use for punishment is deliberate understatement, a device the Quran employs elsewhere when the reality being named is severe.
From a root describing a date breaking out of its skin. The picture is something leaving the covering that held it, so the failing named is stepping outside a known limit rather than not knowing it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Boundaries in that world were real and marked. Grazing rights, water rights and the protected months around the sanctuary were all limits a man could see and could choose to cross. Crossing them was a public act with a name. Nobody stepped outside such a boundary in ignorance. The vocabulary of this verse belongs to that setting, where a limit was known before it was broken.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb for defiance here comes from a root that describes a ripe date pushing out of its skin. The early Arabic dictionary writers kept that plain sense alongside the moral one. The image is exact. Something that belonged inside a covering comes out of it, still itself, but now outside what held it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The consequence is tied to a named cause, and it is stated with a light verb. That keeps the passage from reading as a threat made in anger. The difference between denial and defiance matters too. A person is described here by what they did with a boundary they could see, not by an inner state only God can look at. That fits a book which keeps refusing to sort people by their unspoken beliefs.

crossReferences.why: Matches the weight of a return to the act that earned it, evil repaid with its like.
States the same link between what hands earn and what befalls, while noting how much is pardoned.
Stands immediately before this verse as its counterpart, promising the absence of fear and grief.

studies.applyIt: Think of a limit you know about and have been treating as flexible: a time you promised, a line someone asked you to keep. The word in this verse is about stepping outside something you can see. Put yourself back inside that one line today, and tell nobody. Then notice how little it actually cost.
studies.explainEasier: People who turn down God's signs will be touched by punishment. The reason given is what they did, not what they thought. They stepped over a line they knew was there.

studies.title: I Do Not Say
studies.meaning: Three claims are refused here in a row, and each was one the audience had demanded or assumed: wealth beyond measure, knowledge of what is hidden, and the nature of an angel. What is left after the subtraction is one clause. He follows what is revealed to him. Early scholars observe that prophethood gets defined by what it is not. Then the verse closes with a line about the blind and the seeing, which hands the work of thinking back to the listener.
studies.historicalContext: Mecca, where the demands being answered are recorded right through the surah. A treasure to prove favour, knowledge of the future to prove access, an angel to prove authority. The Prophet's ordinary life was public knowledge in a small city. That is why an honest denial was possible at all. The classical sources treat this as a general answer, not a reply to one occasion.

keyTerms.note: The plural of a word for a locked store where valuables are kept. It implies a keeper with access, which is the claim being declined, rather than wealth itself, which is what the audience heard.
What lies beyond perception, whether in the future or simply out of view. The word covers both, so the disclaimer turns down fortune-telling and hidden knowledge in one phrase.
A passive verb from a root for swift, quiet communication. The passive is the point: the one speaking is the recipient, not the source, which is exactly what the three refusals leave standing.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Mecca had its diviners and its keepers of oracles. Men went to them about lost camels, marriages and journeys, and paid for the answer. Their standing rested on a claim to hidden knowledge. A man arriving with a message from God fitted that familiar slot exactly. This verse turns it down flatly, giving up the one role the city already had a place and a fee for.
studies.didYouKnow: Almost the same three-part denial appears elsewhere in the Quran, spoken by Noah to his own people. Two messengers separated by a huge stretch of time are given nearly the same words. That makes the refusal part of the office itself, rather than a reply to one situation.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Prophethood is cut away from power, from inside information, and from a different order of being. What is left is passing on what was given. That keeps the message from turning into a cult of the messenger. It also keeps the messenger safe from claims he could not meet. The words at the end add the other half. Sight is not produced by argument, which is why the passage ends by asking for thought rather than agreement.

crossReferences.why: Puts nearly the same threefold disclaimer in the mouth of Noah, answering his own community.
Extends the point: had he known the unseen, he would have secured good and avoided harm.
States that he is nothing new among messengers, and does not know what will be done with him.

studies.applyIt: Notice the next time you are asked something and the honest answer is that you do not know. Say that, plainly, before you offer anything else. Most of us fill the gap with a guess delivered in a confident voice. This passage is a model of the alternative, and it costs less standing than you expect.
studies.explainEasier: The Prophet said he does not own God's treasures. He does not know what is hidden, and he is not an angel. He only follows what God sends him. The blind and the seeing are not the same.

studies.title: No Protector Besides Him
studies.meaning: The instruction narrows the audience on purpose: warn those who already fear being gathered before their Lord. Early scholars read that as naming who a warning can actually reach, not as barring anyone from hearing it. The words between them describe everyone, though, not only the fearful. There is no protector and nobody to speak up for you apart from Him. The hope at the end uses a particle of possibility, so even the aim is left open rather than promised.
studies.historicalContext: Mecca, in a passage about who responds to a message and who does not. The city's religion assumed a chain of go-betweens, lesser powers who could speak for a person to the highest one. This verse removes the chain in a single clause. The argument comes back through the surah in different forms, because it was the central point of disagreement.

keyTerms.note: A passive verb used of driving people together into an open space, as flocks or an army are assembled. The passive removes any choice about attending, which is what makes it something to be feared.

The relationship of a patron who stands behind someone in a dispute. In Arabian practice it was the difference between safety and exposure, so denying it here removes a real social security, not an abstraction.

From a root meaning to make something even by pairing it. Someone who speaks for you joins himself to your case to strengthen it, which is why the Quran allows this only by permission rather than by influence.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Every serious matter in Mecca went through somebody. A man seeking a deal did not go himself. He sent a relative with standing, and the result turned on the weight of the man carrying the request. Access was the whole currency of the place. An arrangement with no go-between was not just strange to that audience. It was frightening at the root.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for one who speaks up for you comes from a root meaning to make a pair, and it gives the Arabic word for even numbers. So the picture is of adding a second to your one. The Quran never denies that this happens. It takes it out of anyone's control by making it rest on permission granted at the time.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Fear here is treated as a capacity, not a failing. Those who already sense that they will stand somewhere and answer are the ones a warning can reach, which makes a certain kind of unease a form of openness. Taking away the go-betweens rearranges everything else. If nobody can be sent ahead on your behalf, the relationship stops being managed and becomes direct. That is harder, and much simpler.

crossReferences.why: States the same limit for a day when no soul helps another and no plea is accepted.
Answers the question of who holds that power by assigning all of it to God alone.
Allows someone to speak for another only by permission, which is the balance this verse assumes.

studies.applyIt: Think of a request you have been routing through someone else because approaching directly felt harder. Not every case can be changed. Pick one that can, and make the approach yourself this week. This passage describes a relationship with nobody in the middle, and practising that with people makes it less strange in prayer.
studies.explainEasier: Warn the people who are afraid of standing before their Lord one day. They have no one to protect them and no one to speak up for them except Him. Maybe they will take more care.

studies.title: Do Not Drive Them Away
studies.meaning: The people to be kept close are identified by one activity: calling on their Lord at both ends of the day, wanting His face. Nothing is said about their standing, and early scholars note that this silence is the point. The words in the middle remove the ground on which they could be judged, since their account is not his and his is not theirs. Then the verse states plainly what dismissing them would amount to.
studies.historicalContext: The classical scholars report that leading men of Mecca offered to sit and listen, on one condition. The poorer believers had to be sent away first, since they would not be seen among them. The reports name different individuals, and the sources vary in detail. What they agree on is the shape of the demand and the answer given to it.

keyTerms.note: The verb for chasing off an animal or turning someone out of a gathering. It is physical and slightly harsh, which measures exactly what was being requested behind the polite framing of the offer.
Used through the Quran for God Himself as the object of attention and the aim of an act. The idiom names what a person is actually after, which is why it appears where motive is being described.

The word for a tally of debts and credits. Placing it on both sides of the sentence, theirs and his, makes answering for what you do strictly individual and closes off judging anyone by their circumstances.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Meccan gatherings were arranged by rank. Where a man sat, who spoke first, and who was present at all were public statements about a family's standing, and being seen with the wrong company cost something real. Freed slaves and men without clans were at the bottom of that arrangement. Asking for them to be absent was not thought of as cruelty; it was ordinary manners.
studies.didYouKnow: A nearly identical instruction appears in surah 18, using the same phrase about calling on their Lord morning and evening and seeking His face. It adds that the eyes should not pass over them. Two surahs from the same period keep the same wording, which suggests a pressure that came up more than once.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Access to a prophet is put out of the reach of social rank. The reason given is not kindness but accounting. Nobody carries anyone else's record, so nobody's presence can be traded for anyone's approval. The passage also names the cost of such a trade without softening it. What was on offer was influence over powerful men. The answer treats that as not worth the sentence that would have to be said afterwards.

crossReferences.why: Repeats the instruction almost word for word, adding that the eyes should not pass beyond them.
Records a related correction, where attention given to the influential cost attention owed to a seeker.
States the principle underneath: the measure of rank before God is care, not lineage or wealth.

studies.applyIt: Look at who you make time for this week and ask whether any of it is sorted by usefulness. Then give an unhurried twenty minutes to the person on that list who can do least for you. Not as charity. This passage is about who gets to sit in the room, and the answer it gives has nothing to do with what they bring.
studies.explainEasier: Some people call on their Lord all day and want nothing but Him. God says not to push them away. Their record is theirs and yours is yours. Sending them off would make you one of the wrongdoers.

studies.title: Are These The Ones
studies.meaning: The test described here runs in both directions: some are tried by means of others. Early scholars explain that the wealthy were tested by the poverty of those who believed first, and the poor by the scorn they met. The sentence quoted carries an unmistakable tone, asking whether these are really the people God singled out. The answer is not an argument. It is a question about who is in a position to know, and the measure it names is thankfulness rather than status.
studies.historicalContext: Mecca, straight after the instruction not to dismiss the poorer believers. The early community drew heavily on people with no clan to protect them, including freed slaves and men of small means. The city's leaders found that hard to square with a message claiming to come from God. Scholars treat this verse as the general rule behind the specific instruction just given.

keyTerms.note: From a root for smelting metal to separate it from ore. The word covers both the fire and the sorting, so a trial in Arabic names a process with a result rather than an ordeal without one.
A verb for granting a favour freely. The same root produces the word for reproaching someone with a favour given, so Arabic keeps generosity and its abuse inside one set of letters.
An active participle naming a settled quality rather than a single act. Set against the sneer just quoted, it proposes a measure that is invisible from outside and unaffected by what a person owns.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Mecca's ranking showed in daily detail: who had clients, who walked with an escort, whose name was worth using at a market. A freed slave had no line of ancestors to name and no protector to threaten anyone with. Men used to reading rank in a second saw such people addressed as first among the guided. To them that was not a problem about God. It was a social absurdity.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran records this reaction in several places. It puts nearly the same sentence in the mouths of much earlier peoples. In one passage the objection to Noah is that only the lowest among them follow him, said with the same disbelief. The complaint survives across the Quran's whole span of history, and the wording barely changes.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Social difference itself becomes the instrument of a test here. So the arrangement everyone stands in is not a side detail before God. Rank becomes a question rather than a fact. The measure offered in reply cannot be checked from outside, and that is deliberate. Nobody can rank anybody by it, which removes the whole activity the sneer depends on.

crossReferences.why: States the same principle broadly: some are made a trial for others, and patience is asked.
Records an earlier version of the sneer, that only the lowest among the people follow him.
Preserves the same reasoning: had it been any good, they would not have got there first.

studies.applyIt: Catch yourself the next time you size someone up from what they are wearing or driving or doing for work. Everybody does this and it takes about a second. Once today, notice the estimate arriving and set it aside without replacing it with a better one. This verse names a measure you cannot see, which means the honest position is not knowing.
studies.explainEasier: God tests people through each other. Rich people looked at the poor believers and asked if these were really the ones God had picked out. God knows who is thankful, even when no one else can tell.

studies.title: Say Peace To Them
studies.meaning: The instruction here is about a greeting. When believers come, the first word is peace, before anything is taught or corrected. What follows is given as the content of that greeting. Mercy is a written promise, and the conditions attached are unusually gentle: wrong done in ignorance, then turning back, then repair. Early scholars read ignorance broadly. It covers anyone who acted without weighing what they were doing, which is most people much of the time.
studies.historicalContext: The verses just before describe pressure on the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) to send away his poor followers, who had nothing to offer. The leading men of Mecca wanted to listen without losing face. The refusal of that demand is what this passage follows. The greeting instructed here is addressed to exactly the people he was being asked to dismiss.

keyTerms.note: From a root for wholeness and being free of defect. As a greeting it declares that no harm is intended, and it is the word the Quran uses of the greeting exchanged in the Garden.
Not a lack of information. Early scholars explain it as acting without regard for the consequence, the state of a person who knew and did not weigh it, which is why the term covers so much ground.

A verb for repairing what has broken, used of mending relations between people. It adds a third step after regret and turning back, and it points outward at the damage rather than inward at the feeling.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Greetings in Arabia set people in their place. Who you greeted first, whether you greeted at all, and which words you used all declared rank in public. A man of standing was greeted before he greeted. Being passed over was a known humiliation. Telling the Prophet to open with peace towards followers of no consequence turned a rule upside down, and everybody watching would have noticed at once.
studies.didYouKnow: The clause about mercy being written appears twice in this surah, and the difference between the two is instructive. At 6:12 it stands inside an argument with opponents about who owns the world. Here it sits inside a greeting to believers. The same sentence works once as evidence and once as reassurance.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Forgiveness is described in three moves rather than one: the act, the turning, and the repair. That refuses a version of repentance that stays entirely inside a person. The passage also puts the offer inside a greeting, which changes its register. This is not a warning with a concession attached. It is news delivered to people already in the room. The verse after it says that clarity itself exposes the other path.

crossReferences.why: Names the same condition, wrongdoing done in ignorance followed by turning back soon after.
Shows the angels greeting the patient with peace, the same word used here.
Refuses the demand to drive away those who call on their Lord morning and evening.

studies.applyIt: The next time someone comes to you with something they have done wrong, notice what your first sentence is. Try making it an ordinary greeting, the kind you would give anyone, before you say anything about the matter. The order in this verse is deliberate. It puts the person in the room before the problem.
studies.explainEasier: God tells the Prophet to greet believers with peace when they come to him. He is to tell them that God has promised to show mercy. Anyone who does wrong without thinking, then turns back and puts it right, will be forgiven.

studies.title: I Will Not Follow Your Desires
studies.meaning: Refusing an offer is easier when the refusal was not yours to make. The first thing said here reports a ban received, so it is not a personal preference. The second names what he would actually be following if he agreed. Not their gods, but their desires. Early scholars read that as naming the real source of the practice. The words at the end are conditional and unsparing. Were he to do it, he would be among the lost, with no exemption claimed for his office.
studies.historicalContext: Mecca, in a period when compromise was still being explored. The classical sources record offers of shared worship, taking turns between his God and theirs. That was part of the bargaining the city tried before it turned to pressure. This verse belongs to a family of answers given across several Meccan surahs, and all of them refuse the arrangement in similar terms.

keyTerms.note: A passive verb, so the speaker reports rather than decides. The construction places the refusal outside his own judgement, which is why the sentence carries no argument to be negotiated with.
The plural of a word for what a self leans toward, from a root meaning to fall. It names appetite rather than belief, which reclassifies the whole practice being defended.
A participle for those who have found a way and are following it. Its use in a conditional sentence about himself removes any suggestion that guidance, once given, cannot be walked away from.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabian religion made room for everything. Tribes took up each other's gods, sanctuaries held images from several regions, and adding one more cost nothing. That flexibility was useful for a city living on visitors. Against that background, a refusal to include anything was not heard as principle. It was heard as bad manners, and it would cost the city trade.
studies.didYouKnow: The word used here for desires is the same one the Quran uses elsewhere of someone taking his own leaning as a god. Putting it in an argument about idols moves the discussion inward. On this reading, what is finally being worshipped is the self's preference, not the object it settles on.
studies.theologicalSignificance: This puts the alternative to God not in rival gods but in appetite, which is why the refusal cannot be settled by a compromise about names. It also places the speaker under the same terms as everyone else. He states what would happen to him if he gave way, in the same words used of others. So the message binds its bearer first, and gives him no separate standing.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same refusal its fullest form, separating two ways of worship without hostility.
Names the underlying condition: taking one's own desire as the god one actually serves.
Repeats the declaration in similar words, adding what he does worship instead.

studies.applyIt: Think of a preference of yours that you have quietly promoted into a principle. A routine, a taste, a way things ought to be done. Name it accurately for what it is, just once. This verse relabels desires honestly, and doing that on something small makes the larger version easier to spot later.
studies.explainEasier: The Prophet was told not to worship what they pray to besides God. He says he will not follow what they want. If he did, he would be lost and off the right road.

studies.title: The Decision Is Not Mine
studies.meaning: The reply separates two things that were getting confused. He stands on clear evidence from his Lord, and that is what they have rejected. What they are demanding, the punishment they keep asking him to produce, is not his to give. Early scholars note the exactness of the wording: not that it will not come, but that it is not in his possession. Judgement is then placed where it belongs, with a God described as one who tells the truth and separates cases.
studies.historicalContext: Mecca, where the demand behind this comes back through the surah, sometimes as a challenge and sometimes as a taunt. Asking a warner to produce the warning showed an audience that nothing followed from ignoring him. The classical sources treat the exchange as typical of the period. They do not tie this verse to any single day or speaker.

keyTerms.note: Something that makes a matter plain, used in Arabic for legal evidence. The word claims clarity rather than persuasion, which is why the sentence goes straight on to note that it was rejected anyway.
A form meaning to demand that something be brought forward. It names impatience as a request, and the Quran uses it repeatedly of people asking for exactly what they would not want to arrive.
From a root meaning to cut apart. A judge in this vocabulary is one who separates a tangle into its parts, so deciding is pictured as clarifying rather than as choosing a side.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Disputes in Mecca went to judges chosen by both sides. Their job was to cut a tangled matter into parts everyone could see. Their standing came from being trusted to separate rather than to favour. A well-known judge's ruling could hold across tribes. The word used here of God belongs to that role, and the audience would have heard a familiar job being named.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb describing what God does with the truth here is the same one used for telling a story, and it is the root of the Quranic word for narrative. Some early readers of the text read the verb slightly differently, giving the sense of deciding rather than telling. The classical commentaries record both.
studies.theologicalSignificance: This draws a firm line between carrying a message and controlling what follows from it, which protects the messenger and the audience from a false bargain. It also describes judgement in an unexpected way. Rather than a verdict handed down, it is truth told and a tangle cut apart. So the day of decision is shown as the day when things are finally described accurately.

crossReferences.why: Opens with the same phrase about standing on clear evidence from one's Lord.
Answers the same impatience: the punishment would have arrived already, but for an appointed term.
States the same principle in the middle of a story, that judgement belongs to God alone.

studies.applyIt: Notice a place where you have been carrying responsibility for an outcome that was never yours to decide: a verdict, a diagnosis, another person's choice. Say to yourself, in one sentence, what part is actually in your hands. Then do that part today and leave the sentence where it is. This verse is a model of the division.
studies.explainEasier: The Prophet says he is standing on clear proof from his Lord, and they have turned it down. The punishment they keep asking for is not his to give. God decides, and He decides best.

studies.title: The Matter Would Be Settled
studies.meaning: The reply is a conditional that quietly turns the demand around. Had the punishment been in his hands, it would already have come, and the argument between them would be over. Early scholars read that as a note on what human control would have produced. A messenger with power over consequences would have used it. The delay they treat as weakness is exactly what has kept them alive. The words at the end move the question of who is wronging whom out of the conversation entirely.
studies.historicalContext: Mecca, and this is the second of two answers in a row to the same taunt. The community around the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) was being harassed and had every human reason to want something decisive. Both verses say the same thing from different directions. The timing does not belong to him. No occasion is reported for either.

keyTerms.note: A passive verb for a matter concluded and closed. The same form appears earlier in this surah about an angel's arrival, so the two answers to two demands are given in identical words.
A word covering a command, a situation and a decision at once. Its breadth here lets one phrase name the whole dispute between the two sides and the verdict that would end it.

A comparative form used absolutely, so it names knowledge beyond anyone's rather than merely greater knowledge. It withdraws the question of who is in the wrong from human assessment, the speaker's included.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Blood disputes in Arabia were settled by men who had the power to act and chose when. A clan that could strike and did not was making a choice every day it waited. Everyone knew that holding back under provocation was a position, not an absence. The audience for this verse knew how to read a delay. It was held by someone with the means to end it.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase about the matter being settled appears twice in this surah, within fifty verses of each other. Once it is about sending an angel. Here it is about hurrying the punishment. Both times it answers a demand for something decisive, and both times the answer is that the decisive thing would leave nobody still standing there to argue.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Delay is presented here as a form of mercy, not as an absence of power, and that changes how a quiet heaven should be read. The passage also protects the messenger from a job nobody could hold well. A human being able to call down harm on his opponents would be a danger. The verse says so by simply describing what would have happened. Restraint is placed with God, on purpose.

crossReferences.why: States the same point: if God hastened harm as people hasten good, their term would be over.
Records the taunt at its boldest, asking for stones from the sky if this is really the truth.
Says that if God held people to account for what they earn, no creature would be left.

studies.applyIt: Think of a moment when you had the power to end an argument by saying the one thing that would have finished the other person, and did not. Remember what that restraint cost and what it preserved. Then find the smaller version of it today. This verse treats withheld force as a kindness, which is easiest to believe when you have practised it.
studies.explainEasier: If the punishment they keep asking for were in his hands, it would already have come. The whole argument would be over. God knows who is in the wrong.

studies.title: The Keys Of The Unseen
studies.meaning: The image is of keys, held by one holder, to what nobody else can open. Then the description narrows instead of widening. It runs from land and sea, to a single falling leaf, to a seed underground in the dark, to whatever is wet or dry. Early scholars note the movement from the vast down to the tiny. What ends the sentence is not knowledge but a record. So nothing seen is left unwritten.
studies.historicalContext: Mecca, in a surah largely taken up with people who wanted proof, and with the limits of what human beings can settle for themselves. The verses around it describe God taking souls at night and returning them by day. Early scholars record no occasion for this one. They read it as part of the surah's long argument about the difference between what people know and what they assume.

keyTerms.note: The plural can be read as keys or as treasuries, and the classical scholars record both. Either way the point is access: what stands behind them cannot be reached without the one who holds them.
What is absent from perception, not what is mysterious in itself. The word is relative to the observer, which is why the verse has to add that only He knows these particular things.
The singular form with its feminine ending names one individual leaf rather than foliage in general. That grammatical choice is what makes the example small enough to do the work the sentence needs.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: For farmers and herders the buried seed was the standing image of not knowing. You put grain into dark ground and waited months. There was no way of learning what had happened to it, and a season's food hung on that hidden stretch of time. The verse names exactly that, along with the wet and the dry. Those were the two words a desert people used to divide everything that grows.
studies.didYouKnow: This verse is one of a small group in the Quran built entirely as a descending list, moving from the widest category down to the smallest without a break. It carries no command and no address to the listener. Classical scholars return to it when they discuss what the clear record named at its end means.
studies.theologicalSignificance: God's knowledge is described through the trivial rather than the impressive, and that is the harder claim to make. Knowing the count of the stars would say less than knowing about one leaf. The leaf falls below the line at which anything would normally be recorded. That lands in two directions at once. Nothing you suffer is beneath notice, and nothing done quietly goes unrecorded either.

crossReferences.why: Repeats the claim about the smallest weight, in earth or heaven, being in a clear record.
Lists specific things kept with God alone, naming keys this verse leaves unopened.
Insists that no atom's weight escapes Him, answering those who deny the Hour.

studies.applyIt: Think of something you have been doing that nobody has noticed. A repeated kindness, a restraint no one sees, a hard thing you have not mentioned. Let this verse be about that for a moment, rather than about the universe. It is built out of the smallest examples there are, and that appears to be the point of it.
studies.explainEasier: Only God knows what is hidden. He knows everything on land and in the sea. Not one leaf falls without Him knowing. Not one seed sits in the dark earth without being written down in His clear book.

studies.title: He Takes You By Night
studies.meaning: The verb used for what happens at night is the one the Quran uses for death. Early scholars take that seriously: sleep is described as a smaller version of the same event. The daily cycle then becomes a rehearsal. Something is taken, what was done in the light is recorded, and the person is raised again into the same day, until the count of days runs out. The words at the end name what the whole sequence is heading toward, which is being told what you did.
studies.historicalContext: Mecca, where the argument for the resurrection is made to people who accepted a creator and refused an afterlife. It does not appeal to power or to earlier peoples. It points instead at something the audience did every night. The surah uses it because it cannot be denied, and cannot be credited to anyone else.

keyTerms.note: A verb meaning to receive something in full, used of collecting a debt paid completely. The Quran uses it for death and, here, for sleep, which is why the tradition links the two states.
Literally to wound or cut, and by extension to earn with the hands. The physical sense stays audible, so the day's actions are described with a word that also means leaving a mark.
To give weighty news, from the root behind the word for a prophet's tidings. The final act is telling rather than punishing, which places accurate information at the end of the sequence.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Sleep was more exposed then than now. People slept on roofs in summer, in tents on the road, and in houses without locks. A traveller took his rest in the open with animals nearby. Handing over consciousness in that setting was an act of trust performed nightly. Nobody needed persuading that sleep was a state you did not control and did not guarantee waking from.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran uses the same verb for sleep and for death in more than one place. One passage states directly that God takes souls both at death and during sleep, returning some and holding others. Arabic therefore has no need of a comparison here. The two events are described by the identical word.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The resurrection is argued from something ordinary, not from something spectacular. That is typical of this surah. Awareness can be taken away and given back every night by an agency you have no part in. If so, the objection to its being given back once more loses its force. The passage also puts the record and the raising in one sentence. So the day's actions and the account that follows are shown as one process.

crossReferences.why: States the pairing explicitly: God takes souls at death, and those not dead during sleep.
Calls sleep a repose and the daytime a rising, using the vocabulary of resurrection.
Offers sleep at night and seeking provision by day as a sign for those who listen.

studies.applyIt: Tonight, notice the last moment you are aware of before sleep. Tomorrow, notice the first moment you are aware of after it. You do not manage the gap. Doing this once turns an automatic thing into a watched one. That is exactly the move this verse makes, with a night everybody has already had thousands of times.
studies.explainEasier: God takes you at night when you sleep, and He knows what you do by day. Then He wakes you up again, until your time is finished. After that you go back to Him, and He tells you what you did.

studies.title: Envoys Who Never Fail
studies.meaning: A life is described here as accompanied from beginning to end. Guardians are sent over a person. When death arrives, it is not something that simply happens but an errand carried out by envoys who do not fall short. Early scholars note the plural and discuss whether it names a company or those who assist, without settling it. Then the circuit closes. They are returned to their true Master, and the judging belongs to Him, reckoned faster than anyone could count.
studies.historicalContext: Mecca, in a sustained passage on God's authority that opens with the same clause used earlier in this surah. The audience believed in unseen beings and in fate. What they did not believe in was a recorded life answered for afterwards. These verses take the unseen company they already accepted and give it a job description that leads somewhere.

keyTerms.note: A plural from the root for preserving and memorising. The same word covers guarding a person and keeping a record, so protection and documentation are named by one term.
The same word used for prophets sent to peoples. Applying it to those who come at death frames the moment as a delivery of a message rather than an interruption of a life.

A word for the one who holds authority and also gives protection, used in Arabia of a freed slave's former owner who remained his ally. Qualified as true, it distinguishes real patronage from the arranged kind.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A caravan of value travelled with hired guards, and their reliability was the whole question. Everyone had heard of escorts who slept, ran, or were bought. Payment, reputation and family were staked on it, and a guard who failed once did not work again. The phrase saying these envoys never fall short is drawn straight from that anxiety, and answers it in four words.
studies.didYouKnow: The word used here for guardians comes from the root that also gives the Arabic term for someone who has learned the Quran by heart. Keeping a text safe and keeping a person safe are named with the same letters. That is why the language of keeping runs through both subjects in the tradition.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Death is shown as a collection, not an ending, carried out by agents under orders. That takes both randomness and terror out of the picture, without softening it. The passage also joins two ideas the audience kept apart. They accepted an unseen world. They did not accept answering for what they did. Once the guardians are also recorders, the unseen runs straight into the reckoning instead of sitting as decoration around it.

crossReferences.why: Names the same watchers as noble recorders who know exactly what a person does.
Places two receivers at each side, with nothing uttered but an observer is ready.
Answers the same question about death by naming the one charged with taking each person.

studies.applyIt: Choose one ordinary hour today, perhaps your commute, and go through it as though everything in it were being noted, without changing anything for show. Notice how much of that hour you would describe differently afterwards. The passage says a record is kept whether or not you attend to it. Attending to one hour is enough to feel the difference.
studies.explainEasier: God is above everyone He made, and He sends guardians to watch over you. When your time comes, His messengers take you, and they never miss. Then you are brought back to Him, and He decides.

studies.title: Humbly And In Secret
studies.meaning: Two adverbs carry this passage. The calling described is done in lowliness and in hiding, which early scholars read as prayer nobody else witnesses, made when there is no audience to perform for. The vow is quoted in full, with its promise of thankfulness. Then the answer arrives in two moves. God is the one who delivers, and not only from this but from every distress. And the pattern that follows the rescue is stated without comment. You go back to what you were doing.
studies.historicalContext: Mecca, and the people addressed were traders whose lives involved regular exposure to open desert and to sea crossings from the Arabian coast. The surah has already asked what they would call on in an emergency. Here it moves from the imagined to the remembered. It describes something the audience had done, not something they might do. No occasion is reported for these verses.

keyTerms.note: Plural again, as at the opening of this surah. Applied to land and sea together, it covers night, storm cloud and depth at once, naming every condition in which a traveller cannot see a way out.
Concealment, from a root for hiding something away. Paired with humility, it describes prayer stripped of any audience, which is why the tradition treats this phrase as a picture of sincere calling.
A word for grief that presses on the chest and tightens the breathing. It names the bodily feeling of crisis rather than the crisis itself, which is what the promise of deliverance is attached to.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Caravans lost people. A man who wandered from the line at night, a party that missed a well by a few miles, a sandstorm that erased the track: these were ordinary risks, not stories. Sea crossings to Africa and up the Red Sea added their own. Almost every family had someone who had prayed in one of those situations and come home to tell about it.
studies.didYouKnow: Both adverbs in this passage, humility and secrecy, appear together once more in the Quran. They come at the start of the next surah, in an instruction about how to call on God. So what frightened people already do becomes the shape prayer is meant to take at any time.
studies.theologicalSignificance: This picks out the most honest prayer a person makes and places it in a crisis. That is both a compliment and a charge. Nothing is wrong with the calling itself.
