The failure is what comes after it. So thankfulness is not the feeling at the moment of rescue, which everybody has. It is something that has to survive the return to ordinary days, when nothing is pressing on the chest.

crossReferences.why: Asks who answers the one in distress when he calls, and removes the harm afflicting him.
Names the same reflex: every blessing is from God, and to Him you cry when harm arrives.
Shows the prayer from inside the darkness itself, and the deliverance that answered it.

studies.applyIt: Recall a specific time you were rescued from something and remember what you promised while it was happening. Most of us made a promise. Write down the one you made, in the words you used, and do the smallest piece of it this week. The passage does not fault the prayer. It notices what happened after the danger passed.
studies.explainEasier: When people are lost in the dark on land or at sea, they call on God quietly and beg for help. They promise to be thankful. God saves them from that and from every trouble. Then they go back to serving other things.

studies.title: The Violence Of One Another
studies.meaning: Three possibilities are named, and the last of them takes the most room. Something from above, something from beneath the feet, or a splitting of the people into parties who are made to taste each other's force. Early scholars note that the first two are events and the third is a condition. They note too that most of the words go to it. The comment at the end repeats a line used earlier in the surah, about the signs being turned in different directions, so that they might grasp them.
studies.historicalContext: Mecca, and the audience was a city held together by a fragile balance of clans. It had no ruler and no standing force. It worked because rival families found it profitable to cooperate around a sanctuary. Everyone listening had heard of towns and tribes destroyed from within by feud. The third possibility named here was the one they had actually seen.

keyTerms.note: Groups formed around a following, from a root meaning to spread or to follow. The plural describes a body that has separated into camps, each with its own allegiance, rather than a simple disagreement.
From the root for clothing, so the sense is of things becoming entangled and hard to tell apart. Applied to a community, it names the state where nobody can say clearly what the quarrel is.
The causative of tasting, used through the Quran for consequence experienced first hand. Here what is tasted is supplied by other people, which makes the affliction one a community hands to itself.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabian feuds ran for generations. A killing in one season brought an answering killing in the next. The tally could run on past the point where anyone recalled the first wrong. The long war between two tribes near Medina had worn out both sides within living memory. Listeners did not have to imagine a community tasting its own violence. They could name the families.
studies.didYouKnow: The comment that closes this verse, about turning the signs in different directions, appears twice in this surah within twenty verses. One time it ends with a note that they still turn away. Here it ends in the hope that they will understand. The same clause is given two different endings, which is itself an example of what it describes.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Division inside a group is listed beside disasters from the sky and from the ground, as something of the same order. That raises the stakes on how a community treats itself. The passage does not make factions a lesser problem, handled by people while the real events come from elsewhere. It also leaves the whole list in the conditional. What is being described is capacity, and the point of describing it is understanding, not fear.

crossReferences.why: Gives the counterpart instruction: hold to God's rope together and do not scatter into parties.
Names the same fracturing, of those who split their religion, each faction pleased with its own.
Warns that quarrelling among themselves is what drains a community's strength away.

studies.applyIt: Think of a group you belong to that is quietly splitting: a family, a workplace, a neighbourhood. Find the one conversation nobody is having, because everyone assumes someone else should start it. You do not have to solve anything. Ask one person in the other camp what they really think, and then listen to the whole answer.
studies.explainEasier: God is able to send trouble on people from above them or from under their feet. He can also split them into groups and let them hurt each other. He explains this so people will understand.

studies.title: I Am Not Your Keeper
studies.meaning: The rejection is stated plainly, and so is the fact it does not alter: your people denied it, and it is the truth. Then the burden is set down. He is not a keeper over them, which early scholars explain as a release from responsibility for outcomes rather than from the work of delivering the message. Then comes the only thing left to say about timing. Every piece of news has a settled place where it comes to rest, and you will know it then.
studies.historicalContext: Mecca, after a run of verses describing what God is able to do and what the listeners keep refusing. This is where the surah turns and speaks to the one carrying the message rather than to those declining it. The classical sources do not report an occasion. The phrase about his own people has weight in a city where the objectors were relatives and neighbours.

keyTerms.note: The agent who manages another's affairs and answers for them. Denying the role removes both the authority to compel and the liability for the result, which are two halves of one office.
News that carries consequence, the same word used earlier in this surah for what will reach those who mocked. Its reappearance ties this promise back to that one.
A noun of place and time from the verb to settle. It can name where something comes to rest or when, and that openness lets the phrase cover both without choosing between them.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A trusted agent was a real position in Meccan trade. A merchant travelling north left someone with authority over his goods, his debts and his household. That man answered for what happened while he was away. The role carried power and risk together. To say he is not that for them told the audience exactly which relationship was not on offer.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for a settled resting place in this verse turns up elsewhere in the Quran. It is used for the earth as a dwelling and for the sun's course. So it belongs to the language of things reaching their appointed position. Applied to news, it treats a report as something travelling toward a place, rather than merely being true or false.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Responsibility is divided cleanly here: the message is delivered, and the answer belongs to those who receive it. The timing belongs to God. That division is what makes long, unrewarded work bearable, and the Quran gives it to a messenger before anyone else. The second verse adds the piece that makes trust possible. The ending is located, not merely promised, and it has somewhere to arrive.

crossReferences.why: Draws the same line: whoever is guided is guided for himself, and he is not their keeper.
States the limit of the office in two clauses: you are a reminder, not one who controls.
Repeats the release if they turn away, since he was not sent as a guardian over them.

studies.applyIt: Pick something you have been carrying that belongs to someone else: a decision, a habit, a life you cannot live for them. Say the sentence out loud, that you are not the keeper of this. Then name the one part that is genuinely yours and do that. Setting a thing down properly requires knowing what remains in your hands.
studies.explainEasier: His own people said no to the message, and it is still the truth. He is told to say that he is not in charge of them. Every piece of news has a time when it lands, and they will find out.

studies.title: Until They Change The Subject
studies.meaning: The instruction here is unusually practical. When people are wading into talk about God's signs, withdraw. The condition for coming back is stated exactly: until they move to another topic. Early scholars note that no argument is called for, and no confrontation. Then room is made for forgetting, which assumes it will happen. Whoever withdraws is freed from any account for the others. That gives the whole instruction a purpose that is about them, not against them.
studies.historicalContext: Mecca, and the setting is social rather than formal. People mocked the recitation in gatherings where believers were present, sometimes just for fun. The classical scholars describe believers being drawn into defending the Quran in rooms where nothing was being decided. This verse speaks to that. A Medinan passage later repeats the instruction in almost the same terms.

keyTerms.note: The verb for walking into water without knowing its depth. Used of talk, it names the kind of confident discussion that goes further than anybody's knowledge, which is why the Quran picks it for careless speech about God.
The same verb used earlier in this surah for those who turned from the signs. Here it is given as an instruction, so a word describing a fault becomes, in a different setting, a discipline.
Used twice in this passage with two senses: the recollection that ends forgetfulness, and the reminder offered to others. One word covers remembering yourself and being remembered to.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Meccan evenings were spent in company. Men gathered by the sanctuary or in a courtyard, and talk moved through poetry, news and jokes, with reputations made and lost by what somebody said well. Leaving such a gathering was noticed by everyone there. The instruction here has a social cost built into it, which is why the verse names the exact condition under which you can sit back down.
studies.didYouKnow: This instruction appears twice in the Quran. Once here, in a Meccan surah, and once later in a Medinan one. Both use the same verb for wading into talk and the same condition about waiting for another subject. The Medinan version adds a clause about becoming like them, which the earlier version leaves unsaid.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Company is treated here as shaping, not neutral. Where you sit shapes what you get used to hearing. The remedy offered is physical distance, not a better argument. It also allows for human weakness with grace. Forgetting is expected, and answered with an instruction for afterwards rather than a telling off. And the purpose stays pointed at the others. The reminder is offered in hope, not in judgement.

crossReferences.why: Repeats the same instruction in a Medinan setting, with the same condition about another topic.
Describes those who pass by empty talk with dignity, as a settled quality.
Shows the same withdrawal from idle speech, with a courteous parting rather than a quarrel.

studies.applyIt: Notice the next conversation, online or in a room, where people are being clever about something sacred and nobody knows much. You do not need to correct anyone. Leave, or close the tab, and come back when the subject has changed. The verse gives a condition for returning, which makes this a pause rather than a rupture.
studies.explainEasier: When people start making fun of God's words, walk away until they talk about something else. If you forget and stay, get up once you remember. Good people are not answerable for them. It is only a reminder.

studies.title: Religion As A Pastime
studies.meaning: Two words describe what has been done with religion. It has become play and pastime. Early scholars read that as covering both those who mocked and those who kept the forms without weight. The instruction is to leave them, and it is followed at once by an instruction to keep reminding. So withdrawal is not abandonment. The reason given is the danger of a soul being handed over to what it earned, with no ally, nobody to speak for it, and no ransom accepted however much is offered.
studies.historicalContext: Mecca, in a passage about who can be reached, and how. The city's religious life was genuinely festive: seasonal fairs, poetry contests, rites around the sanctuary that doubled as show and trade. Calling that play and pastime was not a stretch invented for the argument. It named the arrangement the city itself would have recognised.

keyTerms.note: Activity done for its own amusement, the word used of children's games. Applied to religion it says the practice is real and the seriousness is missing, which is a sharper charge than hypocrisy.
From a root for being taken in by an appearance, used of a market deal that looked better than it was. The deceiver is named as the present life itself rather than any person.

keyTerms.gloss: it is given up, handed over
keyTerms.note: A rare verb, appearing only in this verse in the Quran, twice. Early scholars gloss it as being consigned or held in pledge, and the range of their explanations reflects how uncommon the word is.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Ransom was an ordinary deal. A captive taken in a raid was priced and bought back. A killing could be settled with an agreed number of camels rather than blood. Every family knew the sums, and most had used them. The line saying no equivalent will be accepted removes the one device the audience relied on for undoing what could not be undone.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb describing a soul being handed over occurs nowhere else in the Quran. It appears twice, both times in this one verse. Rare words like this are the ones the earliest works on Quranic language worked hardest to explain. The commentaries keep several proposed meanings side by side.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Seriousness is treated as part of what religion is. So keeping the shape while dropping the weight is a change in kind, not a matter of degree. The passage also finishes the surah's argument about go-betweens by shutting the last door, which is payment. Nothing can be put in a person's place at that point. What a life actually contained is the only thing left.

crossReferences.why: Names the present life as play, amusement and adornment, then shows what remains of it.
Uses the same verb of deception, warning against being taken in by the present life.
States the same refusal of ransom: an earth-full of gold would not be accepted.

studies.applyIt: Ask yourself what part of your religious life has become comfortable enough to be a routine you enjoy rather than something you mean. Not to give it up. Pick one such practice this week and do it slowly enough to notice what it is for. This verse is about weight going missing while the shape remains.
studies.explainEasier: Some people treat religion as a game and a way to pass the time. Leave them alone, but keep reminding. On that day nobody can help a soul or pay anything to buy it back.

studies.title: Turned Back On Our Heels
studies.meaning: The refusal is put as a question about direction. Calling on something that neither helps nor harms would mean turning back on your heels after being guided. That is movement in reverse, not a change of opinion. Then a picture is drawn. A man is led off by devils, wandering lost in open country, while companions on the road call him to come to them. Early scholars note that the ayah does not say whether he answers. It leaves him mid-scene and turns to the declaration that God's guidance is the guidance.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The pressure behind it was real. People who accepted the message were urged back by families, who framed the return as reasonable and as loyalty to their own. The wording answers that framing rather than the beliefs. No specific occasion is attested. The surah speaks to the situation in several places, using a different image each time.

keyTerms.note: The plural of heel, used in the idiom for turning back the way you came. It describes reversal as bodily movement, which is why the Quran uses it for abandoning a position rather than for changing a view.
A verb built on the root for falling and for desire. It carries both at once, so the luring described is a downward pull toward what the person already wanted rather than an external abduction.
An intensive form for someone turning in place, unable to choose a direction. It appears only here in the Quran, and it names confusion as a physical state rather than an intellectual one.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Getting lost was the standard nightmare of desert travel, and the stories about it were exact. A man leaves the fire to check on an animal. He circles within a mile of the camp all night while people call his name. Sound carries strangely over dunes. The scene in this ayah, with companions calling from the road and a man turning in place, was a story everyone had heard told.
studies.didYouKnow: The word describing the bewildered man occurs only once in the whole Quran, in this ayah. Single uses like that are rare enough that classical scholars made lists of them. They tend to turn up at the vivid centre of a comparison, where a plainer word would have blurred the picture.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Guidance is described as a position already held, not a conclusion still being weighed. That changes what leaving it means. The comparison also says something about how people get lost. They are not seized. They are drawn by something they wanted, while help is audible the whole time. And the declaration that follows moves the standard. Guidance is defined by its source, so the question stops being which road feels right.

crossReferences.why: States the same measure in almost identical words, that God's guidance is the guidance itself.
Describes people who took devils as allies instead of God and reckon that they are guided.
Pictures the reversal differently, as worship on an edge that turns on its face when trouble comes.

studies.applyIt: Think of a good practice you have quietly let go of in the last year, and notice how the letting go was argued for at the time. It usually sounds reasonable. Pick that one thing and restart it this week at half its old size. The ayah describes reversal as movement, which means it can be walked back the same way.
studies.explainEasier: They are asked why they would call on something that cannot help them or hurt them. God has already guided them. Turning back would be like a man led away by devils. He wanders lost while his friends call him.

studies.title: And To Establish The Prayer
studies.meaning: The ayah completes a sentence begun before it. The instruction to submit to the Lord of the worlds runs straight into two more: establish the prayer, and be mindful of Him. Early scholars note that the verb used with prayer is not simply to perform but to set upright. That suggests keeping something standing rather than carrying it out. The closing clause supplies the horizon. It is to Him that you will be gathered, and everything before it is pointed by that.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The prayer described belongs to the earliest stretch of the community's practice, before its later Medinan detail. The classical sources put regular prayer at the centre of Meccan believers' lives from very early on. Much of the harassment they met came when they were seen praying. In the grammar of the sentence, the instruction here is joined to the statements before it.

keyTerms.note: The causative of standing, used of putting up a structure and of maintaining an institution. It asks for something kept upright over time, which is why the Quran rarely says simply to perform the prayer.
From a root meaning to guard or shield oneself. It describes careful attention to a relationship rather than fear of a person, so the English words for piety and fear both fall short of it.
The same passive used earlier in this surah for being assembled before God. Its reappearance here attaches the two instructions to a destination rather than leaving them as good practice.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Standing in prayer was conspicuous in Mecca. There was no separate building and no privacy for it; people prayed in courtyards, at the edge of the sanctuary, in the open where anyone passing could see. Some of the early community went out to the ravines around the city to pray unobserved. The instruction to keep it standing was, in that setting, a public commitment.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran almost always pairs the prayer with the verb for setting something upright. It rarely uses a verb for doing or finishing. The pattern holds across Meccan and Medinan passages, steadily enough that early grammar writers treated the pairing as fixed. The choice keeps the idea of keeping it going, rather than of a performance, at the centre of the phrase.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Prayer is placed here as the practical shape of the surrender just described. So the statement and the daily action belong to one sentence. That link matters more than either half alone. The mention of gathering at the end sets the frame. The practice is not offered as a method for a better life now. It is the ordinary posture of someone who expects to stand somewhere and answer.

crossReferences.why: Gives the prayer a stated purpose in the same imperative form, as a remembrance of God.
Describes what the practice does over time, restraining a person from what is shameful and wrong.
Sets the prayer at the two ends of the day, with good deeds removing what is bad.

studies.applyIt: Choose the prayer in your day that is most rushed, usually the one squeezed against something else, and give it five extra minutes tomorrow. Not more words. Just room around it, so the standing is not immediately followed by moving. The verb in this ayah is about keeping something upright, and things stay upright when they are not knocked into.
studies.explainEasier: Keep the prayer going, and keep God in mind. That is what the words say here. In the end everyone is brought together in front of him.

studies.title: His Word Is The Truth
studies.meaning: Creation is said to be in truth, meaning with a purpose rather than as a game, and that phrase governs everything after it. Then the mode of creation: a word said, and the thing is. Early scholars note the tense, since the sentence describes a day still ahead while using a present verb, which keeps one act of command over both the first creation and the raising. Sovereignty is then named specifically for the day the trumpet sounds.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. It closes a passage that has followed Abraham's argument with his people and then run through a list of prophets. The surah speaks to an audience who accepted God as creator while treating other powers as go-betweens. This verse answers them by leaving no room for a second authority on the day it would matter most. Early scholars report no particular occasion for it.

keyTerms.note: The word covers truth, right and what is due. Saying the heavens were made with it denies that creation is arbitrary, and the same word returns two clauses later to describe God's own speech.
The bare imperative of the verb to be, two letters in Arabic. It is the shortest command the language can form, and the shortness is the point: nothing stands between the intention and the thing.
A curved horn of the kind used to summon people or signal an army. The Quran uses it for the blast that ends and then restarts everything, and here it fixes the moment sovereignty becomes undeniable.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Authority in Mecca was spread among the clans by office and by custom. Nobody held all of it. Decisions were taken in assembly. Alliances shifted. The man who looked dominant one season could be outplayed the next. A claim that rule on one particular day belongs to a single holder, with no assembly and no bargaining, described something nobody there had ever seen.
studies.didYouKnow: The command translated as be is a single word of two letters in Arabic. It occurs several times in the Quran, always in the same construction. Each time the answer is given in the same breath. There is no gap between command and result. The grammar itself refuses any interval in which the thing might not yet exist.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Creation and resurrection are folded into one kind of act. If the first needed nothing but a word, the second cannot be harder. That is the argument the verse makes without stating it. Naming God as knower of both the hidden and the witnessed then closes a gap a listener might use. No area, private or public, is held back from the same authority. The closing names concern wisdom and detail rather than force.

crossReferences.why: States the same command and its instant answer, arguing directly for the resurrection.
Applies the same phrasing to the origination of the heavens and the earth.
Describes the two blasts of the trumpet and what happens between them.

studies.applyIt: Pick one thing you keep postponing because the first step feels heavy. Do the smallest possible version of it within the next hour, not the whole thing. This verse puts no distance between a word and its effect, and while nothing human works that way, most of the distance we experience turns out to be added by us.
studies.explainEasier: God made the sky and the earth for a reason. When he says to a thing, be, it is. On the day the trumpet sounds, everything will belong to him alone.

studies.title: Do You Take Idols As Gods
studies.meaning: The story opens with a question put to his own father, and the question is not aggressive but incredulous. He then states what he sees, using the word for plain error and including the whole community in it. The second ayah steps back to explain the sequence about to unfold. God was showing him the dominion of the heavens and the earth, so that he would be among those who are certain. What follows is therefore presented as instruction rather than as doubt.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. It sits right after a passage about being called back by your own people. Abraham's position matched the early Meccan community's exactly: a person who breaks with the religion of his household. The scholars discuss the name given here for his father. Some treat it as his name, others as a title or a second name. They keep the difference without settling it.

keyTerms.note: Specifically shaped figures, distinguished in Arabic usage from unshaped stones set up for worship. The word emphasises manufacture, which is the point of the question being asked.
An intensified form of the word for kingdom, appearing only a few times in the Quran. It names not the things owned but the fact of their being held, which is what he is being shown.
From a root for knowledge that has settled and stopped moving. It names a state rather than an act, and the ayah presents it as the intended outcome of what he is about to be shown.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Breaking with a father's religion in that world meant losing a household, a name and a trade at once. Religion was not a private choice. It was the property of a family line, kept by the same people who kept the wells and the grazing rights. The Meccan converts hearing this story had made the same break, or were making it. The ayah names the person it costs most to face.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for dominion used here occurs only a handful of times in the Quran, and never for ordinary kingship. It carries a strengthening ending that Arabic uses sparingly. Its rarity marks what follows as a different kind of seeing. It is not simply looking at the sky more carefully than usual.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Certainty is described as something shown, not argued into place. That frames the coming sequence with the star, moon and sun as a lesson rather than a wavering. The passage also shows that the search begins by standing against what you were raised in. And it shows that standing against it can be said respectfully. The question to his father is a question. It is asked before any conclusion is announced to anybody.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same conversation at length, with its gentleness and its repeated address to his father.
Shows him pressing the question further, asking about images to which his people are devoted.
Preserves his declaration of disowning what they worship, apart from the One who originated him.

studies.applyIt: Think of something you believe mainly because it was in the house you grew up in, and it can be small: a view about money, a way of handling conflict. Ask where it came from, once, without deciding anything about it. This passage begins with a question rather than a rejection, and the question is the part worth copying.
studies.explainEasier: Abraham asked his father why he treated carved statues as gods. He said his father and their people were clearly wrong. God then showed Abraham how the sky and the earth are held, so he would be sure.

studies.theme: The Love Between God and the Believer
studies.title: I Do Not Love What Sets
studies.meaning: The reasoning is done aloud, and the conclusion comes with a verb of love rather than of logic. He sees a star in the falling dark and says this is my Lord. When it goes down he says he does not love things that set. Early scholars differ over whether he is reasoning his way forward or arguing with his people in their own terms. Both readings are old. Either way, the test he applies is attachment, and setting is what fails it.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The story sits where the surah is arguing about what deserves worship. Star and planet worship was practised in the wider region and known in Arabia. So the sequence begins with a real option, not an imagined one. The classical scholars treat this as the opening move of a demonstration. It is not a report that Abraham ever believed it.

keyTerms.note: A verb for concealing, from the root that gives the words for a garden, a hidden being and the heart's inner chamber. Night arrives here as a covering laid over him rather than as light departing.
A bright heavenly body, used in Arabic for the wandering ones as well as the fixed. The indefinite form keeps it unnamed, so the argument does not depend on which body it was.
A participle for a body that sinks below the horizon, and by extension for anything that declines and disappears. It is the pivot of the whole sequence, repeated at each stage.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Navigation in Arabia was done by stars, and their risings and settings were tracked closely enough to fix the seasons and the timing of journeys. Herdsmen and guides could name individual stars and knew which appeared when. To this audience, a body that sets was not a poetic idea. It was a working fact used every night, and its regularity was exactly what made it useful.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb used for nightfall here shares its root with three other Arabic words. One is the word for a garden. One names the unseen beings mentioned elsewhere in the Quran. One is the sheltered inner part of a person. All of them are covered or hidden from view, so one set of letters ties hiddenness to what is inside.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage brings in love as a test for what may be worshipped, which is unusual in a surah built on argument. What sets cannot be loved rightly, because attachment to something that goes under has its ending built in. That test also reaches past idols. Anything that reliably departs, including status and strength, fails it. That is why the sequence is remembered outside its original setting.

crossReferences.why: Continues the sequence with the moon, adding a plea for guidance when it too disappears.
Draws the same conclusion directly: do not bow to the sun or moon, but to the One who made them.
Turns the criterion around, describing love that runs from God toward the one who follows the way.

studies.applyIt: Name one thing you are currently attached to that you know will not last: a role, a physical capacity, a season of life you are inside. Do not detach from it. Just say clearly to yourself that it sets. The passage does not ask for coldness. It asks you to know which things are on their way down before they go.
studies.explainEasier: When night came, Abraham saw a star and said, this is my lord. Then it went down. He said he does not love things that set and disappear.

studies.title: Unless My Lord Guides Me
studies.meaning: The second stage repeats the first and then changes the ending. The moon rises, is named, and sets. Instead of a statement about love, he now says something about himself: without guidance he would be among those who go astray. Early scholars note the escalation. He has moved from weighing an object to seeing his own exposure, and the sentence is conditional rather than confident. The reasoning has produced a prayer before it has produced a conclusion.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. It is the middle panel of a three-part sequence the surah presents as teaching given to Abraham. The moon carried religious weight across the ancient Near East, more than any single star. So this stage raises the stakes from the one before. The scholars treat the whole sequence as a demonstration for his people, not a record of belief he actually held.

keyTerms.note: A participle for something breaking into view, used of the moon and sun coming up. The root carries a sense of splitting through, so the rising is pictured as an emergence rather than a smooth arrival.
A conditional particle carrying an oath, so the sentence it opens is sworn rather than supposed. It makes the admission that follows a solemn statement instead of a passing thought.
The same root used through this surah for losing a road, and for what the invented partners do at the end. Applying it to himself puts him in the category he has been describing in others.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The lunar month organised everything. Arabs dated debts, fairs, journeys and the sacred months by the moon's phases, and a new crescent sighted from a rooftop began a month for a whole region. It was the most consequential object in the sky for practical life. Watching it set was therefore not a small observation; it was watching the timekeeper of the year go under.
studies.didYouKnow: The three stages of this sequence move from a star to the moon to the sun, in order of rising brightness. Each stage ends differently. First a statement about love, then a plea for guidance, and finally a declaration. The build is part of the structure, and the middle stage is the only one that is a prayer.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Certainty is shown to include a dependent moment. Even the figure the Quran presents as the model of finding God says he would go astray without being guided. And he says it after reasoning correctly, not before. That puts asking at the centre of the search rather than at its beginning. It also makes fear and hope work together. The fear names a real possibility, and the address turns it into a request.

crossReferences.why: Turns the same request into the daily prayer of everyone who recites it, in almost the same terms.
Gives the previous stage, where the criterion applied to the setting star was love rather than a plea.
Records a similar phrase, hoping the Lord will guide to what is nearer than this to right conduct.

studies.applyIt: Take a decision you are close to making, and add one sentence before you decide. Say that you could get this wrong and would like to be guided. Say it as a request, not a formality. This ayah puts the plea in the middle of good reasoning, not in place of it. The middle is where most of us leave it out.
studies.explainEasier: Next Abraham saw the moon coming up and said, this is my lord. When it set too, he said that without God guiding him he would be one of the people who lose their way.

studies.title: When The Sun Went Down
studies.meaning: The sequence ends here. Abraham has watched a star, then the moon, then the sun, each time calling it his lord and then withdrawing when it set. Early scholars differ over whether he was reasoning his own way towards God or arguing with his people by adopting their premise and following it to collapse. Either way the conclusion is not that the sun is small, but that whatever sets cannot be what he is looking for.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The surah is largely an argument with people who worshipped God alongside other powers. Abraham is brought in as the ancestor they claimed. Early scholars note the strategic point. Mecca traced its line and its sanctuary back to him, and here he is shown rejecting the very arrangement his descendants had settled into. No particular occasion is reported for the passage.

keyTerms.note: A word for something bursting into view, used of dawn and of blood from a wound. It gives the sun's appearance a suddenness that makes its later setting all the more pointed.
A legal term for being clear of a liability or a charge. Using it here makes the break formal rather than emotional, the way a man publicly renounces a debt he will not carry.
One who turns from the surrounding practice towards what is upright. The Quran uses it repeatedly of Abraham, and it describes a direction taken rather than a doctrine held.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Star religion was familiar across Arabia and nearby lands. Some tribes were linked with certain heavenly bodies. Caravans steered by the same stars they called on. Anyone travelling at night knew the order of risings and settings by heart. Abraham's argument works because his hearers were expert watchers. They knew better than anyone that everything in that sky goes down.
studies.didYouKnow: The passage is one of very few places in the Quran that lays out a line of reasoning step by step. The conclusion is reached at the end rather than announced at the start. The classical scholars disagree about what it records. Some read it as Abraham's own search, others as a method of debate. Major authorities have held both readings.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The test applied is disappearance. Whatever cannot stay is ruled out. That test is open to anyone with patience and a horizon. It needs no text and no teacher. The passage also models a public break with inherited practice, which is costly in any society built on lineage. The declaration at the end is about direction, a face turned, rather than about agreeing to a statement.

crossReferences.why: Gives the earlier steps of the same sequence, the star and then the moon.
Tells the other Abraham story, the broken idols and the question put to his people.
Shows him arguing about a lord who gives life, with the sun brought into it again.

studies.applyIt: Take something you rely on for a sense of stability: a job, one person's approval, a number in an account. Ask what happens to your footing if it goes, and answer honestly rather than bravely. Abraham's test was not contempt for what he was watching. It was noticing what those things do at the end of the day.
studies.explainEasier: Abraham watched a star, then the moon, then the sun. Each one rose and then went down again. So he told his people that none of them could be his lord. He turned instead to the one who made the sky and the earth.

studies.title: My Lord Encompasses All Things
studies.meaning: The argument is answered rather than continued. He asks why they dispute with him about God when he has been guided, which relocates the disagreement: he is not offering a theory to be weighed against theirs. Then the threat behind their argument is addressed. He does not fear what they associate, and the only exception is what his Lord wills, so even his safety is not claimed as his own. The reason follows: his Lord's knowledge takes in everything.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The exchange fits a pressure the early community knew well. Warnings that abandoned gods would take revenge were part of how households kept members in line. The sources describe converts being told they would be struck with illness or bad luck. Abraham's answer here meets that argument rather than an intellectual one, which is why it turns on fear.

keyTerms.note: From the root for a proof or argument, in a form meaning to trade arguments back and forth. It names the activity rather than the content, which is what he is declining to continue.
A verb for containing something with room to spare, used of a vessel large enough for what is poured in. Applied to knowledge, it says nothing overflows or falls outside.
A form of remembering that means retrieving what is already held rather than learning something new. The question assumes his listeners possess what they need and are not consulting it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Fear of an offended local god was practical, not abstract. A tribe blamed a drought, a stillbirth or a lost caravan on a shrine neglected or an oath broken. That thinking drove real choices about where to travel and what to sacrifice. Telling a family you had left their god was, to them, news that you had put the household in danger.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb used here for encompassing gives the name of the widest ayah in the Quran. That is the one about the seat that extends over the heavens and the earth. The same root gives the Arabic word for spaciousness and for being at ease. So knowledge and roominess share one set of letters.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Two things are held together that come apart easily. He denies fearing what they worship, and at once adds a condition, so that even his fearlessness is not his own. Nothing is claimed for himself. The passage also treats guidance as a change in standing rather than in opinion. That is why a debate is no longer the right shape for the talk. He is not defending a position. He is reporting one he was given.

crossReferences.why: Records another dispute with Abraham about his Lord, and how the argument was closed.
Puts the same challenge to his people about worshipping what neither benefits nor harms them.
Uses nearly identical wording about a Lord whose knowledge encompasses everything there is.

studies.applyIt: Notice an argument you keep re-entering with someone who has no intention of moving. Ask what you are actually defending, and whether continuing serves it. You can leave a dispute without leaving the person or the position. This ayah's speaker states his ground, gives his reason, asks one question, and stops there.
studies.explainEasier: His people argued with him about God. He asked why, when God had already guided him. He said he is not afraid of the things they worship. His Lord knows everything there is.

studies.title: Which Side Deserves Security
studies.meaning: The argument is turned around. Abraham is being threatened with the anger of the gods. He answers by asking who should be afraid of whom. His opponents had attached partners to God with no warrant sent down for it. The question about which party has more right to safety is left for them to answer. The next verse supplies it. The condition attached, faith not clouded by wrongdoing, is what early scholars discuss most.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, continuing Abraham's dispute with his people right after he disowned what they worshipped. The surah around it applies the exchange to its own audience. They had warned the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) that their gods might strike him. Classical sources keep reports of early listeners troubled by the second verse. They took the word for wrongdoing in its widest sense.

keyTerms.note: A word for a sanction or proof that gives someone the right to act, and later for a ruler. Its use here demands documentation: the practice is challenged for having nothing issued behind it.
From the same root as faith and trust. The word for being safe and the word for believing come from one source, which is why the verse can move between them without changing subject.
A verb for clothing something or covering it over, used of confusing truth with falsehood. Faith is pictured as a garment that can be worn with something else layered on top of it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Fear of offending a tribal god was practical, not theoretical. Shrines were credited with causing illness, drought or a failed journey when slighted. People arranged their travel and their oaths around that. Threatening someone with a god's displeasure was a real threat in that world. Abraham's reply does not deny that the fear is reasonable. It asks which of the two positions is actually exposed.
studies.didYouKnow: The word used for security shares its root with the word for faith. The two stand in the same sentence at the close of the passage. Arabic lets the verse make its point through sound as well as sense. A listener hears the link between believing and being safe before the argument has been spelled out.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Safety is presented as a result of what is true. It is not a result of what is powerful. The question about which party has more right to it assumes that security follows accuracy. A person lined up with reality stands differently from one who is not. That holds whoever happens to be frightened at the moment. The qualifying clause then keeps this from turning smug. Faith is described as something that can be clouded over.

crossReferences.why: Names associating partners with God as a great wrong, the reading given to this passage.
Precedes the argument, where his people dispute with him and he refuses to fear.
Describes God as the ally of believers, bringing them out of darkness into light.

studies.applyIt: Name one thing you are quietly afraid of that has been shaping your decisions this month. Then ask Abraham's question about it: what is it actually able to do, and on what authority. You are not talking yourself out of the fear. You are checking whether it has the standing you have been giving it.
studies.explainEasier: Abraham asks his people why he should fear their gods, when they are not afraid of setting up gods beside God with no proof at all. He asks which side is really safe. The answer is those who believe and do no wrong.

studies.title: That Was Our Argument
studies.meaning: The whole sequence is named and attributed. The reasoning Abraham used was given to him. Early scholars take that as covering the seeing described earlier and the words he spoke. Then a general statement widens it: God raises in degrees whom He wills. The two names that close the ayah keep the raising from looking arbitrary, since it is done by one who is wise and informed. What looked like a private intellectual achievement is reassigned without being diminished.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. It closes the Abraham sequence, before the surah turns to the line of prophets who followed him. The story has been answering people who argued that their inherited religion needed no defence. This closing ayah speaks to the listeners directly by shifting to your Lord. That pulls the argument out of the past and lays it in front of the audience.

keyTerms.note: A word for a decisive case in a dispute, the kind that ends it. Its assignment to God rather than to Abraham is the point of the sentence, since the reasoning was received and not devised.
Steps of a stair, used for gradations of standing. The plural and its indefinite form leave both the number and the measure unspecified, so no scale of ranking is offered to the reader.

From a root for restraining and for sound judgement, the same one that gives the word for a bridle. Wisdom in Arabic includes holding back, which is why it pairs naturally with knowledge of everything.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Skill in argument was prized and taught. A man who could carry a case before an assembly protected his family's interests. The language of proof and reply was familiar to anyone who had watched a dispute settled in public. Handing a winning argument to someone else was unusual there. A good case was a personal credit, like a good poem.
studies.didYouKnow: The clause about raising in degrees appears elsewhere in the Quran, tied there to knowledge. That passage adds that above everyone with knowledge is one who knows more. So the same phrase serves twice. Once for a prophet's reasoning, and once for the ordinary ranks of learning.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Insight is presented as given rather than achieved, which unsettles a natural pride. The sequence with the star, moon and sun reads like a mind working. This ayah says the working itself was a gift. That does not make the effort unreal. It changes what a person can take credit for. The closing names guard the change from turning arbitrary, since raising is done knowingly and with judgement, not by preference.

crossReferences.why: Repeats the clause about raising in degrees and adds that every knower has one above him.
States the same thing plainly, that Abraham's soundness of judgement was given to him beforehand.
Applies the raising in degrees to believers and to those who have been given knowledge.

studies.applyIt: Think of a good idea you had recently and try to trace where it actually came from: a conversation, a book, a mood, a night's sleep. You will not find a clean origin. Sitting with that for a minute is the exercise this ayah proposes, and it makes the credit harder to hold and easier to carry.
studies.explainEasier: That whole argument was given to Abraham by God. It was not something he worked out on his own. God lifts whoever he wants to a higher place. Your Lord is wise and knows everything.

studies.title: Each Of Them We Guided
studies.meaning: A list begins, and its order is not by date. Isaac and Jacob are given first as a gift to Abraham. Then Noah is mentioned as earlier, and then a run of names described as from his descendants. Early scholars discuss whether the pronoun refers to Abraham or to Noah, and both readings are old and defensible. The refrain does the work: each of them We guided. It is repeated so that the achievement in every case is attributed the same way, and the closing line names them as those who do good.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. It follows the Abraham sequence, and it speaks to a city that valued lineage above almost everything. Mecca's leading families traced descent from Abraham through Ishmael and used it as a claim to standing. The list here runs through the same ancestry and measures it by guidance rather than by blood. That quietly changes what an inheritance is.

keyTerms.note: A verb for giving without payment or return, the root behind the Arabic for a gift. It is used through the Quran for children in particular, which places offspring outside anything earned.
A collective noun for what issues from someone, connected by the lexicographers to scattering seed. It covers a line rather than a generation, which is what lets one word carry the whole list.
From a root for beauty and excellence, so the word means doing something well rather than merely doing it. Naming the prophets by this term measures them by quality of action, not by rank.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Genealogy was the memory system of Arabia. Men could recite ancestry back many generations, and disputes over precedence were settled by who could name a longer or better line. Poets were paid to preserve it. A list of names carrying weight was therefore a familiar genre to this audience, and they would have heard this one as a claim about who the real ancestors are.
studies.didYouKnow: This ayah and the two after it name seventeen prophets in one unbroken run. It is the longest such list anywhere in the Quran. The order follows neither the dates nor the alphabet. Classical scholars noted that it groups figures by kinship and by kind. Relatives are placed beside one another rather than in order of century.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Guidance is stated as the one thing shared across an enormously varied set of lives. The list includes a king, a fugitive, a prisoner and a man who preached for centuries. Nothing else in it is shared. That makes the repeated refrain the actual claim of the passage. What these people had in common was not their circumstances or their success. It was the same thing being given to each of them.

crossReferences.why: Describes the same gift to Abraham of Isaac and, in addition, Jacob, each made upright.
Places prophethood and the Book within his descendants, which is what this list then traces.
Gives a parallel list of those to whom revelation was sent, overlapping with this one substantially.

studies.applyIt: Pick one of the names in this list you know least about and read a short account of that prophet this week. Most readers have three or four they know well and the rest as names. Filling in one changes how the list reads, because it stops being a recitation and starts being people whose lives went differently.
studies.explainEasier: God gave Abraham Isaac and Jacob, and guided them both. He had guided Noah before that. From the same line came David, Solomon, Job, Joseph, Moses and Aaron. That is how God rewards people who do good.

studies.title: Their Fathers And Their Brothers
studies.meaning: The list continues. Then, in the final ayah, it opens outward in three directions at once: their ancestors, their descendants, and their brothers. Early scholars note that this closing phrase deliberately refuses to draw a line around the group. Not every relative is included, since the word used means some of them, and not only sons are named. The passage ends with two verbs, chosen and guided, which describe what was done rather than who deserved it.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and part of the longest run of prophetic names in the Quran. The audience included people from the scriptural communities of the region as well as Meccans. Several of these names belonged to traditions the Meccans knew only at second hand. Naming them together in one breath makes a claim. There is a single line of guidance behind traditions the region had come to treat as separate.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to be fit or in good working order, used of a repaired wall or a workable arrangement. Uprightness in Arabic is soundness rather than sanctity, which keeps the word ordinary.

An intensive verb from the root for surplus and what remains over. Favour here is described as something extra given rather than a merit recognised, which fits a passage where everything is attributed.
A verb for gathering something up and selecting it out, used of collecting the best of a crop. It implies picking from among many rather than finding the only candidate available.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabian families were wide and layered. Brothers, half-brothers, cousins raised as siblings, and adopted members who took the family name. A household had one shared identity. Honour or shame travelled through all of it. Against that background, saying that only some of the fathers, descendants and brothers were chosen is a strange claim. In that world, a family line carried the whole family together.
studies.didYouKnow: The list places related figures side by side rather than following the centuries. Moses and Aaron close the previous ayah as brothers. This one opens with Zechariah followed at once by John, a father and his son. The final ayah then makes the rule plain, by naming ancestors, descendants and brothers together.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage separates family line from selection while running them along the same lines. Prophethood is given inside families again and again, and it is never given to a family as such. That distinction protects two things at once. Inherited faith is real, and the Quran treats it as a genuine advantage. It also confers nothing by itself. Being related to guidance is not the same as receiving it.

crossReferences.why: Names families chosen above the worlds, describing them as descendants issuing one from another.
Gathers many of these same figures as those God favoured, from several distinct lines of descent.
States that prophethood was placed in the descendants of Noah and Abraham, with mixed results.

studies.applyIt: Think of the faith you inherited from your family and name one thing in it that came to you already made, that you have never had to build. It might be a habit of prayer or simply the assumption that God is there. Say what it is, and thank whoever passed it down, aloud if they are still reachable.
studies.explainEasier: The list goes on. Zechariah, John, Jesus and Elias. Then Ishmael, Elijah, Jonah and Lot. God chose them and set them above everyone else. He chose some of their fathers, children and brothers too, and led them on a straight road.

studies.title: Such Is God's Guidance
studies.meaning: The long list is summarised in three words and then given a condition. All of that was God's guidance, given to whom He wills among His servants, and the second half states what would have undone it. Had even these figures associated others with God, their work would have collapsed. Early scholars note the force of applying that clause to prophets. The point is not a warning aimed at them but a statement that nothing in the list was secured by the standing of the people in it.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, closing a passage that ran through the whole prophetic line. The Meccans accepted a supreme God and added others alongside Him. The surah has been arguing that the addition is not a small adjustment. This ayah sits at the end of the list. That applies the argument at its strongest point, to the very figures both sides respected.

keyTerms.note: A vivid verb, used of an animal that eats bad pasture and swells before dying. Work that comes to nothing is pictured as something that looks full and then fails, rather than something small.
The same word this surah uses of all humanity. Its use here, in a sentence about prophets, quietly keeps them inside the general category rather than raising them out of it.

The verb of willing, left unqualified. The Quran uses it in this construction without stating a criterion, and mainstream commentators read the silence as deliberate rather than as an absence of explanation.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Grazing was a constant calculation. A herd moved onto rich ground could bloat and die, and the swelling looked at first like the animal thriving. Herdsmen knew the sign and dreaded it, since the loss came exactly when the beast appeared at its best. The verb in this ayah carries that picture, and the audience would have heard it before hearing anything abstract.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb used for deeds coming to nothing appears more than a dozen times in the Quran. It is almost always built the same way, about work made void. Its plain sense, kept in the classical dictionaries, is a beast swelling from bad pasture. That gives the moral word a physical picture: ruin dressed up as plenty.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Everything the passage has described is placed under one condition, and the condition is applied to the highest possible subjects. Nothing builds up a standing that could survive it. That is the surah's central argument at its sharpest. Setting others beside God is not one fault among others. It is the thing that empties the rest. It also explains why a book so patient about most failings returns to this one so often.

crossReferences.why: States the same condition directly to a messenger, that association would render his work worthless.
Describes what this guidance does, leading those who follow it out of darkness into light.
Shows deeds coming to nothing on the same principle, so that no weight is given them at the reckoning.

studies.applyIt: Look at one good thing you do regularly and ask honestly what else is mixed into it: a reputation, a habit of being seen doing it, an obligation to someone watching. You are not obliged to purify it in an afternoon. Just find the mixture and know it is there. This ayah says the mixture is what matters most.
studies.explainEasier: That is God's guidance, and he gives it to whoever he wants. Even these prophets were under the same rule. If they had set anything beside God, everything they did would have come to nothing.

studies.title: Entrusted To Another People
studies.meaning: Three things are said to have been given: the Book, sound judgement, and prophethood. Then the conditional arrives, and it is not a threat but an observation about how this has always worked. If the people in front of you reject these, they have already been entrusted to others who do not. Early scholars note that the sentence is in the past tense, so the alternative is not a plan held in reserve. It has been done already.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The rejection in view is the immediate one, from a city that had heard the recitation for years. The classical scholars differ over who exactly is meant by the people entrusted. Some read it of the emigrants and helpers who would form the community. Others read it more broadly, of anyone who receives it in any generation. The reading is left open.

keyTerms.note: From the root for restraining and deciding, covering wisdom in judging a matter. Placed between scripture and prophethood, it names the capacity to apply a text rather than merely to receive it.
From the root for an agent given responsibility for another's affairs, used earlier in this surah when the Prophet is told he is not such an agent over anyone.
A demonstrative for people present and close at hand. Its use makes the sentence concrete: the rejection being discussed belongs to the room, not to a category of humanity.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Trades and offices passed within families, and they could be lost. One clan held the keys to the sanctuary. Another held the right to water the pilgrims. These jobs were inherited, argued over, and now and then moved on when a line failed or fell out of favour. Everyone knew that such a charge could pass to another house. The ayah uses that familiar machinery for something much larger.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb for entrusting in this ayah comes from the same root as a word used a few pages earlier. There the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) is told he is not a keeper over his people. So the same letters mark two things. The duty he is released from, and the duty given to those who receive the message.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Revelation is described as never being at risk. Only its keepers are. That moves the worry somewhere else. The question is not whether the message survives but who is carrying it, and the answer to that has changed before and can change again. The passage also gives an odd comfort to a small, pressured community. The succession does not depend on the people who currently hold the standing.

crossReferences.why: Names the same three gifts, the Book, judgement and prophethood, given to an earlier community.
States the replacement principle plainly: turn away and others will be brought who are not like you.
Describes a people God will bring in place of those who turn back, loved by Him and loving Him.

studies.applyIt: Think of something valuable you are the current holder of: a family practice, a piece of knowledge, a role in a community. Ask who you are handing it to and whether you have started. Nothing in this ayah is about loss of the thing itself. It is about who ends up carrying it, and that is decided by whoever bothers.
studies.explainEasier: Those are the people God gave the Book, good judgement and prophethood. The people here may turn all that down. If so, it has already been put in the care of others. Those others will not turn it down.

studies.title: I Ask You No Reward
studies.meaning: The instruction is to follow their guidance, and early scholars are careful about what that means. It is not to copy the particular laws given to earlier communities. It is to take the same path they were on, since the ayah has just described that path as one thing. Then the address turns to the audience with a denial about payment. Nothing is being charged for this. The final clause states what it is instead: a reminder, offered to everyone, with no deal attached.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The denial answers a live suspicion. Religious jobs in the city brought in money, from care of the sanctuary to fees for fortune-telling. A new claim about God was naturally read as a bid for a share. Several Meccan surahs record the same denial in almost the same words. So the suspicion kept coming back rather than arising once.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning a model or standard, in a form that means taking someone as a pattern. The final letter is a rare orthographic feature that most reciters preserve, marking the word as a stopping point.
The ordinary word for pay owed for work done, used of a hired labourer. Its plain commercial sense is what makes the denial concrete rather than pious.
Not new information but the retrieval of something already known. Describing the whole message this way limits the claim: what is offered is recollection rather than a novelty being sold.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Mecca's religious trade was out in the open. Water rights for pilgrims, care of the sanctuary, and the fairs around it brought income and status to certain families. Poets and diviners were paid for their work. Anyone speaking about the gods in that city was assumed to be angling for a share. That is the assumption this ayah steps around by naming it.
studies.didYouKnow: The denial of asking for payment runs through the Quran in the mouths of many messengers. It appears in earlier stories too, always in similar words. In one surah alone it is repeated five times by five different figures. That steadiness makes taking no money a feature of the office rather than a personal virtue.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Removing payment removes a motive. The passage offers that as evidence rather than as a claim to virtue. If nothing is being collected, the usual account of why someone keeps going is not available. Calling the whole message a reminder makes a further point about its content. It claims to recover something people already have, not to introduce a system. That is why it can be offered to everyone without adjustment.

crossReferences.why: Repeats the same two clauses almost word for word: no payment asked, and only a reminder to the worlds.
Gives the one exception ever named: that whoever wishes may take a way toward his Lord.
Puts the identical disclaimer in the mouth of an earlier messenger addressing his own people.

studies.applyIt: Pick something you do for others and check what you are quietly collecting for it: thanks, a reputation, the sense of being the reliable one. Do the same thing this week without any of it reaching you, if you can arrange that. Notice whether you still want to do it. That is the whole experiment this ayah suggests.
studies.explainEasier: Those are the people God guided, so follow the way they took. The Prophet asks for no pay for any of this. It is only a reminder for everyone.

studies.title: They Did Not Value God
studies.meaning: The charge is stated as a failure of estimation rather than of belief. Saying that God has revealed nothing to any human being is treated as underrating Him, since it denies Him the ability to speak. The answer is a question with a fact inside it: who sent the Book Moses brought, described as light and guidance. Then the handling of that Book is described, put onto sheets, some shown and much concealed. The instruction that closes it is to say the answer and walk away.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The classical scholars differ over who is being addressed in the middle of the ayah. Some read the whole ayah as aimed at Meccans who denied revelation outright. Others read it as turning to those who held the earlier scripture and handled it selectively. The shift between plural addressees in the Arabic is what produces the disagreement. The tradition records both readings.

keyTerms.note: A verb for assessing size or worth, used of weighing a load or judging a distance. The failing named is therefore a mismeasurement rather than a denial, which is a subtler and more common error.
The plural of the word used earlier in this surah for a writing sheet, and its only other occurrence in the Quran. Both appearances fall within these ninety ayat.
The noun from the verb for walking into water of unknown depth, used a few ayat earlier in this surah for careless talk about God's signs. Its return here closes a loop.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Scripture in that region existed as scrolls, kept by communities who could read them. Access ran through the few people able to do so. A text was read aloud to a gathering by someone who chose the passage. That was normal, and it gave real power to the reader. What was not read aloud did not exist for the people listening.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase about not valuing God as He deserves appears three times in the Quran, always in this exact form. Each time it introduces a different failure of judgement. Here it is the denial that God speaks to human beings. Elsewhere it comes before descriptions of His power over creation on the day of resurrection.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Denying revelation is treated as a claim about God, not as caution about what people claim. To say that nothing has ever been sent down is to describe a God who does not speak. The ayah says that this is a shrunken picture. The mention of Moses then does the work of the argument. The Book he brought was acknowledged across the region, and its existence answers the general denial without any appeal to the present case.

crossReferences.why: Uses the identical phrase about not appraising God with the appraisal He is due.
Describes the same Book brought by Moses in the same terms, containing guidance and light.
Names the covenant to make scripture clear to people and not to conceal any part of it.

studies.applyIt: Ask whether your working picture of God includes His speaking to people. Many of us hold the idea of a maker easily and the idea of being spoken to awkwardly. Read one page of the Quran today as something said rather than something written, aloud if you can. The difference is not soft. It is what this ayah says was being underrated.
studies.explainEasier: They did not think of God highly enough. They said God never sent anything down to any person. But God sent the Book that Moses brought, and it was light and guidance for people.

studies.title: The Mother Of Cities
studies.meaning: Four things are said about this Book in one sentence. It was sent down. It is blessed. It confirms what came before it. And it has a purpose: to warn a particular city and what surrounds it. Early scholars identify the Mother of Cities as Mecca, and they discuss how far the surrounding area extends. Answers range from the nearby settlements to the whole earth. The last clause names who responds, and it links belief in the hereafter to a habit rather than to an opinion.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and the phrase naming the city belongs to that setting. The surah addresses the place where it was being recited. The word for confirming what came before assumes an audience aware of earlier scripture. The Meccans were, through trade and through the communities on their routes. No occasion is reported for this ayah in the classical sources.

keyTerms.note: From a root for a camel kneeling and settling, giving the idea of good that stays in place. Blessing in Arabic is abundance that has come to rest rather than a burst of it.
A phrase for the settlement from which others derive, the way a mother is the origin of a family. It names Mecca by function rather than by size, since it was not large.

An intensive form of the verb for preserving, the same root that gives the word for the guardians mentioned earlier in this surah. Applied to prayer, it means keeping something rather than performing it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Mecca was small, dry and poor as farmland. It mattered because of the sanctuary and the trade routes that met there. Settlements around it lived off the pilgrimage season and the caravans the city organised. Calling it the mother of cities described a real dependence that the region knew about. It had nothing to do with the size of the place or its wealth.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase naming the city appears only twice in the Quran, here and in a later Meccan surah. Both times it sits in a sentence about warning. The other passage adds that the Quran was revealed in Arabic for that purpose. The classical commentaries read the two together as a pair.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The Book is described as continuous with what came before it, not as a replacement. That shapes how the earlier scriptures are to be regarded. The final clause makes a quieter point. Belief in the hereafter is tied to guarding the prayer. So a conviction about what comes later shows up as a practice now, and the passage treats the practice as the visible form of the belief rather than as its result.

crossReferences.why: Names the same city and the same purpose, warning it and those around it, in an Arabic recitation.
Describes the revelation with the same word for blessed, and asks whether they will deny it.
States the confirming relationship at length, as a criterion over the scriptures that came before.

studies.applyIt: Notice whether your prayers are things you perform or things you keep. The verb in this ayah is about guarding something, the way you guard an appointment you would not miss. Pick the prayer most likely to slip this week and protect it in advance, by deciding now where you will be and what will be paused.
studies.explainEasier: This Book was sent down too, and it is blessed. It agrees with the books that came before it. It is there to warn the Mother of Cities and the places around it. People who believe in the next life believe in it and keep up their prayers.

studies.title: In The Floods Of Death
studies.meaning: The question about who does greater wrong returns, now with three specific answers. Inventing against God. Claiming revelation that never came. Offering to produce something like what God sent down. Early scholars connect these clauses to men who made such claims in that period, and their identifications differ. Then the scene shifts abruptly to a deathbed. Angels reach out and command the soul to be given up, and the reason is stated in the same breath: what was said about God, and pride before His signs.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, in a passage about who may speak for God. The claim to produce something comparable was made publicly in the city. The Quran elsewhere records the challenge to attempt it. The classical sources name different individuals behind the middle clauses and do not agree. So the ayah is best read as describing a kind of claim rather than a single person.

keyTerms.note: Water deep enough to cover a person entirely, from a root for submerging. Death is described as a rising level rather than a blow, which matches how dying is usually experienced from inside.
The participle for spreading something open, used of an outstretched hand. Arabic uses the same gesture for giving and for taking, so the image is direct without being explained.
From a root for being light in weight and therefore of little account. The punishment is named by the loss of standing rather than by pain, which answers the pride mentioned at the end.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Drowning was the particular terror of a people who mostly could not swim and who crossed the Red Sea for trade. Flash floods in the valleys were more familiar still. A dry valley bed could fill in minutes after rain somewhere out of sight. People camped in them died without warning. The word used here for death belongs to that experience of water arriving and rising.
studies.didYouKnow: The opening question of this ayah, asking who does greater wrong, is the same one that opens an earlier ayah in this surah. The surah uses it more than once. Reading the two together shows the second expanding the first. One clause about inventing against God becomes three distinct claims about speaking in His name.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Speaking falsely for God is placed at the far end of wrongdoing. The reason given at the end of the ayah pairs it with pride before the signs. The two belong together. Claiming to speak for God and refusing what He has said are both ways of putting the self where revelation should be. The scene at death then removes the chance of going on, which is what makes it the natural end of the passage.

crossReferences.why: Opens with the identical question earlier in this surah, with one clause where this has three.
Gives a parallel scene of angels taking souls, described from outside rather than through the dying.
Records the answer to the third claim: an invitation to produce a single comparable chapter.

studies.applyIt: Notice how often you attach God's name to your own preferences in conversation, in phrases that make a personal view sound settled. Everybody does it and mostly without noticing. Once today, catch yourself before the phrase and say the opinion as your own instead. It is a small correction, and this ayah is about the direction it points in.
studies.explainEasier: The worst wrong is lying about God. Or saying a revelation came to you when none did. Or offering to make something like what God sent. At death the angels reach out and tell such people to hand over their souls.

studies.title: You Have Come Alone
studies.meaning: Three things are named as absent. The company is gone, since each arrives singly as they were first created. The possessions are gone, described as left behind the back, which early scholars note is the position of something you are walking away from rather than something taken. And the intercessors are gone, along with the claim that they had a share in you. The last clause states the result as a cutting: whatever ran between you has been severed.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The society it addresses was organised entirely around belonging. A person in Arabia was a member before being an individual, protected by a clan and known by a family line. Wealth was held and shown off together. Describing arrival as singular removed every structure the audience relied on for identity. That, rather than any description of punishment, is what gives the scene its force.

keyTerms.note: A plural formed from the word for one, so the Arabic says many people each alone. It describes a crowd of individuals rather than solitude, which is a more precise and stranger picture.
An intensive verb for granting property and dependants into someone's charge. The root is connected to livestock and management, so what is given is described as placed in one's keeping.
An intensive form of cutting, suggesting something broken apart at many points rather than divided once. Applied to the link between people and what they relied on, it names a thorough separation.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A Meccan's standing could be counted: camels, dependants, clients, sons. These were shown off at gatherings and recited in poetry. A man who lost ground in any of them lost ground everywhere. Even a burial was shared, in the ground of a family.
