The picture of arriving with none of it, in the state of a newborn, cut across every way the audience had of describing a person.
studies.didYouKnow: The word used here for people arriving one by one is a plural built on the singular for one. Arabic uses that construction sparingly. It occurs twice in the Quran. The other place is an instruction to stand for God in pairs and singly. So the same rare form describes both a discipline and a destination.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage strips a person down to what cannot be handed on, and says that this is what arrives. Property was given and remains given. The wording never denies that it was real. What it denies is that any of it belongs to the person in the sense they assumed. And by naming the intercessors as absent, the ayah closes the surah's long argument about go-betweens with a picture rather than another statement.

crossReferences.why: Uses almost identical words about coming as you were first created, against a claim of an appointment.
States the same singularity: every one of them will come to Him on that day alone.
Names what will not help on that day, neither wealth nor sons, leaving only a sound heart.

studies.applyIt: Look around the room you are in and pick the three things you would find hardest to lose. Not people, objects. Say what each one does for you, in a sentence. The ayah describes them being left behind the back rather than confiscated, which is a gentler picture and a more accurate one. Knowing what they carry makes them lighter.
studies.explainEasier: You come back to God one by one, the way you were first made. Everything you were given is left behind. The ones you said would speak for you are not there. Whatever tied you to them is cut.

studies.title: Who Splits The Seed
studies.meaning: The picture is agricultural and very small. God is the one who splits the grain and the date stone, which is the moment nobody watches, underground, when a hard closed thing opens. Two reversals follow, the living drawn out of the dead and the dead out of the living, and early scholars read these both literally, of seed and egg and corpse, and more broadly. The closing question is not rhetorical decoration. It asks how a person turns away after that.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and the beginning of a long run of ayat about the natural world that follows the surah's argument with the deniers. The audience farmed at the oases and lived on dates and grain brought in by caravan. The passage does not argue from anything remote. It starts with the two things most likely to be in a Meccan storeroom.

keyTerms.note: An active participle for splitting something open lengthwise. It is used again in the next ayah for the dawn, so the same action covers a seed cracking and the horizon opening at first light.
The collective noun for cereal grains, the staple of the diet. Pairing it with the date stone covers the two crops the region depended on, one imported by caravan and one grown at the oases.
A passive verb for being diverted from a direction, used of something overturned. The passive form is notable: the question asks what is turning them, not simply why they turn.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Date stones were everywhere. They were fed to camels, burned as fuel, and pressed into the ground to grow new palms, and a farmer knew that a stone had to be kept damp for weeks before anything happened. Nothing about the process was visible while it worked. The ayah picks the least dramatic event in the agricultural year and makes it the evidence.
studies.didYouKnow: The word used here for splitting appears again as the first word of the very next ayah, applied to daybreak. The repeat links the smallest scale in the passage to the largest, with no connecting phrase. Arabic allows that compression, and English translations usually have to spell it out.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The argument moves through the ordinary, not the rare. That is typical of this surah after its long dispute about miracles. Nothing here breaks the usual order. It is the usual order, set down exactly. The two reversals also answer the question of rising again, sideways. Bringing life out of what is dead is already happening in every field. It runs on a timetable everybody plans their year around.

crossReferences.why: States the same two reversals in a prayer, bringing the living from the dead and the reverse.
Puts the identical question to the same audience: who is it that brings the living out of the dead?
Offers dead ground revived and grain brought out of it as a sign, using the same argument.

studies.applyIt: Put a few seeds in damp cotton wool on a windowsill this week, or a date stone in a pot of soil. Look at it once a day. Nothing will happen for a while and then something will. The ayah rests its case on that specific event, and most adults have not actually watched it since childhood.
studies.explainEasier: God splits the seed and the date stone so they grow. He brings living things out of dead ones, and dead ones out of living. That is God, and still people turn away.

studies.title: He Splits The Dawn
studies.meaning: Three things are named in one line, and each is given a purpose. Daybreak is described with the verb used a moment earlier for a seed, so first light is an opening rather than an arrival. Night is made for rest, using a word connected to dwelling and tranquillity. The sun and moon are set for calculation, which is the most practical claim in the ayah. Two names close it, and the tradition reads them as pairing power with the precision that makes such an arrangement work.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, continuing a sequence of signs drawn from the natural world. The audience navigated, dated debts, timed pilgrimages and planned caravans by the sun and moon, and did so with real skill. The ayah does not tell them anything they did not know about the sky. It renames what they already used as something arranged deliberately for their use.

keyTerms.note: A verbal noun for the coming of morning rather than the word for morning itself. It names the transition, the process of becoming light, which is what the verb for splitting is applied to.
From the root that produced the verb used earlier in this surah for whatever comes to rest in night and day. Night is not merely dark here; it is described as a dwelling place.
A noun from the root for counting and accounting. Applying it to the sun and moon makes their motion a measuring instrument, and the same root gives the word for the final reckoning.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arab timekeeping ran by the moon, and it was exact enough to run a trading economy. Debts fell due at named moons. The sacred months when fighting stopped were fixed by the calendar. The two great caravans left at set seasons. Nobody carried a device. The whole system depended on people looking up, which is why calling the sun and moon a means of reckoning described something that worked.
studies.didYouKnow: The root behind the word for reckoning in this ayah also gives the Arabic for arithmetic. It gives the word for the account rendered on the day of judgement too. So the same three letters cover the motion of the sun, the sum a merchant does, and the final accounting. The Quran uses that link more than once.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage gives a purpose to things that would otherwise be bare patterns. The purposes named are human ones: rest and measuring. That says something specific about how the cosmos and the people in it stand to each other. The two closing names guard the arrangement from seeming cold. A system that exact is credited to one described as both irresistible and knowing.

crossReferences.why: Spells out the same purpose, that you may know the count of years and the reckoning by them.
States the sun and moon running by exact calculation, in a surah listing what has been given.
Makes night and day two signs, one erased and one made visible, for the same practical ends.

studies.applyIt: Get up once this week in time to watch the sky change before sunrise, and stay with it from grey to colour. It takes about twenty minutes. The ayah calls this a splitting, and the word only makes sense if you have seen the whole process rather than the finished result on your way somewhere.
studies.explainEasier: God splits open the dawn. He made the night for rest, and the sun and the moon for counting time. That is how he set it up, and he is mighty and knows all.

studies.title: Guided By The Stars
studies.meaning: The stars are given one purpose here, and it is practical. You find your way by them in the darknesses of land and sea. The plural for darkness comes back from earlier in the surah. So does the pairing of land and sea. Early scholars note how modest the claim is. Nothing is said about the stars' influence or their meaning. That was the common assumption across the region. Here they are simply markers. The ayah then closes by naming who reads a sign like this.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and part of a run of ayat about the natural world. It speaks to people who knew the sky as part of their work. Star religion existed across the ancient Near East, and it had left traces in Arabian practice. The passage about Abraham earlier in this surah takes it on directly. Here the stars are given a use rather than a status. That move is itself the argument.

keyTerms.note: The plural of a word whose root means to appear or rise. The same root gives the verb for something occurring in due course, so a star is named by its arrival on schedule rather than by its brightness.

keyTerms.gloss: that you may find your way
keyTerms.note: The same verb used through the Quran for being rightly guided. Applying it to navigation lets the physical and the moral senses stand in one sentence without a comparison being made explicit.

keyTerms.gloss: We have set out in detail
keyTerms.note: An intensive verb for separating something into distinct parts, used of jointing a carcass. It describes explanation as taking a whole apart so the pieces can be seen individually.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Desert guides were specialists. They were hired for their memory of stars and ground, and a good one cost a lot. In summer they travelled at night to dodge the heat. They steered by certain stars whose seasonal places they had learned as boys. A caravan's survival rested on one man's recall of the sky. This ayah describes how they worked, and it names where the method came from.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb for being guided here is the ordinary word for finding a road. The Quran uses that same root for guidance in every religious sense. Arabic keeps no separate words for the two. So every mention of the straight path carries a traveller's meaning underneath it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The stars are cut down and honoured in one breath. They are not powers to ask about a marriage or a journey's luck, which was the practice of the region. They are placed there on purpose for people who need to get somewhere. That pairing is the surah's method throughout. Nature is emptied of rival authority and filled with intent. The closing phrase ties the reading of such a sign to knowledge.

crossReferences.why: States the same use in fewer words, landmarks on the ground and stars by which people are guided.
Uses the same phrase for the darknesses of land and sea, there as the place where people call out.
Describes the lamps set in the nearest sky, giving them a different assignment in the same register.

studies.applyIt: Go outside tonight and find one star or planet you can pick out. Learn its name if you do not know it. Then find it again tomorrow. Two nights is enough to see that it has moved. It is also enough to feel why someone would trust it to point out north. That familiarity is what this ayah assumes.
studies.explainEasier: God made the stars so people can find their way in the dark, on land and at sea. The signs are made clear like this for people who know how to read them.

studies.title: From A Single Soul
studies.meaning: Humanity is traced back to one origin. Then come two words that early scholars have read in several ways. One means a place of settling. The other means a place of deposit. The readings offered include the womb and the loins, the earth and the grave, and life and what comes before it. The tradition keeps the whole range rather than picking one. What the ayah sets out is not which reading is right but the shape. Every person is passing through stages, some settled and some temporary.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and set inside a run of signs drawn from creation. Common descent carried social weight here. This was a society built on lineage, where a family argued its worth from its ancestors. Putting everyone's origin in one soul cut straight across that. The surah has already argued that guidance and standing do not travel through blood.

keyTerms.note: A verb for raising something up and developing it, used of growing a plant or founding a settlement. It implies a process rather than an instant, which suits an ayah about stages.
A noun of place from the verb to settle, used earlier in this surah for where news comes to rest. Here it names a stage where something stays for a period.
From the root for entrusting something to someone's keeping, as goods are left with a custodian. What is deposited is by definition collected later, so the word carries impermanence in itself.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Deposits were a familiar arrangement. A traveller leaving Mecca left goods, money or a family member with someone he trusted. He collected them on his return. Nothing was written down, so the whole system ran on reputation. Everyone had held something for someone, or left something behind. The word in this ayah comes from that practice. It names the difference between where you live and where you are being kept.
studies.didYouKnow: The two words at the centre of this ayah are read differently by different classical authorities. The commentaries list the possibilities side by side and never settle them. Open cases like this are rarer than readers expect. This is one of the clearest. The tradition records that the meaning is disputed, and leaves it there.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Common origin is stated as a fact about creation, not as a moral appeal. The ethics follow anyway. If everyone came from one, then the divisions people build are arrangements rather than natures. The stages named add a second point. Some of what a person occupies is a home and some is storage. Knowing which is which changes how tightly anything is held, including a body.

crossReferences.why: Opens a surah with the same origin from one soul, and draws an obligation about kinship from it.
Repeats the phrase and continues into the making of a mate and the beginning of a family.
Describes the stages further, creation after creation within three layers of darkness.

studies.applyIt: Think of the person you feel most distant from by background. A different country, class, or generation. Hold the thought that they came from the same origin you did. Do not turn it into a resolution. It is a fact rather than a feeling. Letting it sit for a minute does more than deciding to be tolerant.
studies.explainEasier: God started all people from one single person. After that, each of us has places we stay for a while and places we are only kept for a time. The signs are spelled out for people who think.

studies.title: Watch The Fruit Ripen
studies.meaning: The ayah moves like a camera. Water comes down. Then vegetation of every kind, then green shoots, then grain packed in layered clusters. Then palms with their fruit hanging low, then vineyards and olives and pomegranates, similar and dissimilar. Early scholars note that this order follows the real order of growth. Then comes the one command in the passage. Look at the fruit when it forms and when it ripens. Attention is what is being asked for.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and the plants named belong to the wider region rather than to the bare valley of Mecca. Olives and pomegranates grew in Syria and Yemen, along the routes Meccan traders used. Dates came from the oases. The audience knew all of them as goods, and as landscapes seen from the road. The list describes the world they moved through.

keyTerms.note: A participle for things mounted or stacked in layers, from the root for riding. Applied to grain it describes an ear of wheat exactly, with the seeds overlapping in rows.
A plural for the heavy bunches that hang from a date palm. The adjective attached means near or within reach, which is a farmer's observation about a mature tree bending under its load.
A noun for fruit coming to maturity, used only here in the Quran. Its rarity marks the second half of the instruction, since watching the forming and watching the ripening are named as two acts.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A date palm was a household's security. It took years to bear and then produced for decades. Its yield was counted, sold forward, and used to settle debts. Families knew their trees one by one. The detail about clusters hanging within reach is not decoration. It describes the moment in the season when a tree is worth what it is worth. Everyone waited for it.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for ripening in this ayah appears nowhere else in the Quran. The list around it is unusually exact. It names four crops in a single sentence, which is more plant detail than almost any other passage carries. The command to look comes after all that detail rather than before it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage asks you to watch rather than to agree, which is an unusual move. Its argument is not that growth cannot be explained. It is that growth is worth watching. The phrase about fruits similar and dissimilar points at one thing. The same water and the same soil produce different results. Difference coming out of identical conditions is offered as the sign, and the ayah trusts a careful looker to notice it.

crossReferences.why: Makes the point explicit: neighbouring plots watered with one water, and some are made to excel others.
Lists the same crops after rain, naming olives, palms, vines and every kind of fruit.
Issues the same instruction to look, then walks through the growth of food step by step.

studies.applyIt: Find one growing thing you pass often. A tree on your street, or a plant on a sill. Look at it properly twice this week, a few days apart. Notice what changed. The ayah asks for this and nothing more. It asks twice because the change is the part you cannot see in one glance.
studies.explainEasier: God sends down rain, and out of it grows every kind of plant: grain, dates, grapes, olives and pomegranates. Some look alike and some do not. Watch the fruit as it grows and ripens.

studies.title: Without Any Knowledge
studies.meaning: Two claims are named, and each is undercut in the same breath that reports it. Unseen beings are made partners to God. The ayah adds that He created them, which settles the matter without an argument. Then sons and daughters are invented for Him. The phrase attached is the sharp one: without any knowledge. Early scholars note that this is the real charge. The claims are not just wrong. They were made about something nobody had any way of knowing.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and both practices named were live in Arabia. Unseen beings were treated as powers to be kept happy. Some Arabian groups described certain deities as daughters of the high God. The surah has been arguing that speaking about God without warrant is among the worst wrongs. Here it names two familiar examples of exactly that.

keyTerms.note: A verb whose basic sense is tearing or boring through something. Used of invention it suggests forcing a hole where none existed, so the claim is described as damage rather than as decoration.
A recurring Quranic phrase for asserting what one has no access to. It names the procedural fault rather than the content, which is why it can be applied to claims that happen to be about God.
A verbal noun from a root for swimming or moving freely, used to declare God far removed from something. It functions as a denial with a gesture of distance built into it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Unseen beings were part of the practical landscape. A traveller in a strange valley would call on its resident power before making camp. Illness and sudden luck were both put down to them. None of this came from a text or a teaching. It was inherited practice, passed on without anyone claiming to have found anything out. That is exactly the situation the ayah describes.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb used here for inventing appears in that sense only once in the Quran. Everywhere else it means to tear or to pierce. The early Arabic dictionary writers linked the two through the idea of making an opening in what was whole. A made-up claim is pictured as a hole cut into something intact.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The failure named here is one of method, not just of content. Claims about God are being made by people who have no source for them. The Quran treats that as the root of the error the rest of the surah argues against. The standard also cuts in every direction. It reaches anyone who is confident about matters they have been told nothing about.

crossReferences.why: Names the same claim of kinship between God and unseen beings, and what those beings themselves know.
Records the attribution of daughters to God alongside what the same people wanted for themselves.
Describes the practice behind the belief: men seeking refuge in unseen beings and adding to their burden.

studies.applyIt: Pick a confident opinion you hold about something you cannot observe. Trace where it came from. Not to drop it. Just find out whether it was told to you, worked out, or soaked up. This ayah's charge is about a missing source. Most of us have never checked which of our certainties have one.
studies.explainEasier: Some people treated unseen beings as partners of God, even though God made them. Others made up sons and daughters for Him without knowing anything at all. God is far above what they say.

studies.title: How Could He Have A Son
studies.meaning: The answer turns on a single word. God is called the Originator of the heavens and the earth. The term means making with no model to copy. The question follows at once: how could there be a son when there was never a consort. The reasoning is biological on purpose, since offspring need a pair. Early scholars note that the ayah does not argue about status or worth. It points out that the word being used belongs to creatures. Then it adds that He created everything there is.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and the claim being answered had more than one source in the region. Arabian practice described some deities as daughters of the high God. Other communities nearby used the language of sonship in their own ways. The ayah answers the shape of the claim rather than any one version of it. That is why it works from the meaning of the word itself.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to begin something with no prior example, which also gives the Arabic word for an innovation. It names making that has no model, as distinct from shaping existing material.
The feminine of the ordinary word for a companion, used of a spouse. Its plainness is the point: the argument uses a domestic term, not a theological one, to show where the claim comes from.
An interrogative covering both manner and origin. It asks by what route such a thing could be the case, which is a stronger question than simply whether it is true.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Descent was the organising fact of Arabian life. A person was placed by naming a father. Property, protection and marriage all followed from that. Sons secured a line and daughters made alliances. To speak of offspring in that world was to call up a whole system of pairing, inheritance and continuation. That is the system this ayah quietly holds up against the word being used.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for Originator appears only twice in the Quran. Both times it sits in this exact phrase about the heavens and the earth. Its root later became the standard Arabic term for a novelty or an innovation. So a name for God and a word for something brand new share the same three letters.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The argument shows that the language of offspring belongs inside creation. It cannot be lifted out of it. Anything with a child has a partner, a beginning and a line. The surah has already denied each of those. The closing clause finishes the case in a few words. Everything that exists was made by Him, so nothing is left over to be related to Him in that way.

crossReferences.why: Makes the same denial at the shortest possible length, including neither begetting nor being begotten.
Uses the identical name for God and continues into the manner of His decreeing something into being.
Answers the claim of a son at length, describing how grave the tradition takes the statement to be.

studies.applyIt: Notice how often you picture God through a family model without meaning to. A father figure, a stern parent, a distant relative. Most people carry a default image of that kind. Name yours once today. Hold it beside this ayah's point that the categories are borrowed. You do not need a replacement picture to see that.
studies.explainEasier: God made the sky and the earth from nothing. He never had a wife, so He cannot have a son. He made every single thing there is, and He knows all of it.

studies.title: No Vision Can Grasp Him
studies.meaning: The first verse gathers a long argument into a conclusion. It names God as Lord and maker of everything, and draws worship as the result. The second verse states a limit. Sight does not reach Him, while He reaches sight. Early scholars record a long discussion of what exactly that rules out. The two divine names that close it are unexpected. Not power or majesty, but fineness and expert awareness, words about closeness rather than distance.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. It closes a passage arguing against giving God children and partners. The surah speaks to people who accepted a creator and then hedged that with go-betweens they could see and handle. The verse about vision speaks straight into that. Early scholars read the pairing as an answer to a demand for something visible to worship, not as an abstract statement.

keyTerms.note: The term for an agent entrusted with another's affairs. Applied to God over all things, it makes maintenance rather than mere origination the point: the world is not left running on its own.
A verb for catching up with something and encompassing it, used of a pursuer reaching what he chases. What is denied is comprehension by sight, which is where the classical discussion begins.
From a root for fineness and delicacy. It carries both being too fine to be perceived and being gentle in dealing with small things, and early scholars keep both senses active here.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Worship in Mecca was tactile. Idols were washed, dressed, touched for blessing and carried on journeys, and the sanctuary held images a pilgrim could stand in front of. Religion was something done with the hands and the eyes. Telling that audience their sight could not reach the one they should worship removed the ordinary equipment of devotion and left only words and conduct.
studies.didYouKnow: The two names that close the second verse appear together several times in the Quran. Almost always they come in passages about hidden things: a grain inside a rock, a deed nobody saw, a private grief. The pairing joins fineness of perception to gentleness of treatment. That is why translators struggle to render the first with any single English word.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage guards worship against its likeliest failure. That failure is not disbelief but shrinking God down. If what is worshipped could be caught by sight, it would be one object among others. It could be handled as one. Denying that, while saying that He catches all sight, reverses the usual relation between the seer and the seen. The closing names then keep the being out of reach from reading as being far away.

crossReferences.why: States that nothing is like Him, closing with names about hearing and seeing.
Records Moses asking to see, and what happened to the mountain instead.
Uses the same name for subtle awareness, asking whether the creator would not know.

studies.applyIt: Notice the picture that appears in your mind when you pray, whatever it is: a direction, a light, a presence somewhere above. Do not try to correct it into nothing. Just let it be inadequate rather than accurate, and carry on. The verse is not asking you to stop imagining; it is telling you what your imagining is not.
studies.explainEasier: God is your Lord, and there is no god but him. He made everything and he looks after everything. Eyes cannot take him in, but he takes in everything the eyes can see.

studies.title: Whoever Sees, Sees For Himself
studies.meaning: The word translated as insights is a plural for the power of seeing, not for what is seen. So what has arrived is the means of perception itself. The results are then handed out one person at a time, and evenly. Whoever sees, it is for his own soul. Whoever is blind, it is against it. Early scholars note that both outcomes stay with the person. Nothing passes to anyone else. That is why the ayah closes with the speaker denying that he is a keeper over them.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and spoken to an audience that had heard the surah's arguments about creation, revelation and answering for what you do. The closing disclaimer comes back several times in these pages. The classical sources treat it as typical of the Meccan setting. The message was going to people who could not be forced. They were not being misled about what was at stake.

keyTerms.note: The plural of a word for the faculty of discernment rather than for eyesight. What has come is described as the capacity to perceive, not merely as information to be considered.
The plain verb for lacking sight, used through the Quran for a refusal to perceive. Its pairing with a verb of seeing keeps both outcomes in the same register, as two responses to the same light.
The same root used earlier in this surah for the guardians set over a person, and later for guarding the prayer. Denying the role here separates delivering a message from watching over its reception.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: In Arabia, answering for a wrong was a shared matter. A clan answered for its members. It paid for their offences and collected for their injuries. A man's actions were his family's business, in a practical and financial sense. Against that background, this sentence gives the outcome of seeing or not seeing to one soul alone. The audience had no everyday model for that arrangement.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for insight here shares its root with the word for the sight taken away earlier in this surah, in a case that never happened. The two uses frame the argument. First came the question of who could give sight back if it were removed. Now a different kind of seeing has arrived.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The thing given here is perception, and that shifts what a revelation is taken to be. It is not first of all a set of statements. It is a way of seeing that a person can use or decline. The consequences are then kept strictly personal, and the closing disclaimer protects that. Nobody is being steered toward an outcome. So the outcome truly belongs to whoever reaches it.

crossReferences.why: Describes the recitation itself as insights from the Lord, using the same rare plural.
States the same symmetry: whoever is guided is guided for himself, and whoever strays only against himself.
Repeats the division and closes with the same denial of being a manager over anyone.

studies.applyIt: Think of advice you were given that you can now see was right. Remember how long the gap was before you saw it. Then give the same patience to something you are being told now and cannot yet see. The ayah says the seeing is yours when it comes. That also means it arrives on your own schedule.
studies.explainEasier: Clear proof has come to you from your Lord. Anyone who sees it helps himself. Anyone who stays blind to it only hurts himself. Nobody is standing over you to make you look.

studies.title: You Have Been Studying
studies.meaning: An objection is expected, and then folded into the purpose. The signs are turned in different directions. One result is that they will say he has been taught. Another is that it becomes clear to people who know. Early scholars note that the same variety produces both responses. So the accusation is not a failure of the method but a result of it. An instruction in three parts follows. Follow what is revealed, hold to the single statement about God, and turn away from those who set up partners.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and the accusation was specific. The city suggested that the recitation came from human teachers. The Quran elsewhere records the charge that one particular foreigner was teaching him. The range of the material, and how well it held together, was the point of dispute. That is why this ayah names the varying and the accusation in one breath.

keyTerms.note: An intensive verb for turning something in different directions, used three times in this surah of the signs. Each occurrence pairs it with a different outcome among the listeners.

A verb for reading a text repeatedly until it is learned, from the root that gives the word for lessons. The accusation is not of invention but of schooling, which is a different and more plausible charge.
The same verb the surah uses for those who turn from the signs, given here as an instruction. Its return in the imperative makes withdrawal a discipline rather than the fault it names elsewhere.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Learning in that world meant sitting with someone. A poet trained under a master. A scribe was taught by a scribe. A man's knowledge was traced back to whoever gave it to him. There was no other model. So the charge that he had studied was the most natural explanation on offer. Naming a teacher was how anyone would have accounted for unusual material.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb behind the accusation is the root of the modern Arabic words for lesson, school and student. Early readers of the text differed over how to vowel it. The readings shift the sense between you have studied and it has been studied. The classical commentaries record the variants side by side.
studies.theologicalSignificance: A hostile reading is treated as expected, not as a problem to be solved. That changes how a believer can hold an objection. Not every response to revelation is a failure of the revelation. The instruction that follows draws the practical conclusion. Its order is worth noticing: follow, affirm, and only then withdraw. Pulling back comes last, and only after something positive has been secured.

crossReferences.why: Names the same accusation of a human teacher and answers it by pointing at the language itself.
Records a fuller version of the charge, that ancient tales were written down and dictated to him.
Uses the same verb for varying the signs and reports that it only increased their aversion.

studies.applyIt: Notice a criticism of your beliefs that you carry as though nobody had answered it. Then look up how it has actually been addressed. Ten minutes is usually enough to find that it is old. This passage names an objection in the same breath as the thing that caused it. That is a calmer stance than either ignoring the objection or fearing it.
studies.explainEasier: God turns the signs around in many ways. Some people will say all this was simply learned from a teacher. Others will see it clearly. The message is to hold on to what God sent down, and to leave behind those who worship other gods.

studies.title: Not A Manager Over Them
studies.meaning: Three clauses, and each one lifts something off the messenger's shoulders. Had God willed, they would not have set up partners with Him. That puts the outcome where it belongs. Then two denials follow. He was not made a keeper over them, and he is not a manager of their affairs. Early scholars read the pair as covering both watching and acting. He is not charged with observing their conduct, and he is not empowered to arrange it. Nothing here criticises the effort. It marks the limits of the office.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and the ayat around it deal with the strain of long refusal. The same denial appears more than once in these pages, and in other Meccan surahs. That suggests a burden that kept returning rather than one low moment. No specific occasion is reported. The wording speaks to one person while the passage around it speaks to everyone.

keyTerms.note: One who guards and keeps a record. Denying the role removes the duty of surveillance, which is the half of responsibility that exhausts a person before any action is even taken.
The one entrusted with another's affairs and empowered to act in them. Paired with the previous word, the two denials cover watching over people and deciding for them.
The verb of willing in a conditional that did not happen. The Quran uses this form repeatedly to state what God could have brought about and did not, without explaining the reason for the restraint.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A Meccan household ran on handed-down authority. A senior man appointed someone to handle a marriage deal, a debt or a caravan's cargo. That agent's decisions bound the family. It was a real office. It carried real liability. The denial comes twice, in two different words. It told the listener exactly which two burdens he was not being given.
studies.didYouKnow: Both words denied here come back elsewhere in the Quran as descriptions of God. He is named the Keeper, and the one in whom trust is placed. The same terms mark the edge of a human role and the character of the divine one. The Quran uses that pattern more than once.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage separates persuading someone from answering for them, right where the two are easiest to confuse. A person who cares about another's belief starts to feel answerable for it. This ayah says that feeling has no basis. The opening clause is what makes the release possible. If the outcome was never outside God's will, then failing to produce it was never a failure. The effort keeps its value either way.

crossReferences.why: Repeats the same denial of being a manager, immediately after naming God as keeper over them.
States the same conditional: had He willed, He would have guided all of you together.
Says plainly that God could have guided all people, in a passage about signs that were demanded.

studies.applyIt: Name one person whose choices you feel answerable for and are not. Write the sentence out: I am not the keeper of this. Then decide what you will still do. Usually that means staying present and stopping the steering. The ayah lifts two burdens and leaves the relationship in place. That is the part most of us drop while carrying the rest.
studies.explainEasier: If God had wanted, nobody would have worshipped anything beside Him. God did not make His messenger a guard over these people. He is not the one who runs their lives.

studies.title: Do Not Revile Their Gods
studies.meaning: The instruction comes with its reason attached. The reason is about what follows, not about whether anything is true. Abuse aimed at what others call on brings abuse aimed at God. It comes back out of hostility and without knowledge, so the result is worse than silence. Early scholars are clear that the ayah does not soften the surah's case against idols. It addresses the manner of speech. The passage then widens. Every community finds its own conduct appealing, and every one of them returns to be told what it did.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and the classical scholars report an occasion in general terms. As the message pressed harder on the city's gods, its leaders warned that they would speak against God in return. The reports differ in detail. They do not name one incident consistently. But they agree on the situation. An exchange of insults was starting, and this ayah stopped one side of it.

keyTerms.note: A verb for insulting speech specifically, not for disagreement or refutation. The distinction matters, since the surah spends most of its length arguing against exactly what this ayah declines to mock.
From the root for running and for overstepping a limit, which gives the word for an enemy. It names retaliation that goes past its provocation, which is what an exchange of insults reliably does.
The same verb used earlier in this surah of conduct made to look good. Its repetition here, applied to every community without exception, extends the observation to the listener as well.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Verbal attack was a recognised weapon. Poets were hired to mock rival tribes. A well-made insult could travel across Arabia and damage a clan's standing for a generation. Exchanges grew because each side had to answer. Anyone in that culture knew that starting such a contest meant seeing it through. The second insult was never the last one.
studies.didYouKnow: The clause about every community finding its own deeds appealing uses a verb from earlier in the surah. It was applied there to people whose hearts had hardened. Placing it here, right after an instruction to the believers, changes its reach. A description of other people becomes a general remark that includes the ones being addressed.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Restraint rests on effect, not on respect for the beliefs themselves. That is a precise basis, and an unsentimental one. The surah has been taking the practice apart for a hundred ayat and takes back none of it. What it shows is that mockery gains nothing the argument wants. The harm it stirs up lands on the name of God. The general clause that follows removes any smugness from the instruction.

crossReferences.why: Describes the manner of calling others: with wisdom, good counsel, and argument in the better way.
Portrays those who answer the ignorant with peace rather than by returning what was said.
States the general principle, that repelling with what is better can turn hostility into closeness.

studies.applyIt: Think of a group whose beliefs you find easy to mock. Notice the joke you already have ready about them. Retire that one joke this week. Not the disagreement, which you may keep in full. Just the line you use to get a laugh. Then hear what the conversation about them sounds like without it.
studies.explainEasier: God tells people not to insult the things others pray to. Otherwise those people may insult God back, out of anger and without knowing better. Every group thinks its own way looks good. In the end they all return to God.

studies.title: Their Most Solemn Oaths
studies.meaning: The promise is made with all the weight they have. They swear by God with the strongest oaths available, and the promise has a condition. If a sign came, they would believe. Two answers follow. Signs are with God, which takes the deal out of human hands. Then a question is turned on the believers themselves. What makes you think they would believe if one came. Early scholars note that the second answer is aimed at the community, not at the objectors. That is what makes it striking.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and the demand for a sign runs through this surah from its opening pages. By this point the audience has heard the request answered several ways. The classical sources describe specific requests made in the city. They include moving a hill and making the dead speak. The ayat that follow this one answer exactly those images.

keyTerms.note: Literally the utmost of their oaths, using a word for exertion and strain. The phrase names an oath sworn to the limit of what a person's word can bear, with nothing stronger available.
The same word used for a verse of the Quran and for a marvel in nature. Its indefinite form here means any sign at all, which is what makes the request both sweeping and unfalsifiable.
From a root for fine awareness, connected to the words for a poet and for hair. It names perception at the edge of noticing, so the question asks what gives the listeners their confidence.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Oaths were the strongest tool a person had. They came in grades. The heaviest meant swearing by God at a sanctuary, and it settled disputes that no evidence could. A man who broke such an oath was finished socially. So hearing that oaths of this weight backed a promise nobody meant to keep would have been genuinely shocking.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase for the most solemn oaths appears several times in the Quran. Almost every time it introduces a promise that is not kept. The pattern is steady enough that classical readers treated the phrase as a signal. It marks a pledge made at the highest volume and the lowest reliability.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage turns from the objectors to the believers and questions their hope. That move is unusual and worth sitting with. Hoping that one more piece of evidence will settle someone is natural and generous. The ayah declines to encourage it. That is not cynicism about people. It is a statement about what belief actually rests on. The ayat right after this one spell out how far the point reaches.

crossReferences.why: Extends the answer to its limit: angels, the dead speaking, and everything gathered before them.
States the same conclusion, that every sign together would not move those already settled against it.
Records the demand in another form, asking why God does not speak to them or send a sign.

studies.applyIt: Think of a person you keep hoping will change if the right thing happens to them. Notice how much of your energy goes into waiting for that event. Keep the hope and stop the waiting. This ayah gently questions the assumption. It is not there to make you give up on anyone. It returns the effort to what you can actually do.
studies.explainEasier: They swore their biggest oaths that they would believe if a miracle came. Miracles are with God alone. Even if one did come, these people would still not believe.

studies.title: We Turn Their Hearts
studies.meaning: The verb here is one of overturning. It is the motion of flipping something over and over, and it is applied to hearts and sight together. Early scholars read the clause that follows as the reason. This answers a first refusal rather than coming before it. The word for heart here is not the usual one. It names the organ at its most alive and open. So the most sensitive faculty a person has is turned, and they are left to wander in it.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and it follows straight on from the point that a sign would settle nothing. The passage explains why. Its language has troubled readers in every generation. The classical scholars handle it by reading the whole surah together. There the refusal comes first, and it is described many times before this consequence is named.

keyTerms.note: An intensive verb for flipping something over and over, used of turning meat on a fire or hands in regret. The repetition built into the form suggests instability rather than a single reversal.
A different word from the usual one for heart, connected by the lexicographers to burning and to intense feeling. It names the heart at its most alive, which is what makes its turning significant.
A verb for moving without direction, used of an animal straying in open country. It differs from the word for blindness by describing the behaviour rather than the impairment.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A camel that lost its bearings in empty country did not stand still. It kept walking, confidently and in wide circles. A herdsman watching from a rise could see what the animal could not. The verb in this ayah belongs to that scene. That is why it names motion rather than being frozen. From the inside, the wandering looks like purpose.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for heart used here appears far less often in the Quran than the more common term. It tends to turn up where feeling rather than understanding is at stake. One place is the description of a mother's heart emptied of everything. So its use in this ayah is pointed rather than accidental.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah states a consequence in the strongest terms available. It ties that consequence to an earlier refusal in the same sentence. The mainstream tradition insists on reading the two halves together. What this rules out is one idea in particular. A person cannot decline something without end and find the power to accept it unchanged. Faculties are described as answering to use, and that answering runs both ways.

crossReferences.why: Uses nearly the same closing phrase, leaving them to wander blindly in their overstepping.
States the same order of events, that hearts were turned aside after the people had first deviated.
Places the same wandering after misguidance, and says no guide remains for the one left in it.

studies.applyIt: Think of something you once found moving that now does nothing for you. A passage, a place, a form of worship. Rather than deciding it has gone flat, ask what changed in you between then and now. This ayah's claim is about the receiving end. That end is the one you can reach.
studies.explainEasier: These people said no the first time. So God turns their hearts and their eyes away. He leaves them to wander about, still refusing to see what is in front of them.

studies.title: Even If The Dead Spoke
studies.meaning: Three impossible things are granted in a row, each one bigger than the last. Angels sent down. The dead speaking to them. Everything gathered before them face to face. The conclusion is stated flatly. They would still not believe, unless God willed it. Early scholars note that this exception keeps the sentence from being fatalistic. The possibility is left open on God's side. The final clause names the state of most of them, and the word chosen means ignorance rather than error.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and every item on the list was actually requested. The classical sources record demands made in the city. People asked for angels to appear, for particular dead men to be raised and questioned, and for other displays. The Quran elsewhere keeps a longer version of the same list. This ayah answers all of them at once rather than one by one.

keyTerms.note: Read in more than one way by the early authorities, giving the sense of things brought face to face or gathered in groups. The commentaries record the variants side by side without preferring one.
The same verb used in this surah for the assembling of people on the last day. Its use here for evidence brought together suggests a preview of that gathering rather than an ordinary display.

From a root covering both lack of knowledge and rashness of temper. Pre-Islamic usage leans toward the second, so the word describes people acting without weighing rather than people lacking information.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Consulting the dead was not a strange idea in that region. Diviners claimed contact with unseen beings. Stories went around of voices heard at graves or in ruins. So asking for a dead ancestor to confirm the message fitted the world the audience already pictured. It was not a joke. That is why the ayah answers it in the same register as the others.
studies.didYouKnow: One word in this ayah has several accepted early readings. Each gives a slightly different image: evidence brought face to face, or gathered in groups, or acting as a guarantor. The classical commentaries list them together. That is how the tradition keeps a place where the sense was genuinely open.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage sets a ceiling on what evidence can do, and then puts a door in it. Nothing available to a person would produce belief on its own. Yet the exception is God's will, which is neither predictable nor closed. That pairing removes two temptations at once. One is despairing of anyone. The other is imagining that the right display would settle the matter, if only it could be arranged.

crossReferences.why: Preserves the fuller list of demands, from a spring in the ground to a house of ornament.
Answers the first item earlier in this surah, explaining what an angel's arrival would settle.
States the same conclusion, that every sign together would not move those already committed.

studies.applyIt: Notice a conversation you keep planning to have, where you finally lay out the evidence and are understood. Most of us have one running. Ask whether more evidence is really what is missing. If it is not, spend that energy on the relationship instead. That was the only part that was ever yours.
studies.explainEasier: Angels could come down to them. The dead could speak to them. Everything could be gathered in front of them. They would still not believe, unless God willed it. Most of them simply do not know.

studies.title: An Enemy For Every Prophet
studies.meaning: Opposition is described as standard equipment, not as bad luck. Every prophet is given an enemy. The enemies come in two kinds, human and unseen, and they work the same way. They pass gilded speech to one another in order to deceive. Early scholars note that the word for their exchange is the same one used for revelation. The parallel is deliberate. The ayah then removes any sense of an evenly matched contest. It closes with an instruction to leave them to it.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and the reassurance is aimed at a community that had begun to take organised opposition personally. The surah has already placed the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) in a line of messengers. They were denied and mocked too. This ayah goes further. It describes the opposition itself as part of the arrangement. That turns it from a setback into a feature.

keyTerms.note: The first word names gold ornament applied to a surface. Speech described this way is not false in a way you can hear; it is plated, attractive on the outside and something else underneath.

The same verb used for revelation given to prophets, in its basic sense of swift concealed communication. Using it of the opposition draws an exact and uncomfortable parallel between two kinds of quiet transmission.
From the root used earlier in this surah for being taken in by the present life. It names the effect rather than the intention, so the word describes what the speech produces in a listener.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Gilding was a known craft. Wood or base metal was covered in a thin layer of gold to make an object look solid. Anyone who had traded in the northern markets knew plated goods from the real weight. Applying that word to speech named a familiar trading trick. It moved the trick into the assembly, where reputations were made by phrasing.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for gilding in this ayah gives surah 43 its name. There it appears in a passage about the ornament of this present life. So the same root titles a whole surah about being impressed by surfaces. That is exactly the mechanism described here.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Opposition is given a place in the design, and that changes how it should be read. Its presence is not proof that something has gone wrong. Its absence would not be proof that something is right. The clause about God's will keeps the two sides from being equal powers. The closing instruction is the practical conclusion. Attention spent on answering made-up claims is attention not spent on the work.

crossReferences.why: States the same principle almost word for word, an enemy assigned from the criminals to every prophet.
Describes a companion assigned to the one who turns from the reminder, using a related mechanism.
Names companions who make what lies before and behind a person look attractive to him.

studies.applyIt: Think of something that won you over mainly because it was said well. An advertisement, a confident speaker, a beautifully written argument. Trace what the actual claim was underneath the phrasing. This ayah's image is plating over base metal. The test for plating is weight rather than shine.
studies.explainEasier: Every prophet has had enemies, both people and unseen beings. They whisper fancy words to each other to trick people. God could have stopped it. The message is to leave them to their lies.

studies.title: Hearts That Lean Toward It
studies.meaning: The ayah continues the sentence before it and says what the gilded speech achieves. Hearts lean toward it. Then they become pleased with it. Then they go on to earn what they earn. Early scholars note the three stages: a leaning, then consent, then conduct. The people described are marked by one thing only. They do not believe in the hereafter. The passage treats that as the condition that makes such speech attractive in the first place.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and belief in an afterlife was the sharpest disagreement in the city. Arabian religion had room for many gods and very little answering for what you do. The surah has already recorded the denial in the objectors' own words. This ayah explains what follows from that denial. It describes an appetite for a certain kind of talk rather than an argument.

keyTerms.note: A verb for tilting toward something to listen, used of an ear turned to catch a sound. It names a small physical movement rather than agreement, which is why it comes first in the sequence.
The verb of contentment and approval. Its placement second turns the sequence into a description of how a position becomes comfortable: first you lean in, and only afterwards do you accept it.
From a root for gathering fruit or bark by hand. It describes wrongdoing as something collected deliberately, which distinguishes it from a slip and matches an ayah about a gradual process.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Reputation in Mecca was made and broken by talk. People chose whose talk to sit near. A young man attached himself to a circle and learned its phrases. Within a season he held its opinions as his own. Nobody decided to change their mind. The sequence in this ayah runs from leaning in to being at ease. The audience had watched it happen to their sons.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb for inclining used here appears only twice in the Quran. The other place describes hearts that have swerved. Both times it names a tilt rather than a decision. That fits a vocabulary which treats belief and its loss as slow movements more often than as sudden turns.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage traces a mechanism rather than handing down a verdict. The mechanism is one anybody can recognise. What you listen to becomes what you accept. What you accept becomes what you do. Putting disbelief in the hereafter at the head of the chain also makes a claim about motive. Whether anything follows this life decides how much a person can afford to be persuaded of.

crossReferences.why: Describes buying diverting talk in order to lead others from the way, without any knowledge.
Names the residue such conduct leaves, a stain settling over the heart from what was earned.
Gives the counter-instruction: do not pursue what you have no knowledge of, since each faculty is asked.

studies.applyIt: Look at what you listen to most in a week, whatever plays while you drive or cook. Not to judge it. Just notice which of your opinions arrived that way rather than by thinking. The ayah's first stage is only a tilt of the head. That tilt is the part you can still feel happening.
studies.explainEasier: People who do not believe in the life after death start to like this kind of smooth talk. First they lean toward it. Then they are happy with it. Then they act on it.

studies.title: Shall I Seek Another Judge
studies.meaning: The question refuses a procedure, not an answer. Seeking a judge other than God would put the matter before an authority above the one who sent the Book. The Book is described as already set out in detail, so the case has been stated. Early scholars note the appeal that follows. It is made to people who hold earlier scripture and recognise what this is. The closing instruction is short and personal: do not be among those who waver.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and arbitration was the standard way to settle a serious dispute in Arabia. The two sides agreed on a respected third person and accepted the outcome. The Meccans had proposed such arrangements over other quarrels. The surah has already refused several offers of compromise. This ayah answers the assumption underneath them, that the matter could be bargained over at all.

keyTerms.note: Specifically the arbitrator both sides agree to, not an appointed magistrate. The word names a role that only exists by mutual consent, which is what makes seeking one here a category error.
From the verb for separating something into its parts, used earlier in this surah for explaining the signs. It describes a text laid out clearly rather than one requiring an interpreter's key.
From a root meaning to dispute back and forth, and connected to milking, drawing something out repeatedly. Doubt in this word is an activity rather than a state, something a person keeps doing.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arbitration was a familiar craft, and it had known practitioners. Before the message began, the tribes of Mecca fell out. The quarrel was over rebuilding the sanctuary. They put it to whoever next came in through one particular gate. Then they accepted the result. Everyone knew that agreeing on a judge was the first step and the hardest. The choice usually decided the case.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for arbiter here shares a root with the word for wisdom. The same root gives the word for the bridle placed on a horse. Arabic links judging with holding back. So a judge in this vocabulary is one who holds a dispute in check, not one who wins it for a side.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage puts the disagreement outside the reach of bargaining. That is a hard thing to say gracefully, and here it is said as a question. It also links clarity with finality. A text set out in detail leaves less room for a professional go-between. The closing instruction is addressed to the one carrying the message. It treats steadiness as something asked for rather than assumed.

crossReferences.why: Describes the same Book with the same word, its verses set out in detail for people who know.
Names both stages of the text, verses made firm and then detailed, from one who is wise and aware.
Makes accepting God's judgement in a dispute the measure of belief rather than an optional step.

studies.applyIt: Notice a matter you have settled in principle and keep reopening in your head. You are looking for a second opinion that agrees with you. Everybody has one of these. Name it, and decide today whether you are actually rethinking it or just shopping. This ayah's word for doubt describes a repeated action. That means it can simply be stopped.
studies.explainEasier: Nobody should be asked to judge between us but God. He is the one who sent down the Book, spelled out clearly. People who were given a Book before know it is the truth.

studies.title: Complete In Truth And Justice
studies.meaning: Two qualities are named as the completion of God's word, and the pairing is exact. Truth covers what the word reports. Justice covers what it asks. So statements and commands are both accounted for. Early scholars read completion here as fulfilment rather than a stopping point. They differ over whether the word means the Quran, God's promise, or His decree in general. Then comes the guarantee. Nothing alters His words. The two names at the end tie the promise to attention.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and placed after a passage about seeking arbitration elsewhere. The surah has been arguing with people who kept looking for another authority, another sign, another go-between. This ayah closes that line. It describes the word already given as complete in both directions. Nothing is left outstanding that a different source could supply.

keyTerms.note: A verb for reaching fullness, used of a moon becoming full or a term running its course. It names arrival at wholeness rather than the end of a process of adding.
Truth specifically in speech, the correspondence between what is said and what is so. Pairing it with justice divides the word into what it tells and what it asks, covering both at once.
An active participle in a construction of absolute denial, so the sentence says no such agent exists at all. The same phrase appears earlier in this surah, where it grounds a promise of help.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Agreements in Arabia were spoken. They were held by memory and by witness. A contract could be quietly reshaped over years, as the people who heard it died. Disputes about what had actually been said were common. Written treaties were kept in the sanctuary partly for this reason. A word that nobody can alter is exactly the security a spoken promise lacked.
studies.didYouKnow: The clause about nothing altering God's words appears twice in this surah. The earlier one grounds a promise that help would come to messengers. This one is about the word's completion. So the same phrase does two jobs. It secures a promise for the future and a text in the present.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Truth and justice are joined as two sides of one word. That resists a common split between what is believed and what is practised. An account that is accurate and a demand that is fair are given as the same completion. What follows is not a claim about manuscripts. It is a claim about the word itself. That is why the two names, hearing and knowing, close the sentence.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same clause earlier in this surah, grounding the promise that help reached earlier messengers.
Repeats the guarantee in a passage about the friends of God, as the great attainment.
States it from God's own speech, that the word is not changed with Him, and none is wronged.

studies.applyIt: Think of a promise you made that has quietly changed shape since. Circumstances adjusted it until it meant something easier. Find the original wording, if you can remember it. This ayah's claim is about a word that stays as it was said. Holding one of your own to that standard is a day's work.
studies.explainEasier: Your Lord's word is finished and complete. It is true in what it says and fair in what it asks. Nobody can change His words. He hears everything and knows everything.

studies.title: If You Obeyed Most People
studies.meaning: A count is not an argument. Following most of those on earth is described as leading away from God's path. The reason given is not that they are wicked. It is that they are guessing. Two words carry it: they follow only guesswork, and they do nothing but estimate. Early scholars note that the second word comes from guessing at quantity. It is the trader's rough figure for a crop still on the tree. What is criticised is a method, and the method is agreement nobody has checked.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and the community hearing this was very small. It sat inside a city that agreed with itself. Agreement was more than social pressure in Arabia. Inherited practice was the basis of authority, and the standard argument against the message was that the ancestors had done otherwise. This ayah answers the form of that argument rather than any one version of it.

keyTerms.note: A word covering everything from a strong impression to a bare guess. The Quran uses it for belief held without grounds, and the objection here is to the grounds rather than to the content.
A specific term for assessing a crop by eye before harvest, in order to set a price. It names skilled approximation, which makes the criticism sharper: this is guessing that looks like expertise.
The causative of the verb for losing a road, used through this surah. Following is described as being led, so the fault is located in the act of following rather than only in the leaders.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Date crops were valued before picking. An assessor walked the grove and looked at the trees. He named a figure, and both sides then treated it as the yield for a sale or a debt. He was often close and sometimes badly wrong. Nobody found out until the harvest. That practice gives this ayah its verb for a guess dressed as knowledge.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb for estimating in this ayah is a technical term from farming. It survives in Arabic legal use for assessing standing crops. Here it appears in a passage about belief. A specialist word moves from the grove into an argument about evidence. That move is a favourite of the Quran's Meccan style.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage separates truth from being popular. It does not treat the majority as wicked. That is a fairer criticism, and a more useful one. People are described as guessing, which is what people mostly do. The danger named is inheriting those guesses as though they were findings. So the reader is left with a task, not a suspicion. Ask of any settled opinion how it was reached.

crossReferences.why: States the principle plainly: most follow conjecture, and conjecture avails nothing against truth.
Applies the same point to a specific claim, that conjecture is no substitute for knowledge.
Notes the numbers honestly, that most people will not believe however eager you may be.

studies.applyIt: Pick one thing you believe because everyone around you does. Try to say what the evidence for it is, in two sentences. Not to drop it if you cannot. Most of what any of us holds arrived this way. The exercise is to find out which of your beliefs you have actually examined.
studies.explainEasier: If you went along with most of the people on earth, they would lead you away from God's path. They are only following guesses. All they ever do is guess at the answer.

studies.title: Over Which His Name Was Spoken
studies.meaning: The first ayah closes the argument before it. It hands back to God the judgement of who is astray, which takes the reader out of the business of ranking anybody. The second turns to something ordinary. Eat from what God's name was spoken over. Early scholars note the condition attached: if you believe in His signs. That ties an everyday act to a conviction. The point of the naming, as the tradition reads it, is to acknowledge where the animal and the permission came from.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and the practice described existed before the message. Arabs spoke names over animals at slaughter. Sometimes it was the name of a deity, sometimes of a shrine. The custom carried real meaning about whose the animal was. The surah's closing section takes up several such practices. This passage begins that turn from argument toward the details of ordinary life.

keyTerms.note: The passive of the verb for remembering and for saying aloud. One root covers holding something in mind and speaking it, so pronouncing a name is described as an act of remembrance.
A name spoken over something in Arabian practice marked whose it was and under whose protection it fell. The phrase therefore carries ownership and acknowledgement rather than a formula's efficacy.

The same participle used earlier in this surah, in a sentence where the speaker says he would not be among them if he yielded. Its reappearance keeps the category consistently outside human assessment.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Meat was uncommon, and its slaughter was public. An animal killed for a guest, a wedding or a season of plenty was an event. What was said over it was heard by everyone there. The words marked whose the occasion was and who was being honoured. In a society that ate meat rarely, nobody treated the moment as routine.
studies.didYouKnow: The root behind the word for mentioning in these ayat runs further. It gives the Quranic term for remembrance of God, and the word used for the Quran itself as a reminder. Speaking a name and holding something in mind are one act in Arabic. That is why the tradition treats calling on God as a form of memory.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage moves from a large argument about guidance to a small daily act. It does not change register, which is typical of this surah. Belief in the signs shows up in what is said over a meal. So conviction reaches into the most ordinary dealing a household makes. The first ayah keeps the sorting of people where it belongs. That stops the practice from becoming a badge.

crossReferences.why: Explains why every community was given a rite: that God's name be mentioned over what was provided.
Repeats the same instruction about mentioning the name, and joins it to feeding the poor.
Uses the same phrase in a Medinan setting, alongside the reminder to be mindful of God.

studies.applyIt: Say God's name out loud once before your next meal. Notice how the first mouthful lands differently. That is the whole exercise. These ayat tie a conviction to a small spoken act. They do it at the point where a person is least likely to be thinking about anything. That is exactly when the naming does its work.
studies.explainEasier: Your Lord knows best who has left His path and who is on it. So eat from food that God's name was said over, if you really believe in His signs.

studies.title: He Has Set It Out
studies.meaning: The question pushes back against strictness that is not needed. What has been withheld is described as already set out in detail. So the list is limited and known. An exception is named for real compulsion. Early scholars read the whole passage as answering people who were adding rules of their own. The second half says where such additions come from. Many lead others astray by their own leanings, without knowledge. The closing clause hands back to God the judgement of who oversteps.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and Arabian practice carried an elaborate set of self-imposed food rules. They were attached to particular animals and occasions. The surah names several of them a few ayat later. The early scholars describe the objectors arguing directly with the believers about these customs. That is why this passage answers a dispute about food rather than starting one.

keyTerms.gloss: He has set out in detail
keyTerms.note: The same verb used through this surah for separating something into distinct parts. Applied to what is withheld, it implies a definite list rather than an open field of caution.

A passive form from the root for harm and hardship, meaning driven to something by necessity. Its presence keeps the whole subject humane rather than absolute, and the Quran repeats it wherever such limits appear.
The same plural used earlier in this surah when desires were named as what would actually be followed. Its return here says the additions come from appetite, including the appetite for strictness.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Food rules in pre-Islamic Arabia were local and inherited. Certain animals were set aside after a number of births. Some were left to graze untouched after a vow. Particular parts were kept for men, or withheld from women, depending on the tribe. None of it came from a text. It was custom hardened into duty over generations, enforced by families rather than by any authority.
studies.didYouKnow: The exception for compulsion appears in every Quranic passage that names withheld foods. That is four times, across four surahs. The wording is nearly the same each time. Such steadiness is unusual. The classical commentaries treat the repeat as deliberate. No list of limits is ever recorded without it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage cares as much about additions as about overstepping, which is a distinctive emphasis. Inventing restrictions is described as leading people astray. That is the same verb the surah applies to the deniers. And it is traced to leaning rather than to piety. One principle is left standing. What has been set out is set out. Treating your own caution as though it came from God is its own kind of speaking without knowledge.

crossReferences.why: Gives the corresponding list with the same exception for one compelled, without desire or excess.
Warns against tongues asserting that this is permitted and that is not, inventing lies about God.
Addresses the opposite error, of declaring unlawful the good things that were made lawful.

studies.applyIt: Notice a rule you keep that nobody gave you. A standard about work, hospitality, or how a home should look. Ask where it came from and whether it serves anyone. This passage is uneasy about a self-made restriction dressed as principle. The first step is simply telling the two apart.
studies.explainEasier: There is no reason to avoid food that God's name was said over. He has already spelled out what to stay away from. There is one exception, for when you are forced by need. Many people lead others off the path with their own ideas.

studies.title: Outward Sin And Inward
studies.meaning: Wrongdoing is split into what shows and what does not. Both are named together in one short instruction. Early scholars read the inward half as covering hidden acts. It also covers the movements of the heart. They note that Arabic uses the same pairing for the visible and hidden parts of anything. The ayat that follow return to what is eaten, and to the arguing around it. The warning is that being argued into something has consequences. Those reach beyond the matter under discussion.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and the surrounding passage answers a live dispute about inherited food customs. The classical scholars describe the objectors pressing the believers hard. Their arguments were framed as reasonable questions. This passage names that pressure directly. The instruction about sin, outward and inward, opens the section. It gives the specific dispute a wider frame before that dispute is addressed.

keyTerms.note: What is visible on the surface, from the root for a back or an exterior. The word gives the Arabic for something manifest, and it is used across the Quran as one half of a standard pair.
The interior, from the root for a belly. Paired with the previous word it covers a thing completely, so naming both halves of wrongdoing leaves no category of it unaddressed.
The same verb used earlier in this surah for the gilded speech passed between enemies. Its repetition ties the argument about food to the mechanism described a few ayat before.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Reputation was a full-time job in a city where everyone knew everyone. A man's outward conduct was watched constantly. His standing depended on it. So the gap between what was seen and what was not could be wide. Naming both halves in one breath spoke to a society that had refined the handling of the visible half into an art.
studies.didYouKnow: The pairing of outward and inward here is the standard Arabic way of saying all of something. English does the same with inside and out. The Quran uses these two words elsewhere of blessings, of the sea and of knowledge. So the phrase places wrongdoing inside a familiar figure for wholeness.
