studies.theologicalSignificance: Naming the hidden half makes character the subject rather than reputation. It does this without a word about being watched. The passage then draws a line from a small argument about food to something much larger. Giving in to pressure in a matter framed as trivial is described as serious. What is at stake is not the matter but who is being followed. That is a claim about how loyalty actually shifts.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same pairing, naming what is apparent of immoralities and what is concealed of them.
Describes those who avoid the greater wrongs and forgive when they are angry, as a settled quality.
Notes that the ones who avoid the great sins are still known best by the One who formed them.

studies.applyIt: Take one thing you do only when nobody can see. Then take one thing you do only because someone can. Write both down on the same piece of paper. You do not have to act on either today. This passage puts the two halves in one sentence. Seeing them side by side is most of the work.
studies.explainEasier: Leave sin alone, the kind people can see and the kind they cannot. Do not eat food that God's name was not said over. Bad voices push their friends to argue with you about it.

studies.title: A Light To Walk By
studies.meaning: Two figures are set against each other. One was dead, then given life and a light to walk by among people. The other is in darkness and cannot get out. Early scholars note the detail in the first half. The light is for walking among people, not for private lighting, so what was given shows up in company. The second figure is described without any verb of choosing. He is simply in it. The closing clause explains why that state lasts.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and the classical scholars discuss whether the comparison points at particular people in the city. Different names are offered. Others read it as describing two conditions in general. The reports do not agree, and the wording works either way. What is not in dispute is the setting. Some in the community had accepted the message and others had refused it, living in the same streets.

keyTerms.note: The causative of living, used through the Quran for reviving dead ground after rain. Applying it to a person makes the change a resurrection in miniature rather than an improvement.
Indefinite and unqualified, so the ayah does not specify what the light is. Commentators offer faith, the Quran and understanding, and the tradition records the range without narrowing it.
An active participle in a negative construction, so the denial is of the person as an emerger rather than of a single exit. The grammar makes the condition a description rather than an event.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Walking at night in a town without lighting meant carrying a flame, or knowing the ground by memory. A lamp changed everything. You saw the drop, the sleeping animal, the person coming the other way. Those without one waited for dawn, or felt their way along walls. Everybody in that audience had done both, and knew which they preferred.
studies.didYouKnow: The light in this ayah is given for walking among people, not for seeing alone in the dark. The same phrase appears in a later surah, where believers walk with their light going before them. The Quran keeps attaching this image to movement in company rather than to private lighting.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The change described is not an improvement in someone's opinions. It is a restoration of life, which sets the stakes higher than persuasion. And the light's purpose is social. What has been received becomes visible in how a person moves among others. So the difference between the two figures is meant to be noticeable rather than inward. The closing clause keeps the second figure's state explained rather than merely condemned.

crossReferences.why: Describes God bringing believers out of darkness into light, and the reverse for those who refuse.
Shows the same light in motion, going before believers and to their right on that day.
Draws out the other half of the comparison at length, as darkness layered over darkness at sea.

studies.applyIt: Think of one person whose presence makes a room easier to be in. Try to name what they actually do. It is usually small and repeatable: they ask, they wait, they do not compete. This ayah describes light as something you walk with among people. So it is visible in behaviour before it is anything else.
studies.explainEasier: Think of a man who was dead. God brought him back to life and gave him a light to walk with among people. He is not the same as a man stuck in the dark who cannot get out.

studies.title: The Greatest Of Its Criminals
studies.meaning: An observation is made about how towns are arranged. In each one the leading wrongdoers are its most prominent men. Early scholars note the word order. It puts greatness first and crime second, so the phrase names people who are great in the town's own reckoning. Their activity is scheming. The correction follows at once, and it is the ayah's whole point. Whatever they plot lands on themselves, and they do not sense it. That makes the scheming self-directed without their knowing.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and the description fitted the city exactly. Mecca's opposition was led by men of standing. They were heads of clans with wealth, clients and reputations. Their objections carried weight because of who they were rather than what they said. The ayah widens that arrangement to every town, which removes any sense that Mecca was unusually bad.

keyTerms.note: A plural for those greatest in a place, by age, wealth or standing. Its position before the word for wrongdoers makes prominence the first thing said about them, which is how the town itself would describe them.
A verb for planning in secret, not necessarily for evil ends, though usually so in the Quran. It names indirect action, working through arrangements rather than through open force.
From the root for fine awareness, the same one behind the word for a poet. Denying it says the effect is real and below the threshold of their noticing, not that they are indifferent to it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Mecca's power sat with a handful of families. They held the sanctuary's offices and financed the caravans. They could make or break a man by withdrawing protection. They met, discussed, and acted together, with no formal body existing. The word for scheming describes exactly that. A few people decided things in private. Everyone else met the result as circumstances.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran uses the verb for scheming of God as well, in passages where a plot is answered in kind. The classical scholars discuss that usage carefully. The word itself carries no moral charge in Arabic. It names planning that is concealed, and the surrounding sentence supplies the judgement.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage says that harm arranged against others returns to its authors. That is how things work, not an occasional punishment. It is a claim about a moral order built into events rather than laid over them. The detail about not sensing it is what makes the ayah unsettling. The mechanism runs whether or not anyone notices. So a person can be well into their own ruin and still be reading the situation as success.

crossReferences.why: States the principle directly, that an evil plot encircles none but the people who made it.
Names the same class of people, the affluent of a town, as the ones whose conduct decides its fate.
Shows the two sides afterwards, the followers and the ones they followed, arguing about who misled whom.

studies.applyIt: Think about a small arrangement you have made at work or at home that quietly disadvantages someone. You would not describe it out loud in those terms. Most of us have one. Say it plainly to yourself. This ayah's warning is not about being caught. It is about a cost that arrives without being noticed.
studies.explainEasier: In every town God has let the biggest wrongdoers become its leading men, so they can scheme there. But their scheming only comes back on them. They do not even notice it.

studies.title: God Knows Where To Place It
studies.meaning: The objection is finally stated in full, and it is about status. They will not believe until they are given what God's messengers were given. That is a demand to be selected rather than addressed. The answer is a single clause. God knows best where He places His message. Early scholars note that it does not argue about their qualifications. It moves the question, since placement is the sender's decision. No candidate is in a position to judge it.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and the complaint had a concrete form. The classical sources record leading men of the city asking why the message had not come to someone of greater standing. They meant someone in Mecca, or in the town to the east. The Quran preserves that objection elsewhere in almost those words. The claim rested on wealth and clan, which were the city's only measures of importance.

keyTerms.note: A noun for what is sent with a messenger, distinct from the messenger himself. The word treats prophethood as a consignment placed somewhere, which is what makes the verb for placing exact.
From the root for being small in size. It names the reduction of standing rather than pain, which answers precisely what the objectors were asking for, since their demand was about being large.
The comparative of knowing joined to a word for place. The construction is unusual and puts the emphasis on location, so what God knows best is the where of it, not the who.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Honour in Mecca was measured and displayed. Precedence at a gathering was counted publicly. So was the right to speak first, and the size of a man's following. So was the number of guests he could feed. Being passed over for a distinction was a real injury, with money attached. In that world, the demand recorded here was a perfectly ordinary complaint about protocol.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for humiliation used at the end of this ayah appears only once in the Quran. It comes from the ordinary root for smallness. Its rarity marks a precise answer. The punishment named for men who demanded greatness is described by the word for being made small.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Selection is placed outside every visible qualification, which unsettles both the powerful and anyone who ranks themselves. The clause about knowing where to place the message says nothing about merit. It speaks only about the sender's judgement. That closes off two errors at once. One is resenting who was chosen. The other is assuming that being chosen shows anything a person could have arranged.

crossReferences.why: Preserves the complaint in its plainest form, asking why it did not come to a great man of two cities.
States the principle broadly: your Lord creates and chooses, and the choice is not theirs.
Records a related demand, that each of them be handed scrolls of his own, spread open.

studies.applyIt: Think of a time you were passed over and someone else was chosen. Notice whether you concluded anything about your own worth from it. Most of us do. Sit with the possibility that selection tracks something you cannot see, in either direction. That is not consolation. It is a more accurate account of what happened.
studies.explainEasier: When a sign comes, they say they will not believe unless they get what God's messengers got. God knows best where to put His message. Shame and hard punishment are waiting for those who scheme.

studies.title: As If Climbing The Sky
studies.meaning: Two states are described in physical terms. One chest is opened wide for submission. The other is made narrow and tight. Then a comparison arrives that has struck readers in every century: as though he were climbing into the sky. Early scholars explain it as the breathlessness of climbing beyond where air will hold you. That is a remarkably exact description of an experience nobody in that century could have had. What is named is not resistance but tightness.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and the passage answers why some accept and some do not after every argument has been made. The surah has offered signs from creation, from history, and from the shape of revelation itself. This ayah steps behind all of that. It describes the receiving state directly, in a Meccan setting where both responses were on display in the same families.

keyTerms.note: A verb for laying something open, used of cutting meat flat to dry. The same word titles a short surah addressed to the Prophet about his own chest being opened.
Read in two ways by the early authorities, giving either extreme narrowness or a thicket so dense nothing can enter. Both readings survive in the commentaries, and both describe blocked passage.
An intensive form built for difficulty, so the ascent is laboured rather than smooth. The doubling of letters in the Arabic does the work that a whole English phrase about struggling would need.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The Arabs knew height from mountains, not from anything higher. Climbing the peaks around Mecca, or in the highlands to the south, left a person short of breath. The chest works harder for less, and shepherds knew that feeling. So did anyone who had walked up out of a valley in the heat. That is the experience the comparison starts from.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb for opening the chest here is the same one used at the start of a short late-Meccan surah. That surah is addressed to the Prophet. It asks whether his own chest was not opened for him. So the same image describes what happened to him and what happens to anyone guided.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Guidance is described as a change in capacity rather than in argument. That explains why the surah's long case has convinced some and not others. Something has to be open for anything to enter. The passage gives both states to God's will, while the whole surah holds people responsible. The mainstream tradition keeps both without collapsing them. It treats the tightness as following refusal rather than causing it.

crossReferences.why: Asks about the one whose chest God has opened to submission, so that he stands on a light.
Turns the same image into a prayer, where Moses asks for his own chest to be opened.
Opens a short surah with the same verb, asking whether the chest was not laid open already.

studies.applyIt: Notice where in your body you feel resistance when something true and unwelcome is said to you. For most people it is the chest or the throat. It arrives before any thought does. Name it once when it happens today. This ayah describes belief and refusal as physical states. The physical part is the one you can catch.
studies.explainEasier: When God wants to guide someone, He opens up his chest. When He leaves someone to go astray, He makes his chest tight and narrow. It feels like climbing high up into the sky.

studies.title: The Home Of Peace
studies.meaning: The path just described is named as the Lord's own, and straight. The detailed explanation is said to be for people who take a reminder. Then the destination is given a name rather than a description. It is the Home of Peace, held with their Lord. Early scholars note that the word covers safety, wholeness and greeting all at once. The final clause makes God their protector. It attaches that relationship to what they used to do, not to a status they were handed.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and this pair closes the surah's long argument before it turns to specific customs. The audience had been offered warnings for many ayat. The naming of a destination here is one of the surah's few extended notes of promise. No occasion is reported. The word for peace also worked as the ordinary Arabian greeting, which gave the name an everyday warmth.

keyTerms.note: The first word means a dwelling with a courtyard, a family compound rather than a house. The second covers safety, soundness and the greeting itself, so the name promises a settled place free of harm.
A form of remembering that means retrieving what is already held. The audience for the detailed explanation is defined by a capacity for recollection rather than by any prior belief.
The relationship the surah has denied to every other candidate, now affirmed. In Arabian usage it named the person who stood behind you, which makes the promise social rather than only spiritual.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A home in Arabia meant a walled compound with a courtyard, animals, and several generations inside it. It was where a traveller finally stopped. Safety there was assumed rather than negotiated. The greeting of peace was said at its threshold. Naming the destination with that word promised the relief of arriving somewhere you no longer have to watch the road.
studies.didYouKnow: The name given here for the final destination appears twice in the Quran. Both times it is in a Meccan surah. Both times people are invited to it rather than described as living in it. The word for peace inside it is also one of the names by which God is described elsewhere.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The destination is named by its quality rather than pictured. That is unusual in a book with vivid descriptions available. What is promised first is peace, and only afterwards anything else. The closing clause is careful in a way worth noticing. God is their protector because of what they used to do. So the relationship is tied to a life. It is not declared over a category of people.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same name for the destination, saying God invites to the Home of Peace generally.
Gives the greeting spoken at arrival, peace upon you for the patience you kept.
Names the same straight path as a daily request rather than as a description of a group.

studies.applyIt: Say the greeting of peace to one person today whom you would normally pass without speaking. A neighbour, a colleague on another floor, someone at a counter. The word in this ayah names a destination. It also names an ordinary courtesy. Using it on purpose once makes the link between the two audible.
studies.explainEasier: This is your Lord's straight path. The signs are spelled out for people who pay attention. For them there is a Home of Peace with their Lord, and He is their protector because of what they did.

studies.title: We Profited From Each Other
studies.meaning: A gathering is described. Unseen beings are addressed for having taken many humans, and it is their human partners who answer. The answer is unusually frank. We took our enjoyment of one another, and we reached the term You appointed. Early scholars note that no defence is offered. The relationship is described as mutual benefit, which is exactly what it was. The reply that follows names the outcome, with an exception attached that the tradition discusses without settling.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and the arrangement being described was a working part of Arabian religion. Travellers sought protection from the unseen powers of a place. Men consulted diviners who claimed such contacts, and got guidance and standing in return. Both sides gained something concrete. The ayah does not caricature the relationship. It lets one party describe it accurately.

keyTerms.note: A form meaning to seek or acquire a great deal of something. Applied to human beings it treats them as a quantity gathered, which is the ayah's judgement on the relationship stated in a single word.
A verb for deriving use and pleasure from something, the root behind the word for goods and provisions. It names an exchange of advantage, which is how the speakers themselves describe what happened.
From a verb meaning to stay somewhere for a long time. It names a residence rather than a punishment, which makes the sentence a statement of where they now live.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabian travellers entering a strange valley would seek the protection of its resident power. They did this before making camp. Diviners in the settlements claimed ties with such beings. That made them consulted and paid. Both arrangements delivered something. One gave a sense of safety on the road. The other gave a living at home. The exchange described in this ayah was a known feature of ordinary life.
studies.didYouKnow: The reply in this ayah contains an exception: that they remain except as God wills. The classical scholars discuss its scope at length without reaching agreement. It is one of the passages where the tradition openly records that the limit of a statement is not settled. The commentaries preserve the range of readings.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage lets a corrupt relationship be described in its own terms. The description condemns it without help. Nobody claims to have been deceived. They say they profited. That puts the fault in the exchange itself rather than in a misunderstanding. And it names a pattern that outlives the specific practice: arrangements in which two parties benefit and something else is spent quietly between them.

crossReferences.why: Shows the other side of the same scene, with the beings themselves disowning those who worshipped them.
Describes the practice as it operated, men seeking refuge in unseen beings and increasing their burden.
Records a similar speech afterwards, in which the tempter admits he had no power beyond an invitation.

studies.applyIt: Think of an arrangement in your life where two people each get something and neither would describe it out loud. A friendship of mutual flattery, or a work relationship built on cover. Name what each of you is actually collecting. That is the whole exercise here. The naming is uncomfortable. That is because it is usually accurate.
studies.explainEasier: On that day God will gather everyone. The unseen beings and the people who followed them will admit that each side got something out of the other. Now their time is up.

studies.title: Wrongdoers Made Allies
studies.meaning: One short ayah states a principle about how alliances form. Some wrongdoers are made close to others, and the reason given is what they used to earn. Early scholars read this as a natural sorting rather than an imposed punishment. Conduct draws like conduct, and people end up among those whose habits match their own. The verb used is the one for making someone a patron or ally. So what is described is not merely company. It is the protective relationship Arabia was built on.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and it follows a scene where two parties admit openly that each gained. The surah has been describing an opposition that acted together. This ayah explains how such groups form. No occasion is reported. The point would have been instantly clear in a city where alliances between families shifted with shared interest.

keyTerms.gloss: We make allies, set as patrons
keyTerms.note: From the root for nearness that gives the word for a protector, used through this surah. It describes assigning one party to another as ally, not merely allowing them to associate.
From a root meaning to put something out of its place. Wrongdoing in Arabic is misplacement, which fits an ayah about people ending up in the company their conduct has sorted them into.
The commercial verb used at the opening of this surah for what God knows of a person. Its return here makes the alliance a return on conduct rather than an accident of circumstance.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Alliances were formal and sworn. Two clans would bind themselves to defend each other. Such pacts were remembered for generations and recited in poetry. Choosing an ally was the weightiest decision a family made. It was made on shared interest. Everyone understood that you ended up beside people whose way of working matched your own.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb in this ayah shares its root with the word for a protector. The surah has been using that word since its early pages. There it asks whether any protector besides God should be taken. So the same three letters mark two things. They mark the relationship that is denied and the one that forms by default.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Company is presented as a consequence rather than a choice made fresh each time. What a person does draws them toward others doing the same. The passage gives that sorting to God while tying it plainly to conduct. The result is a claim worth taking seriously. The circle you find yourself in is information about you. It built up by a process you were part of without deciding.

crossReferences.why: States the same sorting from both sides, with wrongdoers as allies and God as ally of the mindful.
Describes those who refuse as allies of one another, and warns what follows if that is not answered.
Shows what becomes of such alliances afterwards, when close friends turn into enemies.

studies.applyIt: Look at the five people you spend most time with. Ask what habit you all share that none of you would defend. Not the good things, which are easy to see. This ayah says company forms around conduct. So the shared habit is usually the invisible reason the group works.
studies.explainEasier: In this way God lets people who do wrong become friends and helpers to each other. It happens because of the kind of things they keep doing.

studies.title: Messengers From Among You
studies.meaning: The question put at the gathering is procedural. Did messengers not come to you, from among yourselves, relating My signs and warning of this meeting. The phrase from among you carries the weight, since a messenger of one's own kind removes the excuse of not understanding. The answer is a confession rather than a defence. The ayah adds the explanation without being asked: the life of this world deceived them. Then the confession is repeated, in the narrator's voice.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and the objection answered here has run through the surah from its opening pages. That objection was that a human messenger was not enough. This ayah puts it in the past tense and shows it withdrawn by the people who raised it. The classical scholars discuss the address to both kinds of being. Their readings of how messengers reached the unseen ones vary.

keyTerms.note: Two words that answer the surah's longest-running objection. A messenger of one's own kind is comprehensible and imitable, which is the argument the earlier ayat made about angels at some length.
From the root for following a track, which gives the word for a story. Relating something is described as following its trail, so a narrative is a set of footprints rather than an invention.
The legal verb for giving testimony, used here of the accused testifying against themselves. It turns the scene into a hearing in which the only witness called is the defendant.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A proper hearing in Arabia began by establishing that the parties had been informed. A claim could not proceed if a man had never been told of the duty. Elders would ask first whether notice had been given. The form of the question here follows that procedure exactly. An audience used to arbitration would have recognised the opening move.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb used for the messengers relating the signs comes from the root that gives the Quran its word for a story. The same root produces the verb for tracking an animal by its prints. Narrating and tracing a trail are one action in Arabic. That is why a Quranic story is presented as something followed rather than composed.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage sets out that nobody is answerable for what they were never told. It does so by having the parties confirm it themselves. That makes the whole scene procedural rather than vengeful. The explanation slipped in between the two confessions is the most humane touch. They were deceived by the present life. That is offered not as an excuse but as an accurate account of what happened to them.

crossReferences.why: States the principle plainly, that punishment does not come until a messenger has been sent.
Puts the identical question at the gate, and records the same admission that warners did come.
Gives the fullest version of the exchange, including the answer that a warner came and was denied.

studies.applyIt: Think of a warning you have already received more than once about your health, your work, or a relationship. Not a vague worry, but an actual warning from someone. Write down what it was in one sentence. This ayah turns on whether notice was given. Most of the notices we are given are forgotten rather than refused.
studies.explainEasier: God asks whether messengers from their own kind did not come to them, telling them His signs and warning about this day. They admit that it is true. Life in this world had fooled them.

studies.title: Never While They Were Unaware
studies.meaning: The first ayah gives the reason for the hearing just described. Towns are not destroyed for wrongdoing while their people are unaware. So notice comes before consequence, as a matter of principle. Early scholars read the unawareness as covering those who never received a message at all. The second ayah then refuses a single verdict for everyone. Each has degrees according to what they did. So the outcome is graded rather than sorted into two piles, and nothing anyone did has gone unnoticed.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, closing a sequence about the questioning at the gathering. The surah has spent many ayat on peoples destroyed before. This passage supplies the standard those accounts assume. The Meccans travelled past ruined settlements twice a year, and had been asked repeatedly to consider them. Here they are told what condition every one of those cases met first.

keyTerms.note: From a root for being inattentive to something present. It covers both never having been told and having been told and not attending, and the second ayah's closing clause denies the same quality of God.
Steps of a stair, the same word used earlier in this surah for the raising of Abraham. Its use here for everyone makes the final accounting continuous rather than divided into two categories.
Read by commentators in two ways: destroying them for their wrongdoing, or destroying them unjustly. Both readings are old, and each yields a different emphasis in the same sentence.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabian law worked by warning. A tribe planning to act against another gave formal notice. Treaties were publicly renounced before fighting began. Striking without that step was itself a disgrace. Poetry records the shame of the surprise raid. An audience raised on those customs would hear this ayah as describing a procedure they already took as the mark of honourable dealing.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for heedlessness in the first ayah returns at the end of the second. There it is applied to God in the negative. So the same term does two jobs. It describes the condition that protects people from judgement, and the condition God never occupies. The Arabic makes that symmetry visible, and translations usually lose it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Two principles are stated together, and each limits the other. Nobody is held to what they were never given. Everybody is held to what they did, in degrees. The result is a picture of answering for your life that is neither indiscriminate nor lenient. The final clause also removes the idea that small acts fall below the threshold of notice. That is where most of a life actually happens.

crossReferences.why: States the same rule for earlier towns, that none was destroyed without warners sent as a reminder.
Applies the principle to a mother city, where a messenger is sent before anything is decided.
Repeats the grading of outcomes by what each person did, so that nobody is treated as a category.

studies.applyIt: Notice a rule you enforce at home or at work that people around you have never actually been told. It might be about tidiness, timing, or tone. Say it out loud once this week, before you next hold anyone to it. These ayat make notice the condition of fairness. The same standard is cheap to apply.
studies.explainEasier: Your Lord does not wipe out a town for its wrongdoing while its people have not been warned. Everyone gets a place that fits what they did. Your Lord is never unaware of what people do.

studies.title: Rich Beyond Need, Owner Of Mercy
studies.meaning: Two descriptions are placed side by side, and early scholars note that the pairing does the work. God is free of all need, so nothing is owed to anyone. And He is the owner of mercy, which is why the situation is not what independence alone would produce. What follows is a statement of capacity. He could remove you and put others in your place. That is exactly how you were raised from the descendants of another people. The second ayah closes with a promise that cannot be dodged.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and the reminder about descent from another people had an edge. The city traced its standing through ancestry. Meccan families held their position by lineage and by inherited offices. The surah has already argued that guidance does not travel that way. Here even their existence as a people is described as a succession that replaced someone else.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to be self-sufficient, which also gives the word for wealth. Applied to God it denies need rather than asserting possession, which is why mercy has to be named separately.
From the root for coming after someone, which gives the word for a successor. It names replacement in an office or a place, so the sentence is about position rather than about destruction.
From a root for weakness and inability, in a form meaning to render someone unable. The denial says nothing anyone does can make the promise fail, which is a claim about capacity, not about effort.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabia's history was a history of replacement. Tribes displaced tribes at wells and pastures. The ruins along the trade roads belonged to peoples whose names survived only in poetry. Mecca's own leading tribe had taken custody of the sanctuary from an earlier group. That happened within remembered history. Nobody in that audience needed convincing that one people could follow another.
studies.didYouKnow: The two descriptions opening this passage, free of need and owner of mercy, appear together in this exact pairing only here in the Quran. Each is common on its own. Placed side by side they answer a question the surah has raised repeatedly. Why is anything at all given to people who have nothing to offer.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Independence and mercy are held together, and neither alone would produce what the passage describes. A God who needed something could be bargained with. A God free of need but without mercy would have no reason to send anything. The reminder about succession then removes any sense of entitlement to a place in the world. The promise that follows removes the hope of outlasting the account.

crossReferences.why: States the same two ideas: you are the needy ones, and He could remove you and bring a new creation.
Repeats the capacity for replacement plainly, that He could take you away and bring others.
Says the same thing about creation as a whole, and calls it no great matter for God.

studies.applyIt: Think of a role you hold that will one day belong to someone else. A job, a place in a family, a duty in a community. Picture the person who will hold it after you, without gloom. Then ask what you would want them to inherit from how you are doing it. That question usually clears things up within a minute.
studies.explainEasier: Your Lord needs nothing from anyone, and mercy belongs to Him. If He wanted, He could take you away and put other people in your place. What you are promised is coming, and you cannot stop it.

studies.title: Work, And So Will I
studies.meaning: The instruction sounds almost like a truce, and it is not one. Each side is told to work according to its position, and the speaker says that he is working too. What settles the matter is put off to knowledge that will arrive, not to argument now. You will come to know whose is the outcome of the abode. Early scholars note the confidence in the closing clause. It states plainly that wrongdoers do not come out ahead, so the delay is about timing rather than doubt.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and this formula appears in several surahs from the same period. It is always addressed to a community that had run out of arguments to make. It belongs to the stage where persuasion had been tried at length and was being set down. The classical sources record no specific occasion. The repetition across surahs suggests a standing posture rather than a moment.

keyTerms.note: A noun of place, covering both where a person stands and the standing they have. The word lets the instruction mean work in your own way and according to what you actually are.
From the root for a heel and for following behind, so an outcome is what comes after a thing has passed. The surah has used it earlier when telling listeners to travel and see how peoples ended.
From a root meaning to split open ground for planting, which gives the word for a farmer. Success in Arabic is a harvest reached, so failure here means never arriving at what was worked for.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Farming in an oasis was a long wager. Ground was cleared, water rights secured and palms planted years before anything came back. Nobody claimed a result until the harvest was in the store. The word for success in this ayah belongs to that world. It explains why the answer offered here is not an argument but an invitation to wait for the crop.
studies.didYouKnow: This exact instruction appears in three separate places in the Quran. It tells opponents to work in their own way while the speaker works in his. Each place is a different surah, and each is spoken by a messenger to his own people. The repetition marks it as the standard closing move when persuasion has run out.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage models disagreement that has stopped pretending talk will resolve it. And it does so without hostility. Both sides are told to act. That treats the opponent as a serious agent rather than an obstacle. The appeal is to an outcome rather than to an argument. That places the matter under time, where it can actually be settled. The last clause makes clear that the speaker is not neutral about which way it will go.

crossReferences.why: Puts the identical instruction in the mouth of an earlier prophet addressing his own community.
Repeats the same formula in another Meccan surah, followed by a promise that they will know.
Describes whose the final home is: those who seek no superiority on earth and cause no corruption.

studies.applyIt: Pick an argument you have been having in your head with someone who is not going to agree. Stop making the case. Instead, spend one hour this week doing the thing you have been trying to justify. This ayah's move is to answer a dispute with work. It is usually the only answer that lands.
studies.explainEasier: Keep working in your own way, and I will keep working in mine. You will find out in the end who gets the better home. People who do wrong never come out on top.

studies.title: This Share Is For God
studies.meaning: A custom is described with unusual precision. Produce and livestock were divided in two. One portion went to God and one to the objects worshipped beside Him. Then the accounting is exposed. What was set aside for the partners never reached God, while what was set aside for God found its way to them. Early scholars explain that shortfalls were made up in one direction only. The closing judgement is brief, and it is about the arithmetic rather than the theology.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and the practice was real and locally recorded. Arabian communities set aside a share of harvest and herds for religious use. It was split between the high God and the shrine deities. The produce fed guests, custodians and the poor. The surah's closing section turns from argument to these inherited customs. It describes several of them before answering.

keyTerms.note: A verb for scattering and propagating, used of God producing creatures in abundance. Placing it in the sentence reminds the audience whose the crops and herds were before any division was made.
Land that has been ploughed and what grows on it, from the root for tilling. Paired with livestock it covers the two forms of wealth an agricultural society had, so the custom touched everything.
The same phrase used earlier in this surah for assertions made without support. Inserted in the middle of the sentence, it marks the words this is for God as their description rather than the ayah's.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Harvest allocation was public and watched. A family separated portions on the threshing floor while neighbours saw it done. The shares had names and customary sizes. Livestock were divided the same way at particular seasons. Because everyone could see the piles, any quiet adjustment between them was a social act as much as a religious one. People knew who did it.
studies.didYouKnow: This ayah preserves an unusually specific piece of pre-Islamic religious practice. It describes a division of produce that other sources also record. The surah's closing section works almost as a catalogue of such customs. It names four or five distinct ones in a few ayat. It is one of the earliest written sources for them.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The complaint is not that they gave. It is that the giving was quietly arranged to favour the recipient who could be seen. Everything named was created and provided in the first place. That makes the division a matter of returning rather than donating. The principle reaches past the specific custom. Any portion set aside for God that is later found useful for something else was never really set aside.

crossReferences.why: Records the same practice, assigning a portion of what was provided to what they do not even know.
Asks about provision that people have themselves divided into permitted and forbidden portions.
Addresses the same instinct in giving, not selecting the poorer part to give away.

studies.applyIt: Look at what you set aside for good purposes. Check whether any of it quietly comes back to you: a donation that buys standing, help offered where it will be noticed. You do not have to stop. Just find out which portion is actually leaving your hands. That is what this ayah is measuring.
studies.explainEasier: They took part of their crops and animals. This share is for God, they said, and this share is for our idols. But the idols' share never reached God. God's share always ended up with the idols.

studies.title: Made To Seem Right
studies.meaning: The gravest of the customs is named, the killing of children, and the ayah is careful about how it happened. It was made to look right to them. So the practice arrived dressed as duty rather than as cruelty. Two purposes are given for that dressing. One is to ruin them. The other is to confuse their religion until they could no longer tell what belonged to it. Early scholars note the sentence about God's will, which denies that the practice was beyond preventing. Then comes the instruction to leave them to their inventions.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and the practice was real in parts of Arabia. The classical sources differ on how widespread it was. Motives recorded include fear of poverty and shame at the birth of daughters. The Quran addresses it in several surahs from this period and always names it directly, without softening. That is itself a comment on how it was normally discussed.

keyTerms.note: The same verb the surah uses for conduct dressed up until it looks acceptable. Its appearance here explains how something monstrous was carried out by ordinary people who believed themselves in the right.
From a root meaning to fall into a pit or perish. It names destruction by falling rather than by being struck, which suits a practice adopted step by step and defended each time.
From the root for clothing, so confusion is something laid over a thing. The surah has used the same verb twice already, of confusion put over a question and over a community.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Life at the edge of subsistence made every extra dependant a calculation. Drought years forced households into decisions they would not otherwise face. Daughters also carried the risk of capture in a raid, which brought a family lasting shame. These pressures do not excuse anything. They explain how a custom could be defended by people who thought of themselves as responsible.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran returns to this practice in several passages. Each time it attacks the reasoning rather than only the act. It names the fear of poverty in one place and the shame at a daughter's birth in another. One late Meccan surah puts the question to the child directly, asking for what offence she was killed.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage names the mechanism by which people do terrible things. The thing is presented to them as right. That is a more useful account than calling it wickedness, because it can be checked from the inside. It also names the second damage. Once such a practice is folded into religion, the religion itself becomes unreadable, and people lose the ability to tell what it actually asks of them.

crossReferences.why: Addresses the stated motive directly, answering fear of poverty with who provides for whom.
Describes the shame at a daughter's birth and the decision made in secret from the community.
Puts the question to the child herself on that day, asking for what sin she was killed.

studies.applyIt: Notice something your own society finds normal that you suspect will be looked back on with horror. Say what it is, even if only to yourself. Notice how quickly the justifications arrive. That arrival is the mechanism this ayah names. Catching it working in your own reasoning is the point of the exercise.
studies.explainEasier: Their idols made killing their own children look like the right thing to do. It ruined them and it muddled their religion. God could have stopped it, so leave them to what they make up.

studies.title: Reserved For Whom We Please
studies.meaning: Three customs are listed in one ayah. Certain livestock and crops were declared restricted, with access limited to those the owners permitted. Certain animals had their backs put off limits, so nobody rode them. Over some, no name of God was pronounced. Early scholars explain each as a vow made about an animal after a number of births or a successful journey. The phrase inserted twice does the work: by their claim, and inventing about Him. The restrictions were real. The source they gave for them was not.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and the customs named here appear elsewhere in the Quran under their Arabic names. They are also known from other sources. They were serious commitments. An animal set aside was never worked or sold, which cost the household real wealth, and the practice was regarded as piety. The surah has just described a division of harvest in the same register.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to prevent or enclose, which gives the word for a lap and for a stone enclosure. The term names a barrier put around something rather than a quality the thing has.
The plural of back, naming what was placed off limits. An animal that could not be ridden or loaded was a household's wealth taken permanently out of use, which is what made the vow costly.
The verbal noun from the root used through this surah for fabricating. Placed at the end as a summary, it names the whole set of customs by what they have in common rather than one by one.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A camel dedicated by vow was recognisable and left alone. It grazed where it liked. It was not milked for the household, and it was never loaded. Everyone in the settlement knew which animal it was. The cost was visible and so was the piety. That is part of why the practice held. Giving up a working animal was a public statement about a family's seriousness.
studies.didYouKnow: A later Medinan passage names four of these dedicated animal categories by their Arabic terms. It states that God did not appoint any of them. Take that passage and this one together. The Quran keeps a fairly detailed record of pre-Islamic Arabian religious practice. It is not written down in this much detail anywhere else.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage takes costly and sincere piety and asks one question about it. Where did the requirement come from. Sacrifice does not authorise a claim. That is a demanding standard, and it applies as much to restrictions people put on themselves as to those they put on others. The phrase about inventing against God places the whole practice in the same category as the surah's gravest charge.

crossReferences.why: Names four of these dedicated animal categories directly and denies that any was appointed by God.
Asks who authorised the division of provision into what is permitted and what is withheld.
Warns against tongues that declare things lawful and unlawful, inventing about God.

studies.applyIt: Think of a personal discipline you keep that costs you something and that you privately regard as a mark of seriousness. Ask where it came from. If it is your own good idea, keep it and call it that. This ayah is not against costly practices. It is against the small upgrade from my practice to God's requirement.
studies.explainEasier: They said some animals and crops were off limits, and only the people they chose could eat them. They said other animals must never be ridden. Over some they never said God's name. They made all this up.

studies.title: Reserved For Our Males
studies.meaning: Another custom is quoted, and its structure exposes itself. What is in the wombs of certain animals is reserved for the men and withheld from their wives. Then comes the detail that undoes the whole claim. If it is stillborn, everyone shares. Early scholars note how exact the observation is. A rule presented as a boundary set by God turns out to send the valuable portion one way and the worthless portion to everyone. That is a distribution rather than a restriction.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, in the surah's closing survey of inherited customs. Arabian food restrictions often divided along lines of sex and status. They were understood as religious duties rather than as preferences. The Quran's method here is to state each custom in the practitioners' own words and let the arrangement be seen. This one is described with more precision than the others.

keyTerms.note: From the root for something unmixed, which also gives the word for sincerity. Its use for a portion reserved to one group makes the claim of purity sit oddly beside what the rest of the ayah reports.
The plural of a word meaning one of a pair, used for husband and wife alike. Its presence names exactly who was excluded, so the arrangement cannot be described in neutral terms.
A verbal noun for characterising something in a certain way. What will be repaid is named as the describing itself, so the fault is located in the act of labelling rather than only in the practice.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Meat divided at a household was divided by rank. Everyone present could see who received which cut. Women often ate after the men, and from what remained. In a subsistence economy these shares mattered for health, not only for show. A rule keeping the best portion for one group had physical effects that everyone in the compound felt.
studies.didYouKnow: The word used for the exclusive portion in this ayah comes from a notable root. Elsewhere that root gives the Quran its term for sincerity. It also gives the word for worship made pure for God alone. So the same three letters name undivided devotion and, here, a claim of exclusive right to a piece of meat.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage shows a method rather than only condemning a custom. When a rule claimed to come from God keeps benefiting the people who state it, that pattern is itself evidence about where the rule came from. The test needs no theology to apply. It was offered to an audience who could check it against their own kitchens. What is repaid, the ayah says, is the describing.

crossReferences.why: Applies the same test to another claim, calling a division that favours the claimant an unfair one.
Records the same asymmetry, assigning to God what they did not want for themselves.
Corrects the underlying assumption, since both sons and daughters are given as God wills.

studies.applyIt: Look at a rule in your household or workplace that you helped make, and check who it benefits when it is inconvenient. Not who it was meant to benefit. If the answer is consistently you, that is worth knowing. This ayah's test is simple arithmetic. It works without anyone needing to be accused of anything.
studies.explainEasier: They said the young inside these animals belonged only to their men. Their wives could not have any. But if it was born dead, then everyone could share it.

studies.title: They Forbade What Was Given
studies.meaning: The verdict on the whole sequence arrives, and it puts two very different things in one sentence. Killing children and declaring provision off limits are both named as loss. Both are traced to the same root: acting without knowledge and inventing about God. Early scholars note the word used for the folly, which means lightness of mind rather than malice. What is lost is not property but the people themselves. The closing clause states the outcome twice over.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, closing the survey of inherited customs. The two practices named were not connected in the minds of those who kept them. One was a hard economic decision and the other was piety. The surah joins them because both rested on a claim about what God had set up, made by people who had received nothing on the subject. No occasion is reported for this ayah.

keyTerms.note: From a root for lightness and instability, used of a garment flapping loosely. It names a mind without weight rather than a wicked one, which is a specific and less comfortable accusation.

The verb behind the Quranic word for provision, covering food, livelihood and anything that sustains. Its presence makes the restriction a refusal of something already given rather than an act of restraint.
The commercial verb for a deal ending in deficit, used at the opening of this surah of those who lost themselves. The particle before it marks the loss as accomplished rather than threatened.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Both practices came from the same fear about scarcity. One household worked out whether it could feed another mouth. Another set aside an animal it could not use. Both were managing a thin margin. Both believed they were doing something responsible. The Quran answers that fear directly in other passages. It names who actually provides for whom.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for folly in this ayah is used elsewhere in the Quran of those who are not competent to manage property. It is also used of the one who turns away from the way of Abraham. It describes a lack of weight in judgement. The classical dictionaries connect it to a rope or a garment that will not hold steady.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Two practices at opposite ends of severity are traced to one failure. That failure is speaking for God without having been told anything. That common root is the surah's central concern. Placing an unbearable act beside a merely mistaken one shows something. The range of consequences from a single error can be very wide. The passage also treats provision as given. So restricting it is described as refusing something rather than declining it.

crossReferences.why: Asks directly who forbade the good things of provision that God produced for His servants.
Names the fear behind the first practice and answers it with who provides for parent and child alike.
Warns against declaring unlawful the good things made lawful, and against overstepping in either direction.

studies.applyIt: Notice a decision you are making mainly from fear of not having enough. A hesitation about hospitality, an unwillingness to commit time. Name the fear rather than the reason you usually give. This ayah traces two very different failures to the same fear. And the fear is easier to address than the decisions built on it.
studies.explainEasier: They have lost everything. They kill their own children out of foolishness, with no real knowledge. They ban the food God gave them. They made it up about God, and they have gone off the path.

studies.title: Give Its Due At Harvest
studies.meaning: After the false restrictions comes the real instruction, and it has three parts. Eat of the fruit when it yields. Give its due on the day of harvest. And do not be excessive. Early scholars differ over what exactly the due refers to. Some read it as the later required portion, and others as the general giving to the poor at harvest time. The tradition records the range. The timing is the striking detail: on the day, before the crop has become a stored possession.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and this places the instruction before the detailed Medinan arrangements for giving were set up. That is why the scholars differ about its scope. The gardens described, some trellised and some not, belong to the oasis farming of the region rather than to Mecca's own bare valley. The passage answers the preceding customs by describing what was actually asked.

keyTerms.note: From the root for a structure raised up, used of vines trained over frames. Pairing it with untrellised covers cultivated and wild growth, so nothing that grows falls outside the sentence.
The word for a right owed rather than a favour offered. Calling the portion a due makes the recipient a claimant, which changes the posture of both giver and receiver.
From a root for going past a proper limit. Commentators apply it to both consumption and giving, since exceeding what is reasonable in generosity was also understood as a form of excess.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Harvest day was public in an oasis. The dates were cut, piled and divided while neighbours and the poor of the settlement stood there. The customary shares were handed out on the spot rather than sent later. Giving at that moment cost nothing extra in effort, and it was visible to everyone. Once the crop went into store, it belonged to the household in a different way.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase about not being excessive appears in almost the same form in another Meccan surah. There it is attached to eating and drinking. Both times it closes with the same clause about what God does not love. Pairing a permission with a limit in one sentence is characteristic of these passages.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The instruction begins with permission and ends with a limit, and the giving sits between them. That structure is worth noticing. Enjoyment is not treated as suspect. What is asked is that a portion is recognised as owed at the moment the wealth arrives, before ownership has settled. Calling that portion a due rather than a gift removes the giver's advantage over the receiver entirely.

crossReferences.why: States the same principle about wealth generally, that a known share belongs to those in need.
Repeats the closing clause about excess almost word for word, applied to eating and drinking.
Extends the warning about waste, calling the wasteful brothers of the devils.

studies.applyIt: The next time money arrives unexpectedly, give a portion of it away on the same day. Do not wait until you have thought about it. The timing is the whole instruction here. A sum that has sat in your account for a week feels like yours. A sum arriving this morning does not.
studies.explainEasier: God grows the gardens, the date palms, the crops, the olives and the pomegranates. Eat the fruit when it is ready. Give away its share on harvest day. Do not waste it.

studies.title: The Footsteps Of An Enemy
studies.meaning: Livestock are described by their uses. Some are large enough to carry loads, and some are kept low for other benefits. Early scholars differ over the exact sense of the second word. Then two instructions follow. Eat of what God provided, which reopens what the customs had closed. And do not follow the footsteps of the enemy. The image is precise. Not his commands but his footprints, meaning a path walked one step at a time by someone who never decided to take it.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and the passage is taking apart a system of inherited restrictions that had built up gradually. Nobody in the city had adopted the whole set at once. Each generation had received it and added to it. The image of following footsteps rather than orders describes exactly that process. That is why it appears here rather than in a passage about open defiance.

keyTerms.note: From the verb for carrying, naming animals large enough to bear loads. It classifies livestock by function rather than by kind, which is how a herding household actually thought about them.
From the root for spreading something out, and read by commentators as smaller animals close to the ground, or as what their wool and hides are spread out to make. Both senses are preserved.
The plural of a single stride. Following footprints is different from obeying instructions, since each step is small, plausible and connected only to the one before it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Tracking was a universal skill. A herdsman could read from prints in sand which animal had passed and how long ago. He could tell whether it was loaded. Children learned to follow a trail before they could read anything else. Following footsteps was therefore an image of something done confidently and half-consciously, eyes on the ground, without needing to know where the trail leads.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase about following the footsteps of the enemy appears four times in the Quran. Every one is in a passage about ordinary conduct rather than grand wrongdoing. The subjects are food, wealth, gossip and the treatment of others. The image is kept for gradual drift rather than for dramatic rebellion.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Character is described as forming through steps rather than decisions, which is both a warning and a relief. Nobody chooses a whole direction at once. So nobody has to reverse one at once either. The instruction to eat what was provided also matters here. Undoing a restriction that had no warrant is treated as part of good conduct, not as laxity. That keeps the passage from being read as a call for more caution.

crossReferences.why: Uses the identical phrase, joining permission to eat what is good with the warning about footsteps.
Applies the same image to speech and reputation, where the first step looks entirely harmless.
Describes livestock by their benefits at greater length, including warmth, food and transport.

studies.applyIt: Think of a habit you would not have accepted three years ago, and trace the individual steps that got you there. There will be about five, and each will have been reasonable. This ayah's image is a trail rather than a decision. Trails can be walked back the same way they were walked in.
studies.explainEasier: Some animals carry loads and some give wool and hides. Eat the food God has given you. Do not walk in the footsteps of Satan. He is a clear enemy to you.

studies.title: Eight Pairs Of Livestock
studies.meaning: The argument becomes forensic. Eight pairs are counted out, starting with sheep and goats. Then the question is put with no room left in it. Was it the two males that were withheld, or the two females, or what the females carry. Every possibility is listed, so no answer can be improvised. Early scholars note that the customs being challenged did not fall neatly into any of these categories. That is the point. The demand that closes it is for knowledge, not for an opinion.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and the counting is deliberate. The audience's restrictions applied to certain animals in certain cases. They came from vows and inherited practice, not from any principle. So the whole herd is set out as eight pairs. Then the question asks which group was named. That forces a general rule to be produced where only local customs existed.

keyTerms.note: The plural of a word for one of a pair, so eight pairs means four kinds counted by male and female. The Quran uses the same word of human spouses and of created things generally.
From the root for a garment wrapped around the body. Applied to a womb it describes enclosure rather than possession, which keeps the third option in the question distinct from the first two.
An imperative from the root behind the words for weighty news and for a prophet. Demanding information in that form asks for something with a source behind it, not for a report of what people do.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The four animals named were the whole of a household's wealth. Sheep and goats gave milk, wool and meat, and were counted daily. Camels carried loads and crossed deserts. Cattle worked the land at the oases. A man's standing was stated in numbers of these. Dividing them into eight pairs was how anyone would have taken an inventory.
studies.didYouKnow: The counting of livestock as eight pairs appears again in another surah. There it is listed among God's provisions rather than used as an argument. So the same list serves twice. Once it describes what was given, and once it frames a question about what was withheld.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage insists that a claim about God's requirements be stated as a general rule that can be examined. The demand for knowledge at the end sets the standard. This is a method rather than a doctrine, and it applies wherever practice hardens into obligation. Listing creation as pairs also does quiet work. The animals under dispute are presented first as things given, before they are argued about.

crossReferences.why: Lists the same eight pairs among what was sent down for people, without any argument attached.
Names pairing as a feature of creation generally, among humans and among the livestock alike.
Describes what these animals were given for, which the customs under dispute had partly cancelled.

studies.applyIt: Take a rule you have been told is required, and try to state it as a general principle, in one sentence, without naming the particular case. Some rules survive this and some do not. The ayah's method is exactly that translation. It usually takes about a minute to find out which kind you have.
studies.explainEasier: There are eight kinds of farm animals, counted as male and female. Ask them which ones God banned. Was it the two males, the two females, or the young inside the mothers. Tell me, if you really know.

studies.title: Were You There To Witness
studies.meaning: The same count is repeated for camels and cattle. Then a new question is added that goes past the content to the source. Were you present when God charged you with this. Early scholars note that the demand shifts from producing a rule to producing an occasion, which nobody could do. The ayah then names the wrongdoing directly. And it adds a purpose clause missing earlier: inventing about God in order to mislead people. That makes the fault social as well as personal.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, completing the challenge begun in the previous ayah. Religious authority in Arabia rested on inherited custom, and nobody claimed a moment of instruction behind it. So the question about being present had no available answer. The surah knows that. It is asked to make the absence of any source audible, not to receive a reply.

keyTerms.note: The word covers both being present at an event and testifying to it. The question uses the first sense to expose the absence of the second, since no one can testify to what they did not attend.
A verb for entrusting an instruction to someone, used for a solemn charge and for a will. The same verb returns a few ayat later, introducing what God actually did enjoin.
A purpose clause naming the effect of the invention on other people. It turns a private fabrication into an act with victims, which is why the ayah's judgement is stated in its strongest form.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Testimony in Arabia meant having been there. A man's word carried weight in proportion to whether he had seen the event himself. Hearsay was known to be weaker, even where nothing was written down. Asking whether someone was present when an instruction was given was a standard move in a dispute. Everyone knew what an evasive answer to it meant.
studies.didYouKnow: The question about being present when something was decreed appears in a similar form in another surah. There it is asked of people who described the angels as female. Both times the challenge is the same. A claim about the unseen is met not with a counterargument but with a question about attendance.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage sets a standard for religious claims that is procedural rather than doctrinal. It asks where a rule came from before it asks whether the rule is right. That standard is uncomfortable in every generation. Much of what any community treats as required arrived without an occasion anyone can name. The added clause is about misleading others. It makes clear why the Quran treats this as the gravest kind of wrong.

crossReferences.why: Asks the same question of another claim, whether they witnessed the creation of what they describe.
States the same judgement earlier in this surah, on inventing against God or denying His signs.
Names the practice directly, tongues declaring things permitted or withheld and inventing about God.

studies.applyIt: Ask about one religious practice you keep whether you could say where it comes from. Say it in one sentence, to someone who asked sincerely. If you cannot, that is a research task rather than a reason to stop. This ayah's question is about sources. Knowing yours makes a practice steadier rather than shakier.
studies.explainEasier: Ask the same about camels and cattle. Were you standing there when God told you to do this. Nobody does worse than a person who makes up lies about God to lead people astray.

studies.title: Nothing That I Find
studies.meaning: The answer to a long argument is a report rather than a ruling. He does not find, in what was revealed to him, anything withheld from someone eating, except a short and specific list. Early scholars note the wording. It describes searching a text and reporting the result, so nothing is being decided in the moment. What closes the ayah is not a warning. Someone driven to it by necessity, without seeking it out or overstepping, is met with two names of mercy.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and this is the surah's direct answer to the customs it has been describing. The list given is short, and other passages in the Quran give it in nearly identical terms. The scholars discuss its relation to those parallels at length. What is agreed is the contrast being drawn. An elaborate inherited system sits on one side, and a brief answer on the other.

keyTerms.note: The verb for finding something on searching. Reporting a search rather than issuing a decision keeps the speaker in the position of a reader of what was given, which the whole surah has insisted on.
From a root for raising the voice, which also gives the word for a new crescent moon greeted with shouts. It names the act of announcing a name aloud, which is what makes the dedication meaningful.
Two names that close many Quranic passages where a limit has just been stated. The first covers what is concealed and pardoned, the second a mercy that is given rather than earned.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Necessity was not imagined. Famine years, a caravan that ran short, or a family cut off by drought put people in front of hard decisions. They would never otherwise face them. The sources describe communities in real starvation. The clause about compulsion was not written for an unusual case. It answered a situation many in the audience had seen or would see.
studies.didYouKnow: This list appears in four places across the Quran, in Meccan and Medinan surahs. Every one carries the same clause about someone compelled by necessity. That consistency is unusual for a passage of this kind. The scholars treat the repeated exception as inseparable from the list itself.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Brevity is the argument. After many ayat describing customs added by inheritance and vow, the answer is short enough to remember. That says something about the difference between what was given and what gathered around it. The closing names then govern the whole passage. A limit that ends in forgiveness and mercy is a different kind of thing from one that ends in a threat. The ayah puts them in that order.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same short list with the same exception, in another Meccan setting.
Repeats the list and the clause about compulsion, adding that God is forgiving and merciful.
Sets out the fullest version in a Medinan surah, ending again with the exception for necessity.

studies.applyIt: Think of someone you know who is in a hard spot. They have done something you would not do. Before judging it, ask what their options actually were. This ayah attaches an exception for need to every statement of a limit. Give the same courtesy to a person you know. It takes only a moment's imagination.
studies.explainEasier: In what was sent down to me I find only a short list of food to keep away from. It is dead meat, flowing blood, pork, and meat named for someone other than God. If you are forced by need, your Lord forgives.

studies.title: That Was Their Recompense
studies.meaning: A different and longer set of restrictions is described, given to an earlier community. The ayah is specific about which parts were included and which were not. Early scholars note the detail. The exceptions are named as carefully as the restrictions. The reason given is stated plainly. This was a repayment for a particular overstepping. So the limits were consequences rather than permanent features. The ayah then closes with a claim of truthfulness about the account itself.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and the comparison is being made for the audience in front of the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him). The surah has just described customs invented without authority. Here it describes limits that had a source and a stated reason. Other passages in the Quran describe the same restrictions in similar terms. The classical commentaries read the two accounts together.

keyTerms.note: The word for a claw or an undivided hoof, and the commentators differ over how widely it extends. The range of their readings is preserved rather than settled, which is characteristic of the vocabulary here.
The plural of a word for animal fat, a valuable food in a lean economy. Naming the exceptions in detail keeps the restriction bounded rather than sweeping, which is the ayah's evident concern.
From a root for seeking and then for exceeding a limit. It names a specific transgression rather than a character, which is why the ayah gives a reason instead of a verdict on a people.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Communities following earlier scriptures lived across the region and in Arabian towns. They traded and farmed alongside their neighbours. Their food practices were visible and known. Meccans travelling north met them regularly. So the audience for this ayah knew the restrictions being described. That is why they could be named without explanation.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran describes these restrictions in two other places. One of them adds a detail worth noting. All food had been permitted before, apart from what one forefather had withheld from himself. The three passages together present the limits as arising within history rather than as belonging to it from the start.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage draws a distinction the surrounding ayat depend on. Restrictions can come from God, in which case they have a source, a scope and a reason. Or they can gather without any of the three. Naming a cause for these limits keeps them understandable rather than arbitrary. The closing statement about truthfulness attaches to the account, which the surah offers as something checkable rather than asserted.

crossReferences.why: Notes that food had been permitted before, apart from what one forefather withheld from himself.
Describes the same limits and gives the same reason, naming the specific conduct behind them.
Refers back to this passage and adds that the wrong done was to themselves rather than to God.

studies.applyIt: Think of a restriction you live under that arrived as a consequence of something. A rule at work after an incident, a limit in a relationship after a breach. Ask whether the reason still holds. Rules with reasons can be revisited. This ayah is careful to give one, which is what makes that possible.
studies.explainEasier: For the Jewish people God banned every animal with claws, and much of the fat of cattle and sheep. That was a payback for a wrong they had done. God tells the truth.

studies.title: Mercy Wide, Yet Not Averted
studies.meaning: The instruction for being called a liar is not a defence. Tell them their Lord possesses a mercy that is wide, and then add the second half without softening either. Early scholars note the order. Mercy is named first and at greater length, and the word used for its breadth is the one applied elsewhere to knowledge that takes everything in. The second clause states a limit that is not about severity but about direction. What comes is not turned back from those who have earned it.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and the accusation of lying was constant rather than occasional. The surah has recorded it in several forms already. Placing a statement about mercy in the mouth of someone just called a liar is a striking choice. The classical sources treat it as typical of the Meccan period. Then the answer to hostility was repeatedly a description of God rather than a rebuttal.

keyTerms.note: From the verb for containing something with room to spare, used earlier in this surah of God's knowledge. Applied to mercy it says the same thing: nothing falls outside for lack of capacity.
A passive verb for something sent back the way it came. The denial is about deflection rather than about force, so what is described is a consequence that cannot be redirected once it is moving.
From a root for cutting or severing, connected to harvesting. The word names people by their acts rather than by their beliefs, which keeps the category defined by conduct.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A protector in Arabia could shelter a man from consequences. The whole system of clan patronage worked by turning claims aside. A powerful patron could make a debt or a blood claim simply stop. Everyone in the audience knew that the question was never whether you were guilty. It was whether someone would stand between you and the claim. This ayah addresses that expectation directly.
