studies.didYouKnow: The pairing of an assurance of mercy with a statement of consequence occurs repeatedly in the Quran. It often comes within a single ayah. The mercy is almost always named first. The classical commentaries treat the ordering as deliberate, so that hope is set down before any limit is described.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Both halves are given to the same audience at the same moment. That resists the instinct to sort people into those who need encouragement and those who need warning. The passage assumes a listener can hold both. The word used for mercy's breadth also matters. It is not that mercy is large enough for most cases. It is that capacity is not the constraint at all, which places the question entirely elsewhere.

crossReferences.why: States the same breadth directly, that His mercy encompasses everything there is.
Puts the assurance in its most open form, addressed to those who have gone furthest against themselves.
Places forgiveness, acceptance of repentance and severity in one sequence of names.

studies.applyIt: Notice which half of this you usually reach for. Some of us tend to comfort people and some to warn them. Most of us lean one way and think it is balance. Once this week, say the half you would normally leave out, in the same conversation. The ayah gives both to the same listener in one sentence.
studies.explainEasier: If they call you a liar, tell them this. Your Lord has mercy wide enough for everyone. But what is coming for guilty people cannot be turned away.

studies.title: Had God Willed, We Would Not
studies.meaning: The objection is predicted before it is made, and it is the strongest one available to them. If God had willed otherwise, none of this would have happened, so the practice is evidence of His will. Early scholars note that the ayah does not deny the premise. It observes that earlier peoples argued the same way, and that the argument did not protect them. Then it asks for what the objection lacks: any knowledge that could be produced. What is left is guesswork and estimation.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and the argument recorded here was in active use. The surah has already stated more than once that God could have gathered everyone onto guidance. So the objectors were quoting a principle the message itself stated. The classical scholars treat the response as addressing the use being made of a true statement rather than the statement itself.

keyTerms.note: The verb of tasting used through this surah for consequence experienced directly. Its appearance here marks the end of the earlier peoples' argument, which was not refuted but simply overtaken by events.

keyTerms.gloss: so you may bring it out
keyTerms.note: A verb for producing something from where it is kept, as goods are brought out for inspection. The demand is for evidence to be shown rather than described, which is what an appeal to knowledge means here.
The technical term for assessing a standing crop by eye, used earlier in this surah of the majority. Its return here labels a theological argument with a word from agricultural approximation.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Fate was a serious idea in pre-Islamic Arabia. Poetry gives deaths, losses and fortunes to time or to fate. The attitude ran deep enough to shape how people spoke about their own choices. The objection recorded here was not invented for the occasion. It drew on an existing habit of explaining what had happened by saying it was always going to.
studies.didYouKnow: This objection is quoted in at least three places in the Quran, in almost identical words each time. It is never answered by denying that God's will governs events. The response is always about what the speakers can actually produce. That is a consistent handling of the same argument across separate surahs.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage separates a truth from the use made of it. That God's will governs what happens is stated throughout the Quran, including a few ayat later. What the objectors do is turn it into a defence. The answer points out that they have no access to the premise they are invoking. Nobody can consult God's will in advance. So it cannot work as a reason for a course of action already chosen.

crossReferences.why: Records the same objection almost word for word, and answers by describing what messengers were for.
Preserves another version of it, adding that they have no knowledge of what they assert.
Follows immediately and affirms the premise itself, that He could have guided everyone.

studies.applyIt: Catch yourself explaining a choice you made by saying it was meant to be, or that you had no option. Sometimes that is true. Once today, when you hear yourself say it, ask what you would have done differently if you had believed the choice was yours. The answer is usually available at once.
studies.explainEasier: They say that if God had wanted, they would not have worshipped anything else, and they would not have banned any food. People before them said the same and then felt what came. Ask them to show what they actually know.

studies.title: The Conclusive Argument
studies.meaning: Two short clauses, and the second concedes what the objectors had just claimed. The conclusive argument belongs to God, and had He willed, He would have guided everyone. Early scholars note the word for the argument. It names the case that reaches its destination and settles a dispute. What is denied is not the premise but its ownership. The objectors were using God's will as their argument. The ayah says the argument that arrives is His, and then states exactly what they said.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, placed immediately after the objection it answers. The surah has been making a sustained case for many ayat. This is close to its final word on who can settle the matter. No occasion is reported. The pairing of the two ayat, objection and answer, is one of the clearest examples of the surah's method of quoting an argument fully before responding.

keyTerms.note: The decisive case in a dispute, the same word used earlier in this surah of the reasoning given to Abraham. Both times it is described as belonging to God rather than to the person making it.
From the verb for arriving at a destination, used earlier in this surah of the recitation reaching whomever it reaches. An argument described this way is one that gets all the way there.
An emphatic word for totality placed at the end for weight. It closes off any reading in which some would have been guided and others left, which is the softening a listener might have looked for.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A dispute in Arabia ended when one side produced a case the other could not answer. Everyone present recognised the moment. The word for such an argument was in ordinary use. Saying that the conclusive one belongs to God described the end of a hearing. It did not describe a stage in it. An audience trained on public arbitration would have heard exactly that.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for a conclusive argument appears in the Quran a handful of times. One is in a passage explaining why messengers were sent at all. It was so that people would have no argument against God afterwards. The same term therefore marks both what God holds and what human beings are left without.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah states an uncomfortable premise rather than dodging it. That is what makes the preceding answer honest. God could have guided everyone and did not. What the passage refuses is the move from that fact to a defence. Nobody can invoke a decision they were not party to. The result concedes everything about God's will. It concedes nothing about what people answer for.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same word, saying messengers were sent so that no argument would remain against God.
States the same conditional about people being made one community, and what followed instead.
Holds both sides in two lines: whoever wills may take a way, and willing itself is within God's will.

studies.applyIt: Notice the difference between accepting that something was in God's hands after it happens and using that to decide what to do beforehand. The first is trust and the second is not. Pick one decision you are facing and make it on the reasons available to you. Then hand the outcome over afterwards. That order is what this ayah keeps.
studies.explainEasier: The final proof belongs to God. If He had wanted to, He could have guided every single one of you. That is what the ayah says, and it says nothing more.

studies.title: Bring Your Witnesses Forward
studies.meaning: The challenge becomes a summons. Bring your witnesses who will testify that God withheld this. Then an instruction follows that expects them to appear: if they testify, do not testify with them. Early scholars note the assumption built into the sentence. Witnesses could well be produced, and their number would prove nothing. The rest of the ayah names three things about the people whose leanings are not to be followed. Each is a description rather than an insult.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and the summons uses the vocabulary of Arabian dispute settlement. There a claim was supported by producing men who would swear to it. Numbers and standing mattered more than what the witnesses had actually seen. The surah has been asking for a source for these customs across several ayat. This is the last and most formal version of the request.

keyTerms.note: An imperative of summoning, unchanged for number or gender in the dialect the Quran preserves. Its abruptness gives the challenge the tone of a courtroom rather than of a discussion.
A prohibition against joining a testimony, not against hearing it. It separates the act of witnessing from the act of being present, which is the distinction on which the whole instruction rests.
The same verb that closes the very first ayah of this surah, where those who refuse set up equals to their Lord. Its return here brings the surah's argument back to where it began.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Producing witnesses was how a case was won. A man with more supporters of higher standing prevailed. The content of what they swore to was often less important than who they were. Testimony was an act of alignment as much as of reporting. That is precisely why the instruction here separates being present from adding your own voice to what is said.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb that closes this ayah is the same one that closes the opening ayah of the surah. That ayah describes those who set up equals to their Lord. More than a hundred and forty ayat apart, the two uses frame the whole argument. So the surah's closing challenge returns to the word it began with.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Truthfulness is treated as something separate from consensus, and the instruction makes that separation practical. Others may testify. You are not required to contradict them, only not to join. That is a workable form of integrity for someone outnumbered. That is what the audience for this ayah was. The passage also connects following leanings to disbelief in the hereafter. What a person can afford to say depends on what they expect.

crossReferences.why: Describes standing firm as witnesses for God even against oneself or one's own relatives.
Asks who does greater wrong than one who conceals a testimony that he holds from God.
Asks the same question a few ayat earlier, whether they were present when this was enjoined.

studies.applyIt: Think of the last time a group agreed on something you did not believe, and you nodded along. The ayah does not ask you to argue. It asks you not to add your own voice to it. That is a smaller and much more achievable thing. Practise the silence once, and notice how little it costs.
studies.explainEasier: Ask them to bring people who will swear that God banned this. If they do swear, do not swear along with them. Do not follow people who turn away from God's signs.

studies.title: Come, I Will Recite It
studies.meaning: A public invitation opens the list. The phrasing is careful. What follows is what your Lord has forbidden, recited rather than argued. The items are mostly prohibitions, with one positive command about parents. That command sits inside the series rather than beside it. Killing children out of poverty is answered mid-sentence with a statement about provision. Early scholars note that indecency is named in both its open and its hidden forms.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, from the end of a surah that has spent its length disputing with people over what they had declared off limits on their own authority. The verses just before challenge those self-made bans. This passage answers by reciting what was actually laid down. Early scholars treat the sequence as deliberate. A false list is set aside and a true one is read out in its place.

keyTerms.note: An imperative meaning to come towards a higher place, used to call someone over. It opens the passage as an invitation rather than a summons, and it is addressed to opponents in the middle of a dispute.
Not general hardship but the condition of having nothing left at all. The word names the actual pressure behind the practice being addressed, which the verse answers by naming who provides.
The plural of a word for what is excessive and shameful. The verse divides it into what appears and what is hidden, so the category is defined by the act rather than by whether anyone saw it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Burying an infant in a famine is attested in the poetry and the reports of Arabia before Islam. It was driven by the sums of a bad season. In a household with no reserve, there were mouths that could not be fed. The Quran addresses the practice more than once. Each time it attaches a statement about provision to the ban. That answers the calculation, not only the act.
studies.didYouKnow: This passage and the two verses after it have been read since early times as a parallel to the commandments given to Moses. Classical scholars note the resemblance directly. The list here begins where those do, with associating nothing with God and honouring parents. It closes with a call to understand rather than with a threat.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The list is introduced as recitation. That puts its authority outside the speaker. That is the whole point of the surah's argument. There is a difference between what God has laid down and what a community has decided among itself. Placing kindness to parents inside a series of bans has been read a certain way. It shows that some duties cannot be met by holding back alone. The stated purpose at the end is understanding.

crossReferences.why: Repeats the prohibition on killing children from fear of poverty, reversing the order of provision.
Continues the same recitation through weights, speech, and the straight path.
Lists what has actually been forbidden, open indecency and hidden alike.

studies.applyIt: The verse divides wrongdoing into what shows and what does not. Pick the quietest item on your own list, the thing nobody would ever hear about, and do one concrete thing this week that makes continuing it harder. Not a resolution, an arrangement. The hidden half is the half that survives on being unmentioned.
studies.explainEasier: God tells the Prophet to read out what God has really forbidden. The list says not to set anything beside God, to be good to your parents, and not to kill your children out of poverty. God feeds you all.

studies.title: Even If It Concerns A Relative
studies.meaning: Four things are set out together, and the arrangement is deliberate. Property held for a child who cannot yet defend it. Weights and measures at the market. Speech given about someone. And the covenant with God. Early scholars note the clause inserted in the middle, that no soul is charged beyond what it can bear, which softens the standard for measuring without lowering it. The hardest item is the third, since fairness in speech is asked even where a close relative is involved.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and part of a short sequence that reads like a summary of what was actually enjoined. It is set against the customs the surah has just dismantled. Orphans were numerous in a society where men died young in raids and on journeys. Their property passed into the keeping of relatives with no outside oversight. Measures at the seasonal fairs were similarly unpoliced.

keyTerms.note: From the root for firmness and strength, naming the age at which a person can manage their own affairs. Commentators differ over the exact point, and the tradition records a range of readings.
A word for a share correctly apportioned, distinct from the general term for justice. Its root sense is dividing something into due portions, which suits an instruction about weights and measures.
From the root for balance and equality, the same one used at the surah's opening for setting up equals to God. Applied to speech it asks for an account that does not lean.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Weights and measures were personal property. A merchant carried his own stones and his own measuring vessel. A small difference between the set used for buying and the set used for selling was invisible and profitable. Orphans' estates were held on the same trust basis, with no register anywhere. Both arrangements ran entirely on the character of the person holding them.
studies.didYouKnow: The clause about no soul being burdened beyond what it can bear appears three times in the Quran. Here it sits in the middle of an instruction about measuring. Its placement is unusual. The classical scholars read it as acknowledging that perfect exactness in a weighing is not achievable, while intention is.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Each item names a situation where nobody would find out. A child cannot audit an estate. A customer cannot check a stone. An account given about a relative is not checked against anything. Placing the covenant with God at the end of that list is the passage's argument. What holds in unwitnessed situations is a relationship rather than a rule, which is why the four belong in one sentence.

crossReferences.why: Repeats the same pair almost word for word, orphan property and full measure with a straight balance.
Describes the exact fraud named here, taking full measure from others and giving less in return.
Extends fairness in testimony to cases against oneself, parents and near relatives alike.

studies.applyIt: Think of the last time you described a disagreement involving someone close to you. Tell it again, to yourself, with the other side's version given the same room. That is the third item on this list. It is the one most of us fail without noticing, because nobody is ever there to check the account.
studies.explainEasier: Do not touch what belongs to an orphan, except to help, until he grows up. Give full weight and full measure. Be fair when you speak, even about your own family. Keep your promise to God.

studies.title: One Path And Many Ways
studies.meaning: A contrast is drawn in the grammar itself. The path is singular and described as straight. The alternatives are plural and unnamed. Following them is said to scatter you from His way. Early scholars note the verb, which describes a group being pulled apart rather than an individual losing direction. Nothing is said about where the other ways lead. What is named is only the effect of taking them, which is breaking apart. The purpose given at the end is mindfulness.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, closing the short sequence of what was actually enjoined. The surah has spent its final section describing customs that gathered in different directions. So a warning about many ways answers something concrete rather than abstract. The classical scholars record a report about the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him). He drew a single line, with lines branching from it, to illustrate this ayah.

keyTerms.note: The plural of a word for a track or route, set against the singular term used for the path. Arabic marks the contrast by number alone, which the translation has to do with an adjective.
An intensive verb for a group breaking into separate pieces. The object is the people rather than the road, so what the other routes do first is divide those walking, not mislead them.
The same verb that closes the two ayat before this one, marking the end of each instruction. Its repetition binds the short sequence together as a single charge rather than three separate ones.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A caravan held together by staying on one route. Where tracks branched, a party that split at a fork could lose contact for days or for good. There was no way to signal across distance. Guides argued about routes, and the arguments mattered. Everyone travelling in that country understood that the danger of a fork was separation before it was ever the wrong destination.
studies.didYouKnow: The classical collections preserve a report describing the Prophet drawing a straight line in the sand. He then drew short lines branching off it. He said the first was the way, and pointed at the others as paths with something calling from each. The image is remembered chiefly because it explains this ayah.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Unity is presented as an effect of direction rather than as a separate duty. That is a distinctive claim. People are not asked to hold together and also to follow the path. Following the path is what keeps them together. Leaving it is described first by what it does to the group. The purpose stated at the end is mindfulness rather than correctness. That keeps the instruction from becoming a matter of position alone.

crossReferences.why: Names the same single way given across the prophets, and warns against becoming divided in it.
Uses the same structure: a way ordained to be followed, against the inclinations of those without knowledge.
Turns the same straight path into the request recited in every unit of the daily prayer.

studies.applyIt: Notice a disagreement in your community that is about method rather than anything essential. Ask what it would take for the two sides to keep walking together while still disagreeing. This ayah's first warning is about scattering. The cost of a branch is usually paid in company. It is paid in direction only later.
studies.explainEasier: This is My path, and it is straight, so follow it. Do not follow the other roads. They will pull you away from His path. God tells you this so you will stay careful.

studies.title: Complete For The One Who Did Well
studies.meaning: Four things are said about the Book given to Moses, and the first is the least expected. It was a completion for the one who did well. Early scholars read this in more than one way. It may mean completing what such a person had already been given, or a favour completed upon them, and the tradition holds both. The other three are detail, guidance and mercy. The purpose stated at the end is belief in meeting their Lord. That is the same thing this surah has been arguing for throughout.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and the mention of Moses at this point serves the surah's argument. The audience accepted that an earlier Book existed and was known in the region. The passage that follows uses that acceptance to remove an excuse. The classical sources do not attach this ayah to an occasion. The Arabic word that opens it has been read by scholars as marking sequence in the telling rather than in time.

keyTerms.note: A verbal noun for bringing something to its full state. Read either as completing a favour or as completing what was already held, and the classical commentaries record both without deciding.
From the root for beauty and excellence, so the verb means doing something well rather than merely doing it. The same root gave this surah its word for the prophets in the earlier list.

keyTerms.gloss: and a setting out in detail
keyTerms.note: The noun from the verb used repeatedly in this surah for separating something into its parts. Applied to a scripture it describes a text laid out so that its pieces can be distinguished.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Communities holding the earlier scripture lived along the trade roads north and in the towns of Arabia. Meccan merchants dealt with them regularly. That a Book had been given to Moses was common knowledge in the region. It was not a claim needing support. The fact was uncontested, and that is precisely why the argument built on it in the following ayat works.
studies.didYouKnow: This ayah and the one after it use nearly the same words for two different scriptures. Each is described as sent down. Each is described as carrying guidance and mercy. Placing the two descriptions in ayat next to each other is the surah's way of showing they belong together, without arguing for it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Revelation is presented as completing something rather than replacing it. The completion is aimed at a person who was already doing well. That order matters. The Book meets existing goodness and finishes it rather than creating it from nothing. The stated purpose is belief in meeting their Lord. That ties a whole scripture to the single conviction the surah has been defending since its opening pages.

crossReferences.why: Names the same giving, the Scripture and the criterion, so that they might be guided.
Refers to the same Book and makes it a reason not to doubt the meeting being described.
Describes it as guidance and a reminder inherited by those who came after him.

studies.applyIt: Think of a good practice you already have that could be finished rather than replaced. A habit of generosity without regularity. Or a reading habit without direction. This ayah describes a completion given to someone already doing well. Add the missing piece to one such practice this week, rather than starting something new.
studies.explainEasier: Then We gave Moses the Book. It was a full gift for the one who did good, and it explained everything. It was a light and a mercy, so that people would believe they will meet their Lord.

studies.title: Lest You Should Say
studies.meaning: A purpose is given for this Book that is stated negatively, and it is unusual. It came so that one particular sentence could no longer be spoken. That sentence is this. Scripture was given to two communities before us, and we knew nothing of what they studied. Early scholars identify the two as those holding the earlier scriptures. The excuse being removed is not disbelief but distance. It is the reasonable complaint of people who had heard that revelation existed elsewhere. They had never received any in their own language.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and the complaint was genuine. Arabs knew that scriptural communities existed nearby. They knew those scriptures were studied in languages they did not read. Some in the region had begun searching for something equivalent before the message came. The passage addresses a real grievance rather than an imagined one, which is why it is answered by removal rather than by rebuke.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to kneel and settle, giving the idea of good that comes to rest in a place. The same description was applied to this Book earlier in the surah, in a passage about warning a city.
A dual form for two distinct parties, from a root meaning to go around something. The dual is precise: the complaint named two known communities rather than scripture-holders in general.
From the root for reading a text repeatedly until it is learned, the same verb used earlier in this surah in the accusation that he had studied. The word names sustained schooling in a text.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Scripture was studied aloud in languages Arabs did not know. A Meccan trader in a northern town would see a community gathered around a reader. The reader worked through a text the trader could not follow. He would understand that something of weight was being handled there, and was not available to him. That experience, repeated over generations, is the exact complaint these ayat quote.
studies.didYouKnow: The word used here for study comes from the same root as the verb in an accusation a few pages earlier. That accusation was that the Prophet had been taught by someone. So the same term appears twice in this surah. Once it is a charge against him. Once it is in the excuse his people would have made without him.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Revelation is described as closing an excuse. That places the whole subject inside fairness rather than favour. Nobody is to answer for what was only ever available in a language and a community not their own. That is a claim about how God deals with people generally. And it implies something further. Wherever a genuine excuse of ignorance exists, it is treated as genuine.

crossReferences.why: Describes this same Book in nearly identical words earlier in the surah, with a different purpose attached.
Names the earlier scriptures given before, which the two communities in this complaint held.
Voices the same excuse from the other end, asking why no messenger was sent before the consequence.

studies.applyIt: Notice an excuse you use that is actually true: not enough time, never taught, nobody showed you. Some of them are fair. Pick one and ask what would have to change for it to stop being available. These ayat take a real excuse seriously and then remove it. That is a different thing from dismissing it.
studies.explainEasier: This Book is a blessed one that We sent down, so follow it. Then you cannot say that a Book was given to two groups before you. You cannot say you never knew what they were reading.

studies.title: We Would Have Been Better Guided
studies.meaning: The second excuse is confidence rather than ignorance. Had a Book come to us, we would have made better use of it than they did. Early scholars note the tone. It assumes that the earlier communities failed through some fault the speakers do not share. The answer arrives without argument. Clarification has now come, and guidance, and mercy. So the claim can be tested rather than asserted. The rest of the ayah names what turning away from it amounts to.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and the sentiment is recorded elsewhere in the Quran as an oath sworn before the message came. They swore that if a warner reached them they would be more guided than any nation. The surah quotes the claim after the message has arrived, which changes its status entirely. It is no longer a boast about a possibility. It is a description of what did not happen.

keyTerms.note: A comparative from the root for finding a way. Comparing one's own hypothetical performance to another community's actual record is the exact form the ayah is quoting, and the comparative carries it.

Something that makes a matter plain, the same word used earlier in this surah when the speaker says he stands on clear evidence from his Lord. Its return here places the same thing in the listeners' hands.

A less common verb for veering away, used earlier in this surah of people shying from the signs. It is repeated three times in this one ayah, which is unusual and makes turning away the sentence's subject.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabs took great pride in their memory and their language. They treated the retention of poetry and family lines as evidence of a superior faculty. A community could hold thousands of lines of verse without writing. It had reason to think it would handle a text well. The boast quoted here was not empty vanity. It rested on a real and provable skill.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb for turning aside occurs three times in this single ayah, in three grammatical forms. It appears in the Quran only in this surah. The concentration is deliberate. The last clause states that the recompense matches the turning away, using the same word for both.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage answers a claim about imagined performance by supplying the actual test. Anyone can be confident about what they would do in a situation they are not in. The ayah quietly points out that the situation has now arrived. The repetition of one verb at the end makes a point about matching. What is returned to a person matches what they did. The same word is used for both.

crossReferences.why: Records the same boast as a solemn oath, sworn before any warner had reached them.
States the same test earlier in this surah, that insights have come and the seeing is each person's own.
Names the excuse this removes, that they would have asked why no messenger was sent to them.

studies.applyIt: Think of something you are confident you would handle better than the person currently handling it. Now recall a time you were given exactly such a chance and did about as well as anybody. Hold the two together for a minute. This ayah's answer to an imagined case is simply to point at the real one.
studies.explainEasier: Or you might say that if a Book had come to you, you would have followed it better than they did. But clear proof has now come to you. It came from your Lord, with guidance and mercy.

studies.title: Faith That Comes Too Late
studies.meaning: Three arrivals are named as things they might be waiting for. Then one of them is followed through. On the day some of your Lord's signs come, faith will not benefit a soul that had not believed before, or earned some good through its believing. Early scholars discuss which sign is meant and record several readings. What the ayah sets out is a closing point. After it, belief is no longer a response to anything but a reaction to what is now visible.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, near the surah's close, and the demand for a decisive sign has run through the whole of it. The audience had asked for angels and for God Himself to appear. This ayah takes the request seriously enough to describe what would follow if it were granted. The classical scholars connect it to a wider Quranic account of belief offered at the last moment.

keyTerms.note: The verb for looking and for waiting, used earlier in this surah for the respite granted to people. Waiting and being given time are the same word, which gives the question its edge.

The commercial verb used at the opening of this surah for what God knows of a person. Its appearance here adds a second condition, so belief alone without anything earned through it is not the picture described.
An imperative from the same root as the verb for waiting at the ayah's start. The instruction returns their own posture to them, and the speaker joins it rather than standing outside it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Debt in Arabia ran to a named term. A creditor could extend it, but at the moment the term expired the arrangement changed entirely. What had been a bargain became a claim. Everyone understood that a payment offered the day before and the day after were different acts. Goodwill did not survive the boundary. The words for waiting and respite come from that world.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran describes belief arriving too late more than once. One case is the drowning of a tyrant who declares his faith as the water closes. Each account uses the same structure. The words are correct, the timing is not, and the passage says plainly that the words no longer do anything.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage sets a limit on repentance that is about knowledge rather than severity. Faith held while the outcome is uncertain is one act. Agreement given once the outcome is visible is another. Only the first is the thing being asked for. The second condition is equally striking. Belief is expected to have produced something, so the ayah measures a life rather than a moment of conviction.

crossReferences.why: States the same limit for repentance offered at the moment death arrives, when nothing is uncertain.
Narrates the clearest instance, a declaration of faith made as the sea closes over the speaker.
Describes faith declared on seeing the punishment, and says it did not benefit them then.

studies.applyIt: Think of a good decision you are putting off. You are waiting until circumstances make it obvious. A resignation, a reconciliation, a change in how you live. Notice that the value of deciding now is exactly that it is not yet obvious. This ayah is about the difference between choosing and giving in. The window for the first closes quietly.
studies.explainEasier: Are they just waiting for angels to come, or for their Lord, or for some sign of His. On the day a sign like that comes, believing then will not help. It only helps those who believed before.

studies.title: You Have No Part In That
studies.meaning: Two things are described together, and the second follows from the first. They broke their religion into pieces, and they became parties. Early scholars note that the fracture is named before the factions. So the groups are the result rather than the cause. The instruction is a complete separation from the activity, not from the people. The reason given is about who has the case. Their matter rests with God, who will inform them of what they were doing. That is a statement about who does the sorting.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, near the surah's end, and the classical scholars differ over who is described. Some read it of earlier communities whose unity had broken up. Others read it as a general statement covering anyone who does this. The tradition preserves the range. The surah has already warned against following many ways instead of one, and this ayah names the outcome of having done so.

keyTerms.note: An intensive verb for separating something into fragments. The object is their religion, so what is described is damage to a single thing rather than a disagreement between people about it.

The same word used earlier in this surah, where being split into factions is listed among afflictions God is able to send. Its return here makes the condition a consequence rather than only a punishment.
A word covering a matter, a command and a decision at once. Assigning it to God removes the case from human hands entirely, which is the ground of the instruction that precedes it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabian society was organised into groups that competed for standing. A man's identity came from which one claimed him. Splits within a tribe were common. They produced long rivalries over precedence and inheritance. Everyone knew what it looked like when one body became several. They knew how quickly the line between them became the most important fact about anyone.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for factions in this ayah appears earlier in the same surah. There it sits in the list of what God is able to send upon a people. It stands alongside afflictions from above and below. So the same term names a punishment in one passage and a self-inflicted condition in the other. The vocabulary does not change.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage separates the activity from the people doing it. That separation is what makes the instruction liveable. Judgement is placed with God, plainly, so what is asked of the reader is only not to join in. That is a narrower demand than it first sounds. It leaves relationships intact. It removes the duty to judge between groups. And it names the breaking apart itself as the thing to keep clear of.

crossReferences.why: Warns against becoming like those who divided and differed after clear proofs had reached them.
Describes the same outcome, an affair cut into pieces with each party pleased by its own portion.
Gives the instruction this ayah's condition follows from, one path rather than many scattering ways.

studies.applyIt: Notice a dispute within your own community that you have been drawn into by loyalty rather than conviction. Step out of the argument for a month without stepping away from anybody in it. This ayah puts the judging elsewhere. It asks only that you not join the fracturing, which is something you can do quietly.
studies.explainEasier: Some people broke their religion into pieces and split into groups. You have nothing to do with that. Their case is with God, and He will tell them later what they were doing.

studies.title: Ten For One
studies.meaning: The rate of exchange is stated plainly, and it is not equal. A good deed brought is answered tenfold. A bad one is answered with its like and no more. Early scholars attend to the wording of both halves. The good is multiplied, and elsewhere in the Quran the ceiling is left open. The bad is capped by a word for equal measure. The closing clause explains why the imbalance is not unfair. Nobody receives less than they earned.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, near the end of a surah largely taken up with argument and warning. Its final verses turn from dispute to a statement of terms, and this is one of them. Early scholars record no occasion for it. They read the placement as deliberate. After a long quarrel about what people had invented, the surah closes by setting out plainly how the account is actually kept.

keyTerms.note: The verb for arriving carrying something, rather than for doing it. It pictures the deed as an item brought to a counter, which is why the response is described as a rate rather than as a verdict.

The multiplier is stated as ten likenesses of the thing itself, not ten of something else. What is returned keeps the shape of what was given, magnified rather than exchanged for a different currency.

The passive of the verb for putting something out of its place. Its use here defines fairness as receiving no less than what is due, which leaves the extra given to a good deed outside the calculation.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Meccan trade ran on rates of exchange, and everyone there understood a multiplier. A merchant financed a caravan expecting several times his outlay back. Profit was reckoned in shares agreed before departure. Putting the moral account in that language used terms the audience handled daily. The tenfold figure would have been heard as a rate of return, not as a picture.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran elsewhere raises the multiplier well beyond ten. One passage compares a good deed to a grain that produces seven ears, with a hundred grains in each. It adds that God multiplies further for whom He wills. So the figure of ten here is the floor of what is promised, not its limit. Early scholars read the two together.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The imbalance is the teaching. If mercy is written into the accounting itself, hope is not a mood a person has to work up. It is a fact about the ledger. Capping the penalty at equal measure keeps justice intact, so the generosity costs nothing in fairness. Between them the two halves describe a system tilted one way on purpose. The tilt is stated as policy, not as a favour.

crossReferences.why: Raises the same multiplication far higher with the image of a grain and seven ears.
States that God does not wrong by an atom's weight and doubles a good deed.
Repeats the same asymmetry in a Meccan surah, with better than the deed for the good.

studies.applyIt: Do one small good thing today that you would normally skip because it seems too minor to count: a message of thanks, a plate washed that is not yours. The whole argument of this verse is about scale, and it says the scale is not yours to judge. Your part is only the bringing.
studies.explainEasier: If you do one good thing, God gives you ten times as much back. If you do one bad thing, it counts as one, and no more. Nobody is treated unfairly.

studies.title: The Creed Of Abraham
studies.meaning: The declaration is personal, and it builds. My Lord has guided me. Then four descriptions stack up: a straight path, an upright religion, the creed of Abraham, inclining toward truth. Early scholars note the word describing that inclination. It names a turning away from everything else and a turning toward one thing at the same time. The final clause is the sharpest. Abraham is the ancestor the audience claimed, and the ayah states plainly that he was not among those who set up partners.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and the appeal to Abraham was an appeal to the audience's own family tree. The families of Mecca traced descent from him and held custody of a sanctuary they linked with him. Their religious practice was defended as inherited from that source. Naming his creed and then denying that it included setting up partners cut directly across that claim.

keyTerms.note: From the root for standing, so a religion described this way is one that stands straight and holds others up. The same root gives the verb used elsewhere for establishing the prayer.
A word for the path a community follows, distinct from the general term for religion. It carries a founder's name naturally, which is why the Quran uses it whenever Abraham is being invoked.

From a root meaning to turn away from something and toward another. Pre-Islamic Arabia knew individuals described by this word who had abandoned the local practices without joining any other community.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The sources record a small number of men in Mecca and its region before the message who had rejected the local rites. They went looking for the religion of Abraham, and some travelled as far as Syria in the search. They were known, and regarded as odd rather than dangerous. The word used in this ayah for inclining was the term applied to them.
studies.didYouKnow: The word describing Abraham here appears about a dozen times in the Quran. In almost every case it is followed at once by a denial. He associated nothing with God. The pairing is so consistent that the classical scholars treat the second clause as part of the term's working definition.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The declaration answers a claim of inheritance with a claim about content. Descent from Abraham is not disputed. What is disputed is whether the practice being defended is his. That move separates a tradition from the person it is credited to. It can be made about any inherited religion. The list also puts guidance first, as something received, before any of the descriptions that follow.

crossReferences.why: Answers a competing claim with the same phrase, the creed of Abraham, inclining toward truth.
Issues the same instruction to follow that creed, closing with the identical denial about partners.
Describes him as a community in himself, thankful and chosen, and guided to a straight path.

studies.applyIt: Take one practice you keep because it belongs to your tradition, and check it against the person or period the tradition claims. Not to reject it if it does not match. Just to know which parts you can trace and which arrived later. This ayah makes exactly that distinction about a lineage everyone in the room shared.
studies.explainEasier: My Lord has shown me a straight path. It is a true and upright religion, the way of Abraham, who turned to God alone. He never worshipped anything beside God.

studies.title: My Living And My Dying
studies.meaning: Four things are named and handed over in a single clause: prayer, offering, life and death. The first two are acts of worship. The second two are not acts at all, which is what makes the list unusual. Early scholars read it as extending devotion past what a person does, into what merely happens to them. The declaration then closes with a claim about being first. They explain that as first among this community rather than in history.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. It is the closing declaration of a surah that has argued at length with people who dedicated animals and crops to various powers. The instruction to say this is therefore pointed. The practices disputed throughout the surah are exactly the ones being reassigned here. Early scholars read these verses as the surah's summing up, delivered in the first person rather than as one more argument.

keyTerms.note: A word for the animal offered and for acts of devotion generally. Its root also carries washing and purity, so the term joins a physical offering to the idea of being made clean.
A noun for the whole of a life rather than for the act of living. Paired with its counterpart it covers the span a person does not control, placing that under the same dedication as their prayer.

Early scholars explain first as foremost within this community rather than earliest in time, since the Quran describes earlier prophets in the same terms. It marks priority of commitment, not chronology.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Animals were dedicated by name in Arabia before Islam. A camel might be marked for a particular god. Its ear was slit and its milk kept back. A slaughter was announced with the name of the power it was offered to. Everyone present heard whose it was. In that setting, declaring who an offering was for was a public act of allegiance, not a private intention.
studies.didYouKnow: These two verses are among the passages many Muslims recite inside the prayer itself. They come in the opening supplication reported in the classical collections. So a statement that begins with the word prayer ends up being spoken during one. Early scholars note that circle when they discuss where the passage came to be used.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Sincerity is defined by range rather than by strength of feeling. The list moves from what a person does to what simply happens. So what is offered includes the parts of a life nobody chooses and nobody can perform. That makes the declaration impossible to complete by effort. That is the point of it. It is a statement of ownership, not a report of achievement. The denial of any partner then restates the same sentence.

crossReferences.why: Describes sincere devotion as the whole of what was ever commanded.
Uses the same language of turning one's face over to God while doing good.
States that the flesh of offerings does not reach God, only the awareness behind them.

studies.applyIt: Before something ordinary today, say quietly who it is for. A meal, a commute, opening your laptop. Not a long formula. These verses put living and dying in the same list as prayer. So the offering is meant to cover the plain hours. Those are the ones nobody thinks to dedicate.
studies.explainEasier: God tells the Prophet to say that his prayer, his worship, his life and his death all belong to God alone. God has no partner. That is what he has been told to say.

studies.title: Shall I Seek Another Lord
studies.meaning: The question echoes one asked near the surah's beginning, and it answers the same way. He is the Lord of everything, so there is nothing left over to be lord of anything. Then come two clauses about answering for what you do. The second has become one of the most quoted lines in the Quran. No soul earns except against itself, and no bearer of burdens carries another's. Early scholars read the pair together. The first makes the account personal and the second makes it non-transferable.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and the classical sources record something specific. Opponents in the city made an offer. They would carry the consequences of the believers' conduct if the believers returned to the old religion. The Quran answers such offers elsewhere in similar terms. Whether or not this ayah responds to one case, the arrangement it rules out was a live proposal. It belonged to a society where a clan absorbed its members' debts.

keyTerms.note: The verb for seeking something out, from a root that also produces the word for overstepping. Seeking beyond what is there and going past a limit share the same letters in Arabic.
From the root for a heavy pack, which this surah used earlier for burdens carried on the back. The verb and its object share the root, so the Arabic says a bearer does not bear a bearing.
From a root for coming after or succeeding one another, so disagreement is pictured as positions taken in turn. What is promised at the end is information about the difference, not a rebuke for it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Answering for a wrong in Arabia was shared by design. A clan paid the compensation for a killing by one of its members. It collected for injuries to any of them. This pooling was the whole security of life without a state. A man really could take on another's debt. So the offer to carry someone's consequences was an ordinary deal, not a flourish.
studies.didYouKnow: The statement that no bearer carries another's burden appears five times in the Quran. It is in five different surahs, always in nearly the same words. Few sentences are repeated that consistently. The classical commentaries treat the repetition as setting out a principle. It does not answer any single occasion.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Two ideas that pull in opposite directions are held in one ayah. God is Lord of everything, which is the largest possible claim. Each soul carries only its own load. That is the smallest possible unit. The combination rules out a universe with several authorities. It also rules out a community that can absorb one person's account. What is left is a direct relationship, with nothing and nobody standing in the middle of it.

crossReferences.why: Repeats the same principle and adds that a heavily laden soul finds nobody to carry any of it.
States it as one of the contents of the earlier scriptures, at the head of a short list.
Records the offer to carry another's faults and says the offer will not be honoured.

studies.applyIt: Think of a responsibility you have quietly handed to someone else. A decision you let a parent make, or a moral question you handed to an institution. Take one of them back this week and decide it yourself. This ayah says the load is not transferable. So the decision was never actually theirs to hold.
studies.explainEasier: Should I look for a lord other than God, when He is the Lord of everything. Nobody earns anything except against himself. No one carries another person's load. In the end you all go back to your Lord.

studies.title: Successors Upon The Earth
studies.meaning: The surah closes by naming what people are. They come after others, placed on the earth in turn. Some are raised above others in degrees. The reason given for the difference is a test. The test lies in what you were given, not in what you were denied. Early scholars note that the unevenness itself is called the trial. Two names then close the ayah. One is swift consequence. The other is forgiveness and mercy. The ending stays open at both ends.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. This is the last ayah of a surah that has argued for a hundred and sixty-five ayat. Its subject throughout is who God is, and what may be said in His name. The listeners held rank in a city built on rank. The surah's last word to them calls their arrangement a test, not a verdict. It does not abolish the ranks. It does not approve them either.

keyTerms.note: The plural of one who comes after another, from the root for succession. The word names people by their position in a sequence rather than by any authority, so it describes a turn rather than a title.
Steps of a stair, the third appearance of this word in the surah. It has already been used for a prophet's raising and for the grading of outcomes, and here it names ordinary social difference.
From a root meaning to wear something out by use, as a garment is tested by being worn. A trial in this vocabulary reveals what a thing is made of rather than punishing it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Mecca ran on degrees you could see. Some families held the offices of the sanctuary. Some paid for caravans, some worked them, and some were owned. Nobody there imagined it could be otherwise. The differences showed every day: where you sat, how you spoke, who greeted whom first. To call that whole structure a set of exam conditions was to say something no one in the city had heard.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for degrees turns up three times in this surah. First it is used of a prophet being raised. Then it is used for the grading of every person by what they did. Here it names plain social rank. One word covers being raised by God, the outcome of a life, and a place in the world.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Unevenness is not defended here, and it is not swept away. It is given a purpose instead, which is a harder and more useful position than either one. Whoever holds more is holding a test, not a prize. Whoever holds less sits the same exam with a different paper. The two closing names leave the ending unsettled on purpose. A surah about answering for what you do ends with forgiveness as its last word.

crossReferences.why: Names the same role at the beginning of the human story, one placed on the earth in succession.
States the same purpose for life and death, a test of which of you is better in conduct.
Gives a reason for the raising in degrees, so that people may make use of one another.

studies.applyIt: Take one advantage you hold that you did not earn: where you were born, an education, a body that works. Name it as an examination question rather than a possession, and ask what it is asking of you. This is the surah's last word, and it turns a fact about your life into something addressed to you.
studies.explainEasier: God put people on the earth to take their turn. He gave some more than others, and that is part of the test. What you do with what you were given is the thing being tested.
